  and caught the survivor my script missed (roadmap's Gap R.90 cell, "the one table both backends read their
  messages from").

## Registering a conformance program is a promise to three harnesses, not one (ADR 0309's own miss)

- **A new asserted program owes the record, the matrix and the GC corpus at once.** ADR 0309's probe was
  registered in `conformanceStandalone()` and the matrix row went green (`oracle: match`), so the cycle called
  itself verified — but `TestGCCorpusCollectsAndAgrees` walks the *asserted* cases and fails any whose source
  has no entry in `testdata/interpreter-golden.json` (ADR 0302 made a missing record a failure, not a skip).
  The commit shipped with that failure in the same package, because the verification command run was
  `-run TestConformanceMatrix` and not `go test ./integration/`. The lesson is about the *shape* of the check:
  a targeted `-run` on a package whose cases are inter-dependent through shared artifacts (the record, the
  matrix, the two ledgers) proves less than it looks like it proves — a new registered artifact must be
  followed through every harness that reads the artifact family, and the package-level run is the cheap way to
  do that.
- **`meta.added_after_0302` is the honesty clause of a post-retirement record.** A source that was never alive
  while the engine ran cannot have an answer "from the interpreter". It gets recorded from the reference, and
  what keeps that from being self-certifying is that the matrix row compares the compiled leg to CPython
  independently and the drift ledger fails on any new disagreement — so the entry is witness to two
  comparisons rather than one. The `meta` block now says so, because the alternative is an agent reading the
  record as an oracle that no longer exists.
- **Editing a machine-readable artifact's prose is an interface change.** While filling that entry the record's
  own `meta.fields` still described its columns as `Evaluator.Repr of the snippet's final value` and
  `Evaluator.TypeOf` — API that ADR 0302 deleted. An agent that reads a schema pointing at a deleted type is
  not guided, it is misdirected; the descriptions now say what the record *holds*, and the two historical
  fields (`meta.source`, `meta.record_corrections`) keep their pre-retirement wording, because they report what
  was done, not what is true.

## ADR 0310 — a pair-bound name enters a dict entry and a set member (Gap R.146, L11.1, L12.11)

- **The asymmetry picked the cycle, not the row's own example.** `Gap R.146` has always been illustrated with
  `abs(n)` / `min(n, 3)` / `[n]`, and by the time this cycle started the first and third were paid (ADR 0309,
  ADR 0306) while the container entries still refused: `print([n])` answered `7` and `print({"k": n})` spent
  exit 1 on the same name. That difference was the row, and it was measurable in one line each — which is why
  the cycle began by measuring 60 sources against CPython before any code changed, rather than by reading the
  tracker's prose about them.
- **The fix was the one ADR 0306 already made, asked of the two builders that had the door open.** A dict and a
  set each have exactly one call that takes the tag with the payload — `rt_dict_put_tagged(i32 h, i32 k, i32 v,
  i32 kt, i32 vt)` and `rt_set_add_tagged(i32 h, i32 v, i32 t)` — and both were being fed by `heapElemKind` +
  `elemKindTag`/`dictKeyTag`, which label an element from its **spelling**. A name has no spelling that
  describes what the objects hold. Since a register is an `i32`, the pair's tag could be handed straight to
  those calls, and **`pkg/lang/runtime.go` has no diff in this commit** — which is the check that tells a later
  cycle whether the invariant still holds: if a future "fix" grows a pair-aware dict helper, the invariant has
  been duplicated somewhere rather than kept.
- **Pay the binding in the same commit as the literal, or the table lies.** `print({"k": n})` and
  `d2 = {"k": n}; print(d2["k"])` are the same entry question asked by two roads — the expression road and the
  assignment road, the second of which keeps its own record of a variable's key and value kinds *beside* its own
  tag slots. Paying only the literal leaves `d2["k"]`, `len(d2)`, `k in d2`, `for k in d2`, `str(d2)` and
  `d2 == {"k": "a"}` refusing next to an answering `print({"k": n})`, and a half-paid table is worse than an
  unpaid one because the passing row advertises the family as done. Both were done, and the binding rows are in
  the same tables.
- **A key and a member have a question an element never gets, and a payload cannot answer it.** A dict key and
  a set member must be hashable; CPython raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` / `'dict'` / `'set'`. A
  payload answers "hashable" for every value in the language — a list's handle is an i32 like any other — so the
  tempting implementation would have built a set holding an address and printed `{[1, 2]}` at the exit code of
  success, the one class the suite's refusal counter is blind to. The guard is therefore three compares against
  the tag and three raises spelling CPython's own sentences, emitted in the program and catchable by
  `except TypeError:` — and it is emitted **only** where a pair writes a key or a member, with an IR test that
  fails if a literal whose kinds are all constants starts paying for a question the compiler already answered.
  `Gap R.81` still owns the general hashing rule; the row says so rather than inheriting the credit.
- **A lying arm is a bug with no caller.** `heapElemKind` labelled a **set** element as a `list` and returned a
  dict's entry count tagged as an `int` — the branch that reads an entry count is not the branch that labels an
  element, and a set has no entry count. Both were unreachable, and both stayed unreachable only because the
  taggable-literal gate rejected anything containing a set or dict element first. A dict entry is precisely the
  caller that would have started using them, so they became `unreachable` assertions in this commit with the lie
  written in the message where the next reader will find it (the same shape as ADR 0303's `str_of_int`, which sat
  in the module printing `0` forever because nothing had found it yet).
- **Widen a gate as far as the proof reaches and no further.** The first version of the dict/set gate admitted a
  literal containing an unclassifiable set/dict element because the pair sibling "looked safe", and the sweep
  caught `print({"a": s, 2.5: 1})` regressing from an honest refusal to an answered wrong shape. The gate is now
  a conjunction — the literal holds a pair **and** every other entry is still something the static tag road can
  label — so the mixed case keeps its old answer and the pair case gets the new one.
- **Registering a conformance program is a promise to three harnesses, and this time all three were paid in one
  pass**: the registry entry in `integration/conformance_cases.go`, the record entry in
  `testdata/interpreter-golden.json` (ADR 0302 made a missing entry a failure, not a skip), and the committed
  artifact `conformance-matrix.json` (regenerated, 170 → 171 rows), plus the loud version of the missing-record
  rule (`TestThePairBoundDictAndSetProbeIsOnRecord`) so deleting the entry fails a test instead of skipping it.
  The corpus-gate test that fails on an unregistered program also runs before the probe is added, so a probe
  cannot be introduced into a corpus that is already inconsistent (ADR 0309's own miss, ADR 0308 amended).
- **A tracker row's own owed-list is a claim surface.** `Gap R.146`'s cell, `L11.1`'s cell and `L12.11`'s
  owed-list sentence all named "a dict entry and a set member" as what they still owed. Paid rows have to leave
  those cells in the same commit that pays them — the lesson ADR 0309 learned from a probe program whose prose
  claimed three legs that no longer run — because the next cycle picks its work out of those cells.
- **A compacted summary is not a measurement.** Two doc lines this cycle went to edit did not exist on disk (a
  `docs/language.md` bullet about "statically taggable" and an `AGENTS.md` sentence about the pair arc), and one
  earlier script appeared to have written a CPython-output file that was never there — every one of them was
  plausible text carried in from a summary rather than read from the file. The rule for the rest of the loop:
  `grep`/`sed` the file **in the same turn** you edit it, re-measure any number you did not produce in this
  session (the record's 5642 → 5703 came out of a script that printed the count, not out of context), and when a
  command's output is load-bearing — the 60-case reference sweep, the golden-file merge — run it through a script
  that reports the bytes it read and the keys it changed.

## ADR 0311 — a pair-bound name is written into a container by a statement (Gap R.146's mutation roads)

- **The row's example list had gone stale, so the row lied.** `Gap R.146` still illustrated itself with
  `abs(n)`, `min(n, 3)` and `[n]` — all paid by ADR 0309, 0269 and 0306 — while the shapes that actually still
  refused were `xs.append(n)`, `s.add(n)`, `xs[i] = n`, `d[k] = n`. The next cycle picked the right work only
  because it measured 144 programs first (six slot kinds × 24 bodies) instead of reading the tracker's prose.
  When a row's examples are paid, its examples have to be restated in the same commit that pays them.
- **Measure before you choose, and keep the measurement as the table.** 144 programs → 15 agreeing (every one
  of those "agreements" was both sides failing). The same JSON that produced that number produced the answer
  tables in `pkg/lang/pair_mutation_test.go` and `integration/pair_mutation_test.go`, so the expectations in
  the tests and the numbers in the docs come from one run rather than from memory.
- **A pair arm on a road that already had a tagged door is not the hard part; knowing when NOT to take the arm
  is.** All four mutators already had `(payload, tag)` calls from ADR 0232, and `pkg/lang/runtime.go` again has
  no diff. The bug came from deleting `assignIndex`'s eager `g.value(b, val)` because it refused before the
  pair road got to answer: `xs[0] = xs[0] / 2` then printed `[2]` and `d["k"] = xs[0] / 2` printed `3.0` where
  CPython prints `[3.5]` / `{'k': 3.0}` — two honest Gap R.88 refusals quietly converted into wrong answers at
  exit 0. The eager question is back for every non-pair value; the pair arms take only pairs. The rule for the
  loop: **a row that stops refusing without answering has not been paid, it has been lost** — and the refusal
  table is as much a test as the answer table, which is why this cycle pins both.
- **Widening a shared helper is a much bigger change than it looks.** The tempting patch widened
  `mixedElemTag`/`taggedOperand` (which also serve the folds and the arithmetic roads) so that "everything"
  took pairs; the first attempt regressed `elemKindTag`'s guess for a division answer into a container slot and
  produced the wrong-answer above. Explicit pair arms at the four call sites, plus `promotePairMixed` doing
  `promoteMixed`'s bookkeeping without `promoteMixed`'s `elemKindTag` precondition, kept the blast radius in
  the mutation roads.
- **A record field the harness does not read is not an answer.** The 0310 probe's record entry had been written
  as `{"stdout": ...}` without `hasStdout: true`; `goldenStdoutIs` reads `rec.HasStd`, so that row was silently
  comparing nothing while looking recorded. Every entry this cycle added carries the canonical
  `{hasStdout, stdout}` shape, and the 137 missing flags were fixed in the same commit. When recording by hand
  rather than through the recorder, copy an existing entry's keys, not just its value.
- **Registering a conformance program is a promise to three harnesses** (registry entry, record entry with the
  canonical fields, committed `conformance-matrix.json`), and this cycle paid all three plus the loud
  missing-record test in one pass: 172 rows / 133 conformant, +138 records (5703 → 5841).
- **The remote can reject a push with a server-side 500 while fetch works.** ADR 0310's commit could not be
  pushed (`remote rejected … (Internal Server Error)` on both `main` and a topic branch, retried over several
  minutes). Keep working, keep the commit local, and keep retrying the push each cycle rather than treating a
  dead remote as a reason to stop the loop.

## A CI timeout was not the failure it reported (ADR 0312 budgets, ADR 0313 shards, ADR 0314 oracle pin)

A failing workflow arrived as one line: `panic: test timed out after 10m0s / running tests:
TestTextPredicatesPrintAVerdict/not_verdict_false`, with a goroutine parked in
`os/exec.(*Cmd).CombinedOutput` under `runIR`. The named case is `print(not "1".isdigit())`, which answers in
70 ms. **`go test`'s alarm names the test that was *running*, never the suite that was slow** — the whole
package needed 10m06s pinned to four CPUs (against `go test`'s 10m00s default) and CI's runner has four
cores, so the suite was two-thirds through when the
timer went off and the accused case was scenery. Reading the frame above the exec (`runIR`, and the call
count behind it) was the only way in; reading the test name would have produced a fix to a test that had no
bug. Measuring first was also cheap and decisive: `Compile` is 1 ms, `llc` 58 ms, `cc` 13 ms, `lli` 57 ms,
`python3` ~40 ms — so the suite is a subprocess suite, and `user 8m31s / real 10m06s` on four pinned cores
said the machine's
asking to be used.

- **An unbudgeted subprocess does not fail slowly, it stops being able to fail.** Eleven `exec.Command` sites
  had no deadline, so "hung" was not a possible outcome to report — it was only ever a stuck process. Now
  every tool is started by `pkg/lang/tool_budget.go`, and the two knobs an operator needs (`GUSTY_TOOL_TIMEOUT`,
  `GUSTY_ORACLE_TIMEOUT`) are read at call time so a test can move one. The user's program is deliberately
  excluded: `--file` waiting on the program it was asked to run is a correct wait, and `while True:` is a
  program, not a bug.
- **A tool that stops answering and a tool that says no are different events, and the exit code is where
  that distinction is readable.** A killed `llc` had been about to arrive as `compile error: jit: codegen: llc
  …` — exit 2, the code the contract reserves for "the module is bad", i.e. an accusation against the
  compiler for a loaded machine. `*lang.ToolTimeoutError` is its own class: exit 8, `--json`
  `phase: "toolchain"`, found by `errors.As`. `toolchainFailure` asks for a timeout *before* building a
  rejection, and the CLI checks timeouts before rejections, because the killed tool's own sentence names the
  stage that was running and string checks would blame that stage.
- **Two `os/exec` traps, both found by running the tests rather than by reading:** asking a channel whether
  a context expired loses a race with `Wait` (the CI's exact call came back as bare `context deadline
  exceeded`, no tool, no stage — read `ctx.Err()`), and `Cancel` is not called for a context already expired
  at `Start`, so the kill hook cannot be the timeout signal. Killing only `cc` leaves `as`/`ld` holding the
  pipe open and `Wait` blocks forever with the budget spent: setuid is not enough, **kill the process group**
  (`Setpgid` + `kill(-pid)`, `WaitDelay` as the backstop), and the same helper distinguishes *missing* from
  *stalled* — the advice for a missing `llc-20` is "install LLVM 20", never "raise the budget".
- **`t.Parallel()` was not available, for three reasons that are properties of the system:** `captureFD` dup2s
  the process's fd 1/2 around a loaded program (two programs in one process print into each other), 46 sites
  need process-wide state (`os.Chdir`, `t.Setenv`) and Go runs a parallel test *beside* the serial ones rather
  than after them, and the compiler's program-wide scan tables are plain maps. The process was already the
  unit of isolation, so it became the unit of parallelism: `tools/testshards` deals one package's cases across
  N `go test` processes. **10m06s → 3m30s on four pinned cores**, with the CPU total flat across the two
  (8m31s → 9m00s), which is the proof that the win was idle cores rather than less work; eight shards on the
  same four cores bought nothing, so the floor is toolchain CPU ÷ cores, not shard count.
- **A harness claim is only a claim if a test can fail it.** The shard runner's four properties are tested
  (`-list` is the authority; the partition is reproducible; `-run` is anchored, because `TestFoo` matching
  `TestFooBar` covers a case twice and another never; only `Test*` is admitted, because a `Benchmark` in a
  `-run` runs nothing and looks green), plus the two nobody can assert from a log — that every case ran exactly
  *once*, judged from a file the cases themselves write rather than from the harness's own plan, and that the
  shards genuinely *overlapped*, measured as a ratio so a slow machine cannot fake it and a loaded machine
  cannot flake it. The first run of my own test-name parser invented 200 cases out of `go`'s banner text; the
  real list was 1244.
- **Rejected with numbers, not vibes: caching.** Hashing the IR to skip duplicate compiles looked free until
  measured — 972 distinct modules of 1177, 1760 distinct sources of 1818, so ~8% of the wall for cache keys and
  invalidation in a suite whose entire value is that it does not cache answers. Same reasoning killed trimming
  the grid cases.
- **The flake this exposed was in the witness, not the language.** Red on an unchanged tree:
  `the_a_text_slot_added_to_a_set`, reference `{'a', 1}` vs compiled `{1, 'a'}` — green when run alone. CPython
  randomises text hashing per process, gusty's sets are insertion-ordered, and `python3 -c "s={1}; s.add('a');
  print(s)"` gave the first answer 3 times in 20. `PythonRun` pinned `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` for exactly this reason
  (the matrix is a committed artifact); nine *other* reference-leg spawns had built their own command and
  inherited the environment. **A leg is only evidence if it is a function of the source** — the pin belongs in
  the helper that starts the process, because a call site that must remember it is a call site that forgets it.
  The tempting wrong fix was a `cpython-debt` row, which would have permanently pinned a bug the compiler does
  not have.
- **Re-running the suite is not a verdict when the suite writes ledgers.** The ratchet is a two-way diff of
  rows against *the cases that ran in this process*, so a subset reports every other row as "vanished":
  one shard → `340 recorded, 0 seen, 340 disappeared`, and `TestMain` fails — correctly, since a run that saw
  nothing must not promote paid debt. The artifact-writing modes (`GUSTY_GOLDEN_UPDATE`, `GUSTY_GOLDEN_MISSING`)
  therefore stay single-process by rule; `make test` is that path, and the golden file itself is byte-for-byte
  unchanged under shards because it is written by the missing-record run, not by a shard.
- **Process notes.** `go build -o bin/gustyc ./cmd/gustyc` was a *no-LLVM* binary, so a `--verify` probe through
  it silently reported `skipped:` — build with `-tags=llvm20` before measuring anything that shells out. The
  workflow's LLVM install step is guarded by a `command -v` check that must list **every** tool the suite uses
  (`go.yml`'s list was missing `lli-20` and `llvm-as-20`, which the JIT legs need). And the `r.OK` field of a
  shard report was never assigned: the JSON said "passed: false" about passing shards, which is the kind of bug
  a machine consumer reads as a green run only because it reads the exit code — both fields are now set, and a
  test asserts they agree.


## ADR 0315 — the drift ledger is adjudicated over the whole run, not over one shard (Gap R.199)

### The failure arrived as a green suite

`make testshards` was green for three cycles. The first new test file in `pkg/lang` — 47 cases for the fold
door — moved the round-robin partition, and `TestEvalImportModuleConst` failed with:

```
PAID debt still on the ledger: "import constlib\nconstlib.base + 1" (the program answered where the record
says it traps) now agrees with the record. Remove the row from testdata/interpreter-golden-drift.json.
```

Nothing about that program changed, and `go test ./pkg/lang` — serial — passed it. The row is not paid; what
changed was *which process ran which case*. A clean `HEAD` worktree at `-shards=11` and `-shards=20` passed,
which is the honest proof that the new cases caused it and that the defect predates them: the partition, not
the fold, is the bug.

### The root cause was a legality argument that proved less than it claimed

ADR 0313 justified sharding with "the drift adjudicator already judges only the sources a run actually asked
about, so a shard may be a subset". True of a subset, false of a shard. `checkDriftAgainst` read two
process-global sets — `divergenceSet` (what diverged) and `askedAbout` (what was put a question to) — and each
`TestMain` judged its own process. Serially the process *is* the run; sharded it is a shard, while a ledger
row is a claim about the run. One source, two witnesses, two shards: the shard that merely ran it says PAID
(failing the build and telling the reader to delete a row still owed), the shard holding the divergence says
owed. The mirror case — a NEW divergence whose *asking* is split so no shard both asks and diverges — reports
nothing at all. Neither is detectable from inside a shard, because a shard's evidence is a subset by
construction.

The `askedAbout` guard was written for `-run` subsets, and it kept passing there. A fixture package with two
test cases — `tools/testshards`'s own golden fixture — has exactly one witness per source, so the tool's
tests could not see the defect either. **A test that cannot express the failure mode is not a test of it**:
the new runner tests are written so the merged-evidence case must *not* report the row while the per-shard
reading must still report it, which is what stops the check passing by being deleted.

### The fix is a type, not a flag

`lang.GoldenEvidence{Ledger, Divergences, Asked}` turns the adjudication into a function of its inputs;
`GoldenEvidenceFromLedger` collects it, `MergeGoldenEvidence` unions it (a divergence any shard saw is the
run's; a source any shard asked counts as asked), and `CheckDriftAgainst(evidence, ledger)` — the rules from
the package that owns them, one implementation for serial and sharded — says the run's sentence. `GUSTY_GOLDEN_REPORT`
makes a shard write its evidence and hand the judgement over; `tools/testshards` groups the files by the
**absolute** ledger path each shard recorded (there are two ledgers over one record, and the shard does not
know which package it is) and calls the rules once per ledger. A green run prints the numbers it merged:
`… adjudicated over 20 shard(s) — 338 divergence(s) over 2765 source(s) asked, all on the ledger`.

### Rejected, and why

* *Drop the PAID direction under sharding* — green CI at the cost of half a ratchet, and the ledger stops
  shrinking; the same trade Gap R.190's guard refused.
* *`-shards 1` in CI* — correct, and 10m06s against a 10m00s default timeout: a fix that spends the budget is
  not a fix.
* *Pre-compute the whole run's asked set* — needs a test-name-to-source index that cannot exist: one table
  case asks 60 sources, and the corpus case asks 2900.
* *A shared append-only ledger file* — concurrent writers, and one crashed shard poisons it.

### Small things worth writing down

* `GUSTY_GOLDEN_UPDATE`/`GUSTY_GOLDEN_MISSING` stay deliberately outside the handover: they are per-run
  artifacts and must land on one process. The runner detects them and leaves adjudication in the shard, so a
  sharded re-record cannot have N writers overwrite the ledger one file at a time.
* A shard that *failed* skips the drift verdict. It already reddens the run, and a verdict computed from
  partial evidence invents a second failure for someone to chase.
* `evidence.Asked` marshals as `[]`, never `null`: a machine consumer should not have to distinguish them.
* The evidence file names carry the package path (`…-pkg-lang-005.golden-evidence.json`), because the shard
  index alone collides across the four sharded packages.

## ADR 0316 — the fold builtins answer the pair (Gap R.146's fold clause, L11.1; Gaps R.197, R.198 filed)

### The door is small; the measuring was the work

`print(min(n, 3))` over `n = xs[0]` was exit 1, and the row looked like "hand the fold two pairs, let the run
time pick". It is that — `@rt_pair_fold` writes the winner's payload beside the winner's tag, `sum` is `+`
seeded with the integer `0` through `@rt_num_arith` so the cross-kind sentence stays the operator's own
(ADR 0265), and the raise is emitted at the step site so `except TypeError:` reaches it (ADR 0228). What took
the time was not the door. It was finding out, by running things, what every neighbouring sentence in this
repo is allowed to say.

### Three claims I wrote down before measuring them, and what the run said

* I wrote that `print(type(m))` works. **It does not parse** — `type` is not a call the parser takes. The doc
  block went back to a form both legs print.
* I wrote that `min(t, 3)` over a *text* slot raises `TypeError`. The compiled leg **refuses to build it**; the
  runtime `TypeError` belongs to `min(n, "b")` over an int slot. A refusal and a raise are different exit codes
  and different sentences; docs/language.md may not blur them.
* I wrote `46` inverted pins, `176` conformance rows, `341` divergences. The measurements are **23** pins
  (counted out of the diff, per file), **174** rows / 135 asserted (the matrix's own numbers), **338**
  divergences over 2765 sources asked at 20 shards. Every number in a doc now comes from the artifact that
  holds it, not from a sum in my head.

The lesson is not "check your arithmetic". It is that a claim written from memory of what the code *should* do
is the same class of defect as code that answers from a tag it did not read.

### A container is where the fold was wrong, and it was wrong before this cycle

Measuring the new door found the old road beside it reading a number that is not the container's value:
`min(la, o)` over a built `la` answers **`2`** — the element count — at exit 0 where CPython raises
`TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'list'`; `min(sa, 3)` over a built set answers `1`
where the reference raises; and two *different* containers raise the reference's own `<` sentence at exit 3
where it answers `[1, 2]`, `[3]`, `{1}`. The identity arms (`min(a, a)`) answer correctly, which is the clue:
the comparison is fine, the **element-wise ordering does not exist** — Gap R.97's missing word, in the fold's
seat. Filed as **Gap R.197** with the reference's answers in the debt row, and as **Gap R.198** the four
shapes the door refuses (set literal, container among the values, `key=`, a shadowed builtin).

Rejected along the way, each for a reason worth keeping: comparing two heap handles (a plausible number at
exit 0 — the exact class of wrong this row exists to stop); folding a set literal in source order (`sum({n, 3})`
= `6` vs the reference's `3`); letting the fold's answer register as a container-bound name so `min(n, 3) + 1`
would work (every truncation this compiler has been patched for started by letting one more door read one word
of a pair); and calling the exit-3 raise "an honest refusal" (the reference *answers* those lines — a raise
there is a wrong answer wearing the reference's exit class).

### A probe's comment is part of its record key

`integration/programs/*.gy` sources are keyed into `pkg/lang/testdata/interpreter-golden.json` **verbatim,
comments included**. Re-numbering an `ADR 0315` to `ADR 0316` in a probe's header comment therefore orphaned
its record and the probe started failing the record leg with *no recorded expectation* — a missing-record
failure that looks like a codegen regression and is a comment edit. Renaming the two record keys fixed it. Two
rules follow: edit a probe's header with the record file open, and expect the record key to move with it.

### A `-run` filter that matches nothing is a green light for nothing

`go test ./pkg/lang -run TestPairFold` reported `ok … [no tests to run]` and I nearly took it as a pass: the
fold tests are `TestAFold…`, `TestTheFoldDoor…`, `TestWhatTheFoldDoor…`. The habit that catches it is
`grep -n '^func Test' <file>` before filtering on a name you have not run by its real name — and the commit
gate stays the whole suite, not a filter.

### The conformance arithmetic when a debt gets paid

Registering `probe_pair_bound_name_takes_a_value` as an asserted program did **not** add a row: it was already
a row, as debt. Rows went 172 → 174 (two genuinely new programs) while the oracle's debt count stayed at 33 —
one debt promoted to match, one new debt filed. Reading only `rows` or only `debt` would have "proved" the
promotion never happened. The diff that settles it is per-row: added / removed / changed, keyed by `case.id`.

### Small things worth writing down

* 23 "this must be refused" pins inverted into printed answers across eleven files, and the suite named every
  one of them. That is the design working: a refusal test that never fails is not testing a refusal.
* A gate test's `mustNotHave` list has to be scoped to the code the program generated: `@rt_print_value` is
  legitimate in a runtime block another program's road uses, so the assertion belongs to the *program's* `main`
  (`mainMustNotHave`), not to the module.
* Same for `store double`: the runtime's float-box writer legitimately stores a double, so the ADR 0305 check
  runs line-by-line over the pair slot the program's own binding writes.
* A fold's empty case cannot be reached through a pair argument (a literal always has elements), so the empty
  trap is documented as defensive and the row that reaches it is Gap R.197 — not shipped as if it were covered.

### The gate's own cache was lying about the docs

While re-running `go test ./...` as the pre-commit gate it printed `ok github.com/donutloop/gusty/cmd/gustyc (cached)`
and the reason for a whole new row: a third of this suite asserts things about files outside its own package — the
doc pins over `docs/language.md` and `roadmap.md`, the conformance guards over `integration/programs/*.gy`, the
record guards over `testdata/*.json` — and `go test`'s cache key holds build inputs, not files a test opens. Edit
a doc, run the suite twice, and the second `ok` came from a run that never opened the file. `make test` now ships
`-count=1`, and `tools/testshards` asserts the makefile keeps it (checked by deleting the flag and watching the
guard go red). CI could not have caught this: a fresh checkout has no cache, so the one environment allowed to
certify a build is the one environment where the defect cannot exist (roadmap Gap R.200, ADR 0317).

## ADR 0322 — the block that closed a door for a program was keyed by the program (Gap R.191)

### The coarse thing was not the conservatism, it was the sentence

`numericSlotChains` decides whether `+` and `*` over a container slot the literal no longer describes may be
lowered at all, and it refuses whenever it cannot *prove* the slots hold numbers — because CPython answers
`xs[0] + "a"` with a joined text and `[1] * 2` with a repeated list, and this backend builds neither from a
slot. Its blocking half was one `bool` for the module, commented "coarse on purpose", and coarse is fine while
it only ever refuses more. What made it a defect was the message that came out of it: `w.append("a")` — a text
in a container the arithmetic never walks — produced
`index cannot reach into nested's slots: the name was rebound, mutated, or handed to code this pass cannot
see`. A refusal is an interface; an agent that reads that edits `nested`, and `nested` was the one container in
the program that had not been touched. Lesson worth keeping: **when a pass refuses on a whole-program
property, the property has to be about the thing the message names.** "Coarse" is admissible for a verdict,
never for an accusation.

### Per-name is only safe once a name can be aliased

The obvious fix — key the block by the container the store writes — fixes the reported program and quietly
un-ships a safety net. `ys = xs` / `ys.append("word")` writes into the very container `print(xs[1] * 2)` reads,
and with a name-keyed block that door opens and raises a `TypeError` where the reference returns `wordword`.
The program-wide bit had been covering aliases, loop variables, parameters and unknown callees without ever
saying so; deleting it converts all four into wrong answers at exit 0. So the block now travels a union-find
built by the same walk: `y = xs`, `a, b = xs`, `d = xs[0]`, `for v in xs`, `[v for v in xs]`, and each call site
linking a parameter to the argument that reaches it. **Evidence stays per-name** (an alias can only close a
door, never open one: `ys.append([9, 10])` proves nothing about `xs`), and `blockAll` survives for the stores
that describe no name at all — `xs[0].append("a")`, `self.items.add(b)`, a loop variable over `rows()` — which
is the only place "which container?" genuinely has no answer.

### A table of expectations can be a table of skips

`TestNumericSlotChainGate` is described as "the gate asked directly, so a widening of `+` fails a decision
row". It took the print argument and handed it to `chainDepth`, which answers only for a *bare* subscript.
Every row in the table is written `print(xs[0][0] + 1)` — a `BinOp` — so every row fell through to
`t.Skip("row has no print(...) argument to walk")`. The gate had no test, and the one row whose expected value
this cycle inverted ("text anywhere in any container" → now open) had never run. Two things to copy: a decision
table should **fail** when it cannot find the thing it is about, and the extractor that finds it belongs in the
test file, walking `BinOp`/`UnOp`/`CondExpr`/call args, not in the pass.

### The walk had blind spots that made the coarse bit look load-bearing

Re-reading the pass found stores it never visited: `xs += ["a"]` (an `AugAssignStmt` on a Name — extends the
container without ever naming it as a receiver), `xs[0][1] = "a"` (an item assignment two levels down, whose
target the walk only recognised one level deep), and whole statement forms it skipped — `Comp`, `Generator`,
`Slice`, `Lambda`, `AssignExpr`, `WithStmt`, `MatchStmt`, `ClassDef`, `YieldStmt`, `YieldFromStmt`. A store the
pass does not visit cannot block anything, so the program-wide flag was protecting against a set of shapes the
walk was simply not looking at. Widening the walk is what made narrowing the flag safe.

### Differential across the corpus is the cheap "did I break anything else"

`for f in integration/programs/*.gy; do diff <(gustyc_base --aot --file $f) <(gustyc --aot --file $f); done`
over 187 programs, run before any of the suite: one file differs (the new probe), plus one already-failing
program whose only difference is the temp directory in an `llc` error. That is a five-minute claim no assertion
in the suite gives you this directly, and it is the claim that a widening of a gate is confined to what it
widens.

### Small things

* The corpus asserts every registered program has a record entry, so a new `programs/*.gy` needs
  `tools/recmerge` before `TestGCCorpusCollectsAndAgrees` will pass — the failure message says exactly that,
  and reading it beat guessing.
* Two refusals measured beside this row are not this row's: `xs[0][0] / xs[0][1]` (both sides read from the
  object) is Gap R.101, and `for v in xs: print(v[0] + 1)` is the loop-variable family (Gaps R.91, R.95). Both
  refuse identically on the pre-cycle binary; they are pinned in a filed-not-fixed table with the reference's
  answer written into the row rather than folded into this cycle's answer table.
* Adding one asserted corpus program moves four published numbers at once (programs, matrix rows, parity rows,
  `match` verdicts) plus the record's count in three documents — and `roadmap_snapshot_test.go` /
  `golden_artifact_counts_test.go` name every cell, which is the whole point of ADR 0319.

## ADR 0323 — the membership test and the loop chose their helper from the notebook (Gap R.95)

### The row said "two refusals"; the family held four wrong answers

`Gap R.95` was written as one line: `7 in xs[0]` and `for v in xs[0]` refuse on a container the program built.
Re-measuring the *family* around those two programs — the same slots through a dict key, the same slots holding
scalars instead of containers — turned up four shapes that were not refusals and were much worse:
`d["a"] = [1, 2]` / `for v in d["a"]` printed a single `0` for CPython's `1`, `2`; the same with a text slot
printed nothing at all; `1 in xs[0]` over a number slot answered `False`; and the same slot stepped over by a loop
answered `0`, `1`, `2`, `3`, `4` — five iterations invented from a heap slot — all of them at the exit code of
success. A row filed as a refusal is a *hint* about the shape of the defect, not its extent: the refusal is what
the compiler notices, and the wrong answer is what it fails to notice, so the family around the reported program
is where the actual damage lives. Lesson worth keeping: **measure the neighbours of a reported row before writing
the "before" column of its table** — and rebuild the pre-cycle binary (here, a `git worktree` at HEAD into
`/tmp`) rather than trusting memory for it. One of the six "before" cells in this cycle's tables came out wrong
when it was measured instead of remembered: the loop over a number slot was written down as printing nothing and
really printed five fabricated iterations.

### One root cause, three callers, two of them never told

ADR 0251 fixed exactly this bug for the *read* below a built slot by asking the tag instead of the notebook
(`g.listVars`, `g.runtimeDicts`, `g.mixedLists` describe the container **variable**; the slot's kind is a fact
about the object, written beside the payload by whoever stored it). The membership test and the loop had the same
line of bookkeeping in their own code and were never given the fix, so they kept asking the notebook — which is
how a loop over a dict *value* ended up walking the dict's own `[key, value]` words. When a door is built for
"the shape the compiler cannot describe", grep for the other callers of the notebook it replaced: ADR 0246's
`len`, ADR 0251's read, ADR 0252's ordering and now these two are one defect with five callers, and the fourth
and fifth were found by the row's own wording, not by a test failure.

### An IR absence assertion asserts the call, never the name

The cost half of the change is "a loop the compiler *can* describe must not grow the new doors". The first version
asserted the module does not contain `@rt_iter_len(`. It could never have failed: the three helpers live in the
shared `heapRuntimeIR` block, which is emitted whole the moment any module asks for any heap object, so the
*definition* is in every module that touches a list. The assertion is now on `call i32 @rt_iter_len(`. A helper
defined in a shared runtime block is absent from no module, and the only honest absence is the absence of a call
site.

### Backticks are not markdown inside a Go raw string

`heapRuntimeIR` is a backtick-delimited raw literal, so the IR comments that open a clause with `` `the tag` ``
terminate the literal and the compiler reports `syntax error: unexpected s after top level declaration` many lines
later, in the middle of a string. IR comments inside that block are prose with no quoting machinery available.

### Two questions, two sentences — the ADR 0271 rule, re-earned

`argument of type 'int' is not iterable` (membership) and `'int' object is not iterable` (a loop) differ by more
than word order; CPython keeps them apart, and the third sentence in the family,
`'in <string>' requires string as left operand, not int`, names the **needle** rather than the haystack. Writing
one helper string and using it in both doors is the cheapest way to pass every new test in this cycle and to make
the trap tables wrong, which is what `notIterableSentence` and `notIterableLoopSentence` as two functions — and
the trap table comparing class **and** message — are there to prevent.

### Raise in the module, not in the helper

`@rt_iter_len` could have raised the `TypeError` itself, which would have saved four `icmp`s at the call site. It
does not, because a raise inside an `internal` helper loses the source span and the landing-pad bookkeeping
`raiseTo` owns, and would have to be re-derivable from nothing but two `i32`s. The helpers are reached only from
an arm that already proved the kind iterable, so they answer a count and never a diagnostic. Same reasoning, same
shape as ADR 0265's `@rt_num_arith`, whose raise also leaves through the emitted door.

### Small things

* A roadmap row's `Evidence` cell is a claim about test tables, and the count of rows in a table drifts the moment
  someone adds a case to cover a new arm. Counting them (`python3`, brace-depth at one tab, not `grep -c name:`
  against a table written with positional fields) beat re-reading them, and `TestTheRoadmapSnapshotIsMeasuredNotRemembered`
  is the tripwire for the snapshot half.
* Adding `docs/adr/0323` makes the snapshot's `ADRs` row stale in the same commit — 314 → 315, highest `0322` →
  `0323` — and the guard prints both numbers, so the ADR has to be written *before* the pre-commit gate, not
  beside it (ADR 0319, ADR 0320).
* One row moved *between* tables mid-cycle: a trap that binds the exception (`except TypeError as e:`) is not
  expressible in this language yet (`Gap R.113`), so the catchable half of that shape was rewritten as a plain
  `except TypeError:` parity row rather than dropped. A test that cannot parse is not a witness.
* Landing a row has to break a pin, and this one broke two: a comprehension shape that the honest-refusal table
  had been demanding `"more than one kind"` for became a parity row (`membership_in_a_slot_of_a_built_comp`), and
  the same program's compiled-vs-record debt row retired out of `interpreter-golden-drift.json` (338 → 337). The
  ledger rewrite went through `GUSTY_GOLDEN_UPDATE=1` on a **serial** `go test` — the sharded runner deliberately
  does not take the judgement over, because the ledger is per-process state (ADR 0315).
* Two published counts and one published sentence-trio move together with the ledger: the `Ledgers` snapshot row,
  `docs/operations.md`'s artifact table, and the green-run example line — all three are guarded or checkable, and
  `TestTheArtifactTableCountsAreTheFilesOwn` prints the file's number when they drift (ADR 0319).
* `git push` still fails in this environment — `sign_and_send_pubkey: signing failed for ED25519 … from agent:
  agent refused operation` — so ADR 0322's commit and this one are local-only and the push is retried every
  cycle rather than treated as done.

## A haystack is asked "what object is this", not "how deep is the chain" (L11.1, Gaps R.210 and R.211, ADR 0324)

`Gap R.210` said the membership test and the loop stop one slot deep, and its own `Plan` cell said the fix was
"dispatching a dispatch" — the arms would have to learn to walk a chain of slots. The fix turned out to be a
three-line fall-through to a function that had always walked the chain. `print(xs[0][0])` answers since ADR 0251
because `runtimeSlotPairDeep` reads outward tag by tag, and the pair it returns was sitting one call away from the
two callers that pick a runtime helper. Neither the membership arm (`@rt_contains_tagged(h, t, p, ntag)`) nor the
loop arm (`@rt_iter_len(h, t)`, `@rt_iter_elem(h, t, i)`) has a depth parameter: both ask *what object is at the
end*, and the read had been answering that question for chains of any length all along. Lesson: when a row says
"the mechanism would have to learn X", first `git grep` whether the mechanism already learned X for a neighbour —
the diagnosis in a row's own prose can be exact about the shape and wrong about the missing piece.

### The row you did not file is the one that ships a regression

The two-deep refusals were `R.210`'s, so I went looking for them. The needle-side defects were not refusals at all
and not in any row: ADR 0323 had read a slot-read needle's *kind* from the compiler's notebook and its *payload*
from the slot, so `d["z"] in xs[0]` for two dicts with the same entries answered `False`, and `[1] in xs[0]` over a
dict or a set slot answered `False` where CPython raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` — both at the exit code
of success, one commit after the commit that made them reachable. Both had been honest refusals *before* ADR 0323
opened the door. Lesson: the row you land is a *hint*, not a boundary; the neighbours of a newly opened door —
here, the other side of the same comparison — are where a "fix" hides an invented answer.

### A payload without its tag is an address

Why `d["z"] in xs[0]` was `False` and not a refusal: the comparison compared the two slots' payloads — heap handles —
under a tag inferred from the wrong question, and two equal dicts in two different objects have different handles.
ADR 0187's rule ("the operation that writes a payload writes its tag beside it") is usually quoted about writes;
the same pair is what makes a *comparison* mean something. A slot read is an operand as much as it is a value to
print, and `taggedOperand` answers "what kind does the notebook say" — a question the notebook cannot answer about
a slot at all, because the slot's kind is a fact about the object, written beside the payload by whoever stored it.

### Key an unhashable raise by the *runtime tag*, not by the statically proven kind

The temptation was a shared `hashable(tag)` helper used by both the dict and the set arms. Rejected against the
reference: `{1} in {1, 2}` is `False` (a set needle is looked up as the frozenset it converts to), while
`[1] in {1, 2}` raises. Keyed by the tag, once per arm, the two rows agree without a special case. This is ADR
0311's write-side rule ("an unhashable value raises from its tag") applied to the read side — the same object, the
same question, and a dict and a set want different answers from the same `TypeError`. The guard also enters the
arm's own raise path (one `icmp` chain per arm) so the program's `except TypeError:` catches it, rather than
raising inside a helper where the span and the landing-pad bookkeeping would be re-derived from two `i32`s.

### Three things about the loop, not the code

* A conformance program is the cheapest double-witness: `integration/programs/runtime_slot_haystack_deep.gy` is
  seventeen lines and is run twice — AOT and CPython — and compared, so one file is the reference leg for every
  answer in both new test tables, including all three new `TypeError` sentences.
* Every "cost" assertion over a runtime helper has to name the *call*, not the symbol. The first cost half of this
  change was "the static door grows no new doors" and it could never fail: the helper's *definition* is emitted in
  the shared heap block of any module that touches a container (ADR 0323 learned this; this cycle re-learned it for
  `call i32 @rt_contains_tagged(`).
* The pre-commit gate caught its usual stale numbers — the record 6029 → 6084, the ADR snapshot 315/`0323` →
  316/`0324` — and one new kind: the roadmap's row-count `129b` has to be unique in the queue table or
  `TestTheQueueCounterSeesWhatASplitTableHides` fails. `git push` still fails (`agent refused operation`) and is
  retried every cycle rather than treated as done.

## The tag a writer leaves is the kind every reader must obey (L11.1, Gap R.209, ADR 0325)

An instance appended into a container printed its heap slot, and `len`, membership and the loop all said `int`.
There were not four bugs. The slot's tag said `int`, and ADR 0187 has made every reader obey that word. The fix was
therefore one writer-side decision in `elemKindTag` — a known instance gets `TagInstance` — followed by the renderer
and raise arms that make the tag meaningful. Patching the printer or membership arm alone would have left three
doors reporting a kind the program never stored. This is ADR 0259's bool-slot precedent one object further out, and
it is the clearest evidence so far that the tag table, not each call site, is the language's source of truth.

### The tag says "object"; only the object says which class

`TagInstance` is not enough to print `<__main__.C object at 0x…>` or `argument of type 'C' is not iterable`. The
constructor already stores the dispatch id in object slot 0, so the module emits a class table beside its heap block
and reads that word when a message or identity form needs the name. Qualification differs by place: the TypeError
names `C`, while identity names `__main__.C`. One table for both would eventually make one of them wrong, so there
are `@rt_class_short` and `@rt_class_qual`. The runtime formats the sentence; it does not raise it, because span,
exception code and landing-pad destination belong to the compiler arm, not to a helper reached with two `i32`s.

### A conformance rule may remove an accident, never answer the question

CPython's address is a process fact, and the compiled backend's is a heap-slot fact. The oracle gained
`instance-identity`, which rewrites only the complete `<… object at 0x…>` form and leaves the class inside the
brackets as the assertion. A general `0x…` normalizer would have been a machine for turning unrelated wrong output
into a match. The CLI test also rejects output that is merely a number, which is the old bug and is not removable by
normalization.

### The static binary road was inventing two answers

`c in "abc"` answered `True`, and `"abc" in c` answered `False`, both at exit 0, because the text-membership and
generic-container roads never consulted the instance subject. The two reference raises name opposite sides of the
operation: a text haystack names the needle's class, and a non-iterable haystack names itself. The ordinary binary
arms now consult the same kind question before either road can turn a TypeError into a verdict.

### One tag can expose a forgotten gate

`print({c})` already used the tagged heap builder, but `len({c})` still fell into the static set-literal path because
its gate only asked `literalNeedsHeap`. After the instance tag arrived, the same object could print and refuse to be
measured. The lesson is to make the literal question explicit at every consumer: does this container need the heap,
can its elements label themselves, or did the pair road bind one? A gate copied for one builder is not the rule.

## The fold had no door to the raise (L11.1/L11.3, Gap R.37, ADR 0326)

**Feature (roadmap Gap R.37, owner `aot`).** A constant read whose position, key or text could not be honoured
was a compile-time refusal at exit 1, and the conversions that had been widened instead of refused answered:
`float("x")` and `float(None)` printed `0.0`, `ord("ab")` printed `97`. `pkg/lang/constant_trap.go` is the new
door (`constantTrap`, the sentence table, `intFromText`/`floatFromText`, `unconvertibleArg`); the constant list,
text, dict and comprehension reads, the `int`/`float`/`ord`/`chr` folds and `print`'s unbounded `chr` arm all
route through it. Tests: `pkg/lang/constant_trap_test.go` (17 record-leg, 5 reference-leg, 10 answering, 5
catchable, 3 block-shape, 2 refusal rows), `integration/constant_trap_test.go` (11 exit-code rows, 4 catchable
rows, the matrix-row assertion), the `ord("hello")` module row in `ircheck_test.go`, the method-body and ternary
rows moved from refusal to raise in `method_unwind_test.go`/`string_subscript_test.go`, the CLI's exit-1 list
rebuilt in `builtin_trap_classes_test.go`. Record 6095 → 6130 through `tools/recmerge`; the `pkg/lang` drift
ledger 337 → 332, five rows out as paid; `integration/programs/constant_trap.gy` is the 191st program. Rows:
Gap R.37 ✅ DONE; Gap R.213 ✅ DONE (paid in this door); Gap R.214 and Gap R.215 ⏳ OPEN (measured here).
Docs: `docs/adr/0326-constant-trap.md`, `docs/language.md`, `docs/operations.md`, `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`,
`roadmap.md`, `docs/roadmap-details.md`.

### A raise is a terminator, so the door owns the block after it

The first build of `constantTrap` failed the verifier. `raiseTo` ends the current basic block — it emits the
branch to the function's unwind exit — and the fold, being an *expression*, returned a value to a caller that
immediately emitted more instructions into a block that had already ended. A fold that raises has to open a
fresh block on the far side of the raise and hand that back. It is the same shape `normalizeIndex` already
carries for the dynamic read (`ix.bad` / `ix.ok`), which is the tell that the two roads had never been asked to
share anything.

### "It refuses" and "it raises" are different capabilities, not two settings of one knob

The trap machinery is years old: ADR 0211 gave traps classes, ADR 0181 gave the raise a frame-closing unwind,
ADR 0166 fixed the exit codes. None of that reached a fold, because a fold never had a *route* to it — the code
that decided `[][0]` was a builder, not a program point. Deleting a refusal does not install a raise; the
evidence is that the refusal had been there since the constant reads were written and the raise had been
reachable from every *other* call site the whole time.

### Reusing the dynamic sentence table is what kept the ledger from growing

The tempting version wrote CPython's words (`list index out of range`) into the new raise. That would have made
one error have two wordings — the constant road saying one thing and the dynamic road another — and turned a
paid row into two divergences. The sentences come from `listIndexOutOfRange()` and friends, so Gap R.90 still
owns exactly one rename, for both roads at once. The corollary showed up immediately: `tools/recmerge`
*refused* to record `print([][0])` because the compiled leg and the reference disagree on the wording, and the
right answer was to leave those three sources out of the record and assert both sentences in the test, not to
push a record through. A recorder that will not write an entry the two legs disagree on is the ledger's immune
system; a test that asserts both wordings side by side is what makes paying Gap R.90 break something.

### A widening without a raise is how a wrong answer ships

`float("x")` → `0.0` is not a missing feature, it is a lie at exit 0, and it arrived by the most ordinary
route: the error was swallowed, the empty string went to the parser, the parser returned zero. Two entries in
one file — `int("abc")` (refused) and `float("x")` (answered) — were the same missing check, and only one of
them looked like a gap. When a fold grows an arm, the arm list is the checklist: `int` grew a `bool` arm this
cycle for exactly that reason (Gap R.213), and `print`'s `chr` folding arm had no bound at all.

### Refusing stays correct where nothing is correct

`int("99999999999999999999999999")` is kept as a refusal rather than routed through the new door. The reference
has an unbounded `int`; this backend has a 64-bit slot; a trap there would name the program for a fault of the
representation, and an answer would be the substituted value this contract forbids. Naming the word, and naming
L12.12 as the decision that has to happen first, is the honest third option — and pinning it as
`TestANumberWiderThanTheWordIsStillAnHonestRefusal` means the day the bounded-versus-arbitrary question is
answered, a test has to be edited to answer it.

### A row's neighbour is where the next rows are

Two shapes fell out of probing the door and both are filed rather than bundled: a subscript on a call result
still refuses (`Gap R.214`) though the same position into a literal now raises, and a text key into a dict
literal still refuses (`Gap R.215`) though the same key into a dict *variable* traps. Both are container-source
gaps, not trap-door gaps — which is the useful distinction: this cycle built a door four roads were standing in
front of, and those two roads are still carrying their own missing half.

### Every number a document quotes has to be re-grepped, not recalled

The artifact guards did their job — 6095, 337, 190/179/126 all failed loudly until recomputed — and the same
reflex caught a worse error mid-cycle: two claims about `roadmap.md` (a "Gap R.168 family table" with a
`literal out-of-range index/key` row, and a `Gap R.184` row about `len`) had been carried along as though
measured, and do not exist in the file at all. `grep -c` over the file is the difference between a claim with an
owner and a fabrication wearing a row number; from here, a number or a row name goes into a document only after
a command has printed it in this session.

## The gate was the bug, not the door (L11.1, Gap R.215/R.216, ADR 0327)

`print({"a": 1}["a"])` refused with `index must be a constant` while `d = {"a": 1}` / `print(d["b"])` raised
`KeyError: 'b'`. The tempting description was "the backend cannot read a dict literal with a text key", and the
thing I found in the code was narrower and stupider: the subscript road opens with a gate that accepts a
non-integer key **only when the base is a registered container name**, so `case *DictLit:` below it was
reachable with an integer key and nothing else. Every part of the answer already existed and was in production
use — `heapDictFrom` builds the literal, `taggedSlotPair` reads an entry as `(payload, tag)`,
`rt_dict_has_tagged`/`rt_dict_get_tagged`/`rt_dict_value_tag` ask the object, ADR 0326's raise names the missing
key. A gate, not a missing door. The first question for any "the backend refuses X" row should therefore be
*which check rejects it*, because a gate is a five-line change and a door is a runtime helper.

### A literal is the same value as the name you would bind it to

The rule that paid the row is one sentence: **a dict literal is a dict**, so its entries are read by the door a
dict variable's entries are read by. Where the fold genuinely can read the shape (`{1: 2}[1]`) it answers and the
module carries none of the heap dict — pinned by a negative control, with the positive half asserted in a
neighbouring test so the control cannot pass vacuously. The key rule fell out of reading the key as a *value*
instead of as a spelling: `1`, `1.0` and `True` are one key, `True` finds the entry `1` wrote, and `{0: 1}["0"]`
raises where the payload-read answer was "the key is there".

### A wrong answer at exit 0 is worth an exit 1 refusal, and the pair is the whole difference

Routing the read through the object was easy; keeping the *tag* was the work. `def f(): return {"a": "x"}["a"]`
and `g({"a": "x"}["a"])` both measured as `1` at **exit 0** — the text's `@str_tab` index — because those
positions keep one word for a whole value. They stay refusals, and the refusal says which half is missing and
which row owns it (Gap R.146, plus Gap R.220 filed from the variable side of the same road). The gate asks
whether the entry is a plain integer rather than trusting `strFuncs`; had it trusted `strFuncs`, Gap R.219 (a
function registered as text-returning on the evidence of one arm) would have turned `{"a": 1}["a"]` into a
`1` printed as text. The invariant that keeps the whole family honest is
`TestTheLiteralRoadIsNeverWorseThanTheVariableRoad`: the literal road may answer where the variable road refuses,
must answer the reference's way when it answers, and may refuse only where the variable road is not right either.

### Four rows fell out of probing, and one of them was this cycle's own fold

`{1: 2, 1: 3}[1]` answered `2` while the object road answered `3` — one construct, two answers, and the fold's
was wrong (Gap R.216, paid by scanning the literal's keys from last to first). Three more are filed, not
bundled: a container key raises `KeyError` where the reference raises `TypeError: unhashable` (Gap R.217 — and
the *variable* road says the same thing, which is what "one door" is supposed to buy), a **list** literal read by
a position still answers the payload (`["a","b"][0]` prints `0`, Gap R.218 — the same defect, other base), and a
dict read handed to a call answers the payload (Gap R.220).

### Twice in one cycle I wrote a citation I had not measured

Two failures worth recording, because both were *my* tooling habits rather than the language's. First, I filled
in a test-name citation and a `file.go:line` reference from what the code "must" look like — `compiledRepr`,
`runCompiledRepr`, `pkg/lang/codegen_robject_index_test.go` — none of which exist; the compile caught the first
two, and only a `grep`/`ls` re-run caught the third. Second, I reached for `write` to *append* a section to
`docs/roadmap-details.md` and overwrote 9,873 lines with a placeholder; `git checkout --` restored it because
the file happened to be unmodified, which was luck and not process. So: a helper name goes into a test only after
`grep -rn "func name"` has printed it in this session, a row number goes into a document only after `grep -c` has
printed it, and an append to a big file is an `edit` against an anchor or a shell append — never a whole-file
`write`.

## The element that is a read (L11.1, Gap R.224; ADR 0332)

### A door with one caller left in it

ADR 0331 made a list literal answer the position the program named, and named this row in its own
consequences. Reading the two side by side was the whole planning step: the print door, the binding door,
the membership door and the length door all ask a subscript for a `(payload, tag)` pair, and `pairElemPair`
— the hook that hands a builder both words — admitted a `*Name` and nothing else. One caller in the language
was still asking for one word, and the answer it got was `[1, 2]` where CPython prints `['x', 2]`. The lesson
generalises past this family: when a capability is "paid", ask **which callers of the old question are still
standing**, because the last one is where the next row lives.

### The gate is the row, not the door

The door was four lines: an `*Index` arm that calls `taggedSlotPair`, the same call `print(xs[i])` emits.
The row was the gate — `subscriptIsPairElem`, which asks the door's own two questions in the door's order and
nothing else (does the run time own the container side; can the fold answer this read alone). ADR 0249's rule
says a gate and a door that test different things ship a refusal nobody measured, and the shape it protects
against here was specific and easy to miss: had the gate admitted the fold's shapes, `[[1, 2][0], 3]` would
have started allocating a list to ask a question the compiler can see the answer to. The negative control
(`TestTheFoldStillOwnsTheReadItCanAnswer`, plus the CLI's `--emit-llvm` row) is what makes that claim instead
of a paragraph.

### Three gates asked a narrower question than the builders

`literalHasPairElement` had its own inline `pairName` predicate, weaker than `nameIsPairElem` (it skipped the
origin switch), and `elemTaggableOrPair` asked the name question only. Had I widened `pairElemPair` alone,
the dict and set would have kept their old refusals and the list would have gone to the static-array road and
errored — three behaviours, one change, none of them measured. They now all ask `isPairElem`. When a decision
is asked in more than one place, the diff has to include every place, and the way to find them is to grep the
*question* (`grep -n "literalNeedsTags\|taggableMixedList\|elemTaggableOrPair"`) rather than the answer.

### Do not let a widening convert a refusal into a lie

One shape moved the wrong way while the door widened: `def f(): return [{"a": "x"}["a"], 2]` used to stop the
build with the static-array sentence, and started printing `0`. The refusal had been accidental — the fold
happening to error — and the road it fell to is Gap R.67's, which already answers `0` for `return ["a", 2]`.
Filing it under the row that owns it, and pinning it in the filed-not-fixed table with CPython's `['x', 2]`
beside it, is the honest third option: neither a fix, nor a silence. The rule I applied to the rest of the
family is the same one ADR 0331 applied to its own residue — `[id({"a": "x"}["a"]), 1]` is asserted to **keep**
refusing, with Gap R.146 named, because a green suite bought by relaxing a refusal is a suite that certifies a
wrong answer.

### Derive the parity expectation, even when you are sure

`TestTheElementRoadIsNeverWorseThanThePrintRoad` first composed its expectation by wrapping the print road's
answer in `[…, 2]`. It failed on text — `print(x)` writes `x`, a container writes `'x'` — which is ADR 0258's
str/repr split, not a bug in the parity. The row now asks CPython for the element program's answer inside the
case (`PythonRun`), the way `integration/` derives every expectation from the reference (Gap N's standing
rule). A parity test whose expectation is assembled from the other leg's *rendering* is testing a rendering
theory; asking the reference removes the theory.

### Four rows fell out of probing, and each got its own owner

Gap R.225 (an element that *contains* a read: `[str({"a":"x"}["a"]), 1]` is `[1, 1]`), Gap R.226 (the loop
that unrolls a literal binds the payload while the bound form binds the pair — visible in the IR as a
`store i32 %t8, i32* %_v` with no tag store beside it), and Gap R.227 (a subscript whose base is a subscript
of a literal refuses, Gap R.214's shape one level in). Each has a different owner — an operand gate, the
unrolled loop, the subscript road — and one row with three owners makes two of them undiscoverable.

### The guards earned their keep again

`tools/recmerge` wrote 56 entries and refused the ones the compiled leg would not agree to; the artifact-count
guards caught every number this cycle changed (record 6260 → 6316, programs 195 → 196, matrix 184 → 185,
oracle `match` 131 → 132, ADRs 323 → 324, queue 109/140 → 111/143) and none of them was typed by hand — the
first pass typed two and the test named each one. One new test row was also wrong before it was run: I
expected `strs[9]` (an out-of-range position into a text literal) to decline the gate, and the gate correctly
said "not the fold's" and let the bounds door raise the `IndexError`. A gate decision table written from what
the code should do, rather than from what the code does, is where I keep finding my own assumptions.

## The answer that crossed a `return` (L11.1, Gap R.67; ADR 0333)

### Exit 2 on a two-line program is the bug worth stopping for

`def build(): return [1, 2]` / `print(build())` was not a missing feature — it was `llc` rejecting our module
(`global variable reference must have pointer type`) because codegen had put `@.lst1`, an i32 global, in a
`ret`. Exit **2** is the code the contract reserves for a broken compiler, and it is the only class where the
tool apologises for a program the reference runs. I started by probing the queue's next row (Gap R.214) and
found I could not even *build* its own example; the blocker two rows down was the exit-2 one, and taking it
first was the right call for exactly the reason ADR 0166 gives: a compiler-bug class outranks a missing door.
The lesson is to read the exit code before reading the message. The three shapes in this row's title all
looked like "printing a container is broken"; only the first was a verifier failure, and the two that built
were wrong at exit 0, which the queue ranks above any refusal but which no red `llc` output advertises.

### A call site holds one word and a name, so the kind has to be a record

The design question was whether to return a `(payload, tag)` pair across the `ret`, like the slot roads, or
to record the kind at compile time. The pair is the honest answer when the caller cannot see the callee; here
the caller does not need to — the callee's own source says what it hands back, and a register per call for one
construct is what `pairRetDone` pays for shapes where the kind genuinely is dynamic. So `containerReturningFuncs`
is a whole-program scan beside `strFuncs`, and the interesting part is what it *refuses to believe*: every
`return` must answer one kind, the body cannot fall off its end, a bare `return` condemns the function, and
`containerBodyIsOpaque` condemns any statement form the walk did not visit rather than let it slip past. A scan
that fails open is worse than no scan — the caller has no way to check. Gap R.219 (`strFuncs` registering a
function as text-returning from ONE arm, so the arm returning a number printed a byte string's interned index)
is the cautionary tale, and I wrote the 18 decline-rows before the answer-rows so the scan had to earn each
claim.

### The re-dispatch was the feature; the notebooks were the fine print

The first version lowered a container-returning call to a temp name and printed it. Correct output, wrong
design: `for k in build():` printed `0 1` for `{"a": 1, "b": 2}`, because the loop road asks `dictKeyStr`, not
`runtimeDicts`, and `print([1, "a", …])` printed `[1, 0, …]`, because the printer asks `listElemStr`. Every road
in this backend already consults a per-name notebook for a container *variable*; the win was that
`containerAnswerOperand` writes those notebooks and then re-dispatches the operand as the name, so there is one
answer per shape rather than nine private copies. Two rules came out of it: (a) a name handed to a notebook must be
a rooted temp, because the loop roads read a name back as an operand, and a bare `%t7` would re-read the wrong
row — the same lesson ADR 0273 learned for the pair road's arity, in the other direction; (b) the notebook writer
must be called with the **same predicate as the build site** — `literalNeedsHeap || literalNeedsTags ||
literalHasPairElement`. Asking only `literalNeedsTags` is how the first build printed `[1, 0]` for `[1, "a"]`: the
string slot's tag never got written, and the printer faithfully read the interned index as the number it is.

### The tag question and the build question are one question

That bug is ADR 0249 wearing a new hat — a gate asking a narrower question than the door it stands in front
of — and it is worth restating as a search rule: when a decision has to match an emission, grep for the
emission's own predicate and call *it*, rather than writing the decision from what you believe the emission
does. Every time this cycle I wrote a second predicate I got it wrong, and every time I called the first one I
did not.

### Do not let a new scan steal programs from a road whose refusal is a contract

The scan initially claimed `def pack(v): return [v, 1]` unconditionally, and `print(pack(2.5))` — which the pair
road refuses in words, naming the `(payload, tag)` pair it is missing — started taking the container road and
printing a wrong list. A refusal sentence is a promise about what the compiler knows (ADR 0249), and an
over-claiming table that re-routes the program breaks the promise instead of the refusal. The fix is a
whole-program call-site table: if any call site hands a double, a float-typed name, a pair-bound name or a
pair-returning call into a parameter that lands in a slot, the function is declined and the pair road keeps it.
The decision table's two rows differ by one character in the call — `print(b(2))` is claimed, `print(b(2.5))` is
not — which is the clearest evidence I have that the gate is asking about the *value*, not the shape. Widening a
door must never quietly relax a refusal elsewhere, and the guard for that is a test in the other direction:
`TestThePairRoadKeepsWhatTheContainerAnswerLeavesIt` fails if my table wins a program it should have left alone.

### A refusal that names the door is worth more than a handle at exit 0

Once the answer existed, every position that has no container arm would have printed the handle — the `0` this
row exists to remove. So the ordinary one-word call road asks the table and, for an unasked container answer,
refuses naming the function and the door that does answer, at exit 1. Every one of those is filed with the
reference's answer beside it (`build()[7]` → Gap R.214, `[build(), 3]` and `build().append(3)` → Gap R.229,
`takes(build())` → Gap R.154, `build() + [9]` → Gap R.175, `la = [1,2]; return la` → Gap R.35, `return None` →
Gap R.228), and each row fails the day its door grows. Exit 2 is asserted absent from all of them.

### Probing found the wrong answer hiding under the right one

`print(f())` where `f` returns `None` answers `0`. It has answered `0` on every binary I built this cycle, old
and new, and it sat inside my probe file between two rows I was watching, so for two days it read as "the None
case, still broken, presumably mine". Comparing the *old* binary and the new one on the same probe was what
made it obviously pre-existing, and it is now Gap R.228 with its own row — filed, not bundled, and not quietly
fixed inside a commit whose title is about containers. The probe file itself is the tool worth keeping: 46
programs, and a filter that prints only the ones where the compiled answer differs from CPython's, which is the
only way I noticed the eight that differ for reasons nobody had measured.

### The guards earned their keep again

`tools/recmerge` wrote 50 entries and the artifact-count guards caught every number this cycle moved (record
6316 → 6366, programs 196 → 197, matrix 185 → 186, parity 147 → 148, oracle `match` 132 → 133, ADRs 324 → 325,
queue 111/143 → 112/145); none was typed from memory, and each was named by a failing test rather than by me.
One conformance line had to come *out* of `container_returns.gy`: `print(bool(make_list()), bool(empty_set()))`
printed `False False` where CPython prints `True False`. A conformance program asserts the doors this row
answers; a line that disagrees with the reference belongs in a Gap row, not in a matrix row's expected file —
and the line's own disagreement is now part of Gap R.229's evidence.

## The same read, one statement shorter (L11.1, Gap R.214; ADR 0334)

### One question, three doors — and the missing one asked about the spelling, not the value

`print([1, 2][7])` raises `IndexError: list index out of range`. `ys = build()` / `print(ys[7])` raises it.
`print(build()[7])` printed `codegen: index requires an inline list/dict/set literal` and exited 1. Same
question, three spellings, two answers — and the diagnostic value was entirely in the *fold* spelling: it
proved the language already owned the trap, the message and the exit class, so the third line could not be a
missing feature, only a door in the wrong place. The subscript road dispatches on the **shape of its base**
(`*ListLit` → fold, `*Name` → the variable's read, `*Index` → the object below), which was sound while a call
handed back a global in a `ret` and stopped being sound the cycle ADR 0333 made the answer a heap handle. That
is ADR 0251's sentence again — *the road chose from the base's spelling rather than from what the compiler
holds* — one construct over, and the fix is the same: lower the call to the rooted name the notebooks are
recorded under, copy the subscript node with that name as its base, and let `ys[i]`'s roads answer. Not a
second reader. A second reader is how a "fixed" row comes back as a wrong answer the first time the tag table
grows a kind.

### The rewrite is the whole change only if its position in the print door is right

`print(f()[2])` over `return {1: "one", 2: "two"}` printed `1` on my first attempt. The tagged read had been
asked first, and a dict built from a **literal** carries no per-slot tags: `rt_dict_get_tagged` answered tag 0,
which the printer reads as "int", and the number it printed was the value's `@str_tab` index. The bound form
had always printed `two`, because in the print door the kind roads (`dictValStr`, `listElemStr`, …) run before
the tagged read. So the hoist goes above **every** subscript arm of that door, not above some of them. "Read
it the way a variable is read" is a claim about order as much as about code; if a reader can tell the answer
from the variable by its output, the row is not done.

### A notebook is a claim about bytes, and a tagged object has no single kind

The stubborn one was `def words(): return ["hi", "ho"]` / `print(words()[1])`, which refused with Gap R.82's
"this context needs a single static kind" while `print(words())` printed `['hi', 'ho']` correctly and
`xs = ["hi", "ho"]` / `print(xs[1])` printed `ho`. Three facts localised it: the whole-container printer asks
`mixedLists` **before** the notebooks (so it was unaffected); the slot read asks the notebooks first, and
`listElemStr` was set; and the object was built **tagged**. A container whose slots describe themselves has no
single kind — `heapDictFrom`/`heapSetFrom` have always cleared the notebooks when they set the tag bit, and the
list builder has no variable in hand, so nobody had ever done it for the answer. Clearing on
`mixedLists[name]` made the slot print `ho`. The mistake that hid it was mine: I had "proved" the clearing did
not work by running a probe script that still pointed at the previous binary. Whenever a fix appears to do
nothing, check the artifact under test before checking the reasoning — a false negative here costs a whole
wrong design decision, not a re-run.

### Do not widen a door onto a road that is broken for everybody

The same judgement covers `Index` and `Slice`, and I wrote both, then deleted the slice arm. `print(b()[0:2])`
refused after the deletion, and that is the decision: the slice road answers `[1, 0]` for
`[1.5, "a", [7]]`, and `zs = ys[0:2]` / `print(zs)` answers `1` for `[1, 2, 3]` — at **exit 0**, for a literal,
a variable, a comprehension and an answer alike. Widening the rewrite would have converted one honest refusal
at exit 1 into two more silently-wrong programs at exit 0, which is moving a defect *down* the contract's
ranking while calling it a fix. The filed rows (Gap R.230 for the slice's dropped tags, R.229 for the answer at
that door) now carry the ordering: fix the slice road's tags first, and the subscript's `*Slice` arm lands with
its two test rows already written. The general form: when a door is missing, measure what the road on the other
side answers for **every** base before opening it — a refusal is sometimes the best thing that road can do today.

### Three things that only existed on paper, caught by re-measuring

- A raise row I had copied from a probe file claimed `{0: "zero"}` / `print(f()[0])` raises `KeyError: 0`.
  CPython answers `zero`; the row asserted the wrong thing, and only running the reference caught it. Parity
  expectations get derived from CPython or they do not go in.
- `print(words()[0] in words())` looked like a nice extra matrix line until the CLI refused it with
  `testing &{%!s(*lang.Call=&{0x4000…}) …} against the container "__cans10" …` — a refusal that prints a Go
  struct dump and a compiler temp name instead of the construct. Filed as Gap R.232, with the sentence's honesty
  as half of the row: a refusal is an interface, and an agent scrapes it as noise.
- The conformance corpus is not free: adding `programs/container_subscript.gy` broke
  `TestGCCorpusCollectsAndAgrees`, because every corpus program must have a record (`HasGoldenAnswer`). New
  program ⇒ new records, in the same commit. The same cycle bit me twice on CLI shapes I trusted —
  `--emit-llvm --file x` parses `--file` as a name, and `except IndexError as e:` does not parse at all, so a
  "trap" row in a test table can be a parse error wearing a costume.

### The tracker's shape is part of the feature

Five rows I had filed in the last two cycles (`26m`–`26q`) had **no Status cell** — the row's text sat in the
