Status column, so any reader or agent parsing the queue read "L11.1 (the tag a call hands back)" as the status.
They are fixed to carry ⏳ `PLANNED`, and the new rows this cycle filed (R.230/R.231/R.232) were shape-checked
before committing. `TestTheRoadmapsCitationsResolve` then caught my own evidence cell citing
`constant_trap_test.go::TestTheCallResultStillRefuses` — a test this very commit deletes. A citation to a case
that no longer exists is worse than no citation: it tells the next reader the claim is checked when nothing
checks it. Reworded to name the raise row that answers today.

## A copy is a container: the slice door copies slots, not words (L11.1, Gap R.230; ADR 0335; Gaps R.233, R.234, R.235 filed)

**Feature (codegen)**: `xs = [1.5, "a", [7]]` / `print(xs[0:2])` printed `[1, 0]` and
`ys = xs[0:2]` / `print(ys)` printed `1` — both at **exit 0** — while `print(xs)` printed `[1.5, 'a']` one line
earlier. `rt_slice` copied seven i32s per slot and the tag was not one of them, because nothing had written the
tag: the road that turns a sliced literal into an object asked only `literalNeedsHeap`, the print road asked
only the base's single-kind notebook, and the binding road recorded nothing at all.

- **A "fix" that turns a refusal into an exit-0 answer has to be measured against the previous commit's
  binary, not against its own test table.** The first cut of this row made `print(m()["k"][0:1])` print `3`
  where `gustyc` at HEAD had refused with `index must be a constant`. Nothing in the new tables caught it —
  the row has no row for that shape, which is why the shape is a roadmap entry now (Gap R.235). The check that
  caught it was mechanical: keep `/tmp/gustyc-athead` beside the working build and diff both against CPython on
  a fixed probe file. A refusal that becomes a wrong number moved **down** the defect ranking.
- **The gate is not polish; it is half of the feature.** Once the road could build a copy, the temptation was
  to run on. `sliceBaseIsDescribed` is what made the difference between "the slice road answers correctly where
  it answers" and "the slice road never fabricates an answer": it retired a second exit-2 class
  (`call i32 @rt_slice(i32 @.set1, …)` — a compile-time global where `llc` wants an i32 register, for a set
  literal, a dict literal and a comprehension alike) and a second exit-0 class (`print(s[0:1])` over a set
  printing `[1]`). It is also a pure predicate over the records — no trial emission, no counters advanced, so
  IR-sensitive tests stay emission-order-independent (ADR 0273's rule).
- **A single-element slice is a fold, and folds hide roads.** `print(xs[0:1][0])` answered `1.5` while
  `print(xs[0:2][0])` refused: `[0:1]` collapses to a literal at compile time, so the subscript never reached
  the object road. A probe list built out of `[0:1]` slices therefore "proves" a slice door works when the two
  element case is broken. Probe with two slots, or don't probe.
- **Docs can carry a claim a year after the code stopped being true.** `docs/language.md` had said since ADR
  0294 that the compiled copy takes "payload and tag together". It did not: the sentence described the runtime
  helper's contract, not the compiler's use of it. The section is now measured prose — what answers, what
  refuses, what the reference raises, each with its Gap row — and the stale `len(...) of a slice still refuses`
  line went out with it (`print(len(xs[0:2]))`, `print(len(b()[0:2]))` and a bound copy all answer `2`).
- **Three roads, one question, asked of whoever wrote the bytes.** The print arm, the build site and the
  binding all ask the *same* predicate (`literalNeedsHeap || literalNeedsTags || literalHasPairElement`,
  `containerAnswerCarriesTags`, `mixedLists`) rather than restating it — ADR 0232's rule, and the reason
  `print(xs[0:2])` and `print(xs)` cannot disagree again. Where the tag question cannot be answered, the copy is
  refused; where it can, `rt_print_list_mixed` is picked — and the untagged control (`[1, 2, 3]` sliced, printed
  by `rt_print_list`) is in both packages, because a row that tags every copy has simply not asked.
- **Machine bookkeeping that bites**: `go run ./tools/recmerge -sources FILE.json` is the only way to add record
  entries (no dedupe mode; a second key for the same source is invisible to it) — and never run it while the
  suite runs, or `TestTheRecordHasNoSourceSpelledTwice` fails on a race that is not a defect. The conformance
  matrix rewrites itself the first time a matrix test asks for it, so the snapshot's counts (now 199 programs,
  188 rows → 150 parity + 38 divergences, 135 oracle `match`, 6455 records, 327 ADRs highest `0335`, 116 of 151
  rows owed) are read off the artifact after the run rather than guessed before it.

### A correction on the same row: an oracle column is a citation, and citations get verified

`Gap R.234` as first filed said the reference answers `print({1: 2}[0:1])` with
`TypeError: unhashable type: 'slice'`. It does not: it answers **`KeyError: slice(0, 1, None)`** — a slice whose
bounds are integers is hashable, so the dict hashes it, finds no entry, and names the key it missed, exactly as
it would for any other absent key. Only the **set** shapes raise the `TypeError` (`'set' object is not
subscriptable`). The sentence came from a probe file written from memory rather than from `python3` on the row
being quoted, and it had propagated into five places by the time the measurement was made: the roadmap row's
item cell and its fix cell, the details section's code block and its prose, ADR 0335's filed table, its
"alternatives rejected" bullet, and the two `oracle` columns in the pkg/lang filed rows.

- **An oracle column is the reference's words, not the row's paraphrase.** Same rule as an expectation file: run
  the row, paste the line. The `oracle` column of a filed row is the only place a reader (or an agent) will look
  for what the shape owes, and it is not asserted by any test — the filed rows assert *this* backend's behaviour
  and quote the reference for the reader.
- **A single sentence can hide a class split.** "The reference raises `TypeError` naming the type" covered four
  shapes and was true of two of them; the row's fix cell told the next reader to raise one sentence where two are
  owed, one of them from a different door (the hashing door's `KeyError`, Gap R.217's neighbourhood). The
  corrected row now names both, and the raise table that eventually lands must carry four rows, not two.

## A bound is asked what it is: the slice door's three handles (L11.4, Gap R.233; ADR 0336; Gaps R.236, R.237, R.238 filed)

**Feature (codegen)**: `print(xs["a":"b"])` answered `[1]`, `print(xs[1.5:2])` answered `[2]`,
`print(s["a":"b"])` over `"abcd"` answered `b` — all at **exit 0** — and `print(xs[[0]:2])` was an **exit 2**.
The same door that ADR 0335 had just fixed took seven i32s and never asked what three of them held. The mirror
half was worse to look at: `None` is a bound the reference excuses, and the road set the presence flag beside the
word `None` lowers to, so `print(xs[None:None])` answered `[]` and `print(xs[::None])` was killed with the run.

- **The two halves of a missing question look like opposite bugs.** A text bound taken for a position invents a
  list; a `None` bound taken for a position deletes one. Both came from "the bound is an i32, and an i32 has no
  kind", and one file answers both — `sliceBoundIsAbsent` for the absence, `nonIntBoundTypeName` + `badSliceBoundGate`
  for the kind — because splitting them would have produced a row that raises on `"a"` and still prints `[]` for
  `None`, which is the same hole with a nicer message.
- **Ask the kind before anything is lowered, and the exit-2 class goes with it.** Gap R.222's lesson re-paid: a
  container-valued bound reaches `rt_slice`'s i32 argument as a `@.lstN` global address, `llc` rejects the module,
  and the toolchain exits 2 on a two-line program. A gate that emits the raise and reopens its block never lowers
  the offending expression, so the invalid instruction is never written — asserted by checking the emitted module
  for the absence of `@rt_slice(` on a bad-bound program, not only by the exit code.
- **The order of two gates is the reference's order, not the compiler's convenience.** ADR 0336's bounds gate runs
  **after** ADR 0335's base gate, because `print({1, 2}["a":"b"])` is a complaint about a set in CPython, and a
  toolchain that answers "your bound is not an integer" first is describing a program the reader did not write.
  The same reasoning decided the print-road rewrite order in ADR 0334; it is worth naming as a rule, because both
  times it looked like an implementation detail.
- **A gate's silence is a decision with a price on it, so price it in the tracker.** A bound whose kind travels as
  a *tag* — `ys[0]`, or a call handing back a text — still answers `[1, 2]` at exit 0. The alternative (raise when
  the compiler cannot tell) turns `xs[k:2]` with `k = 1` into a coin flip, because the notebooks are not complete.
  So the row keeps the silence and files **Gap R.237** naming the road that can see the pair
  (`runtimeSlotPairDeep`), beside **Gap R.82** and **Gap R.146** where the same one-word position is already
  priced.
- **Two more wrong answers turned up in the row's own blast radius, and both were filed rather than folded in**: a
  **step of zero** hangs `rt_slice`'s loop and the killed run comes out as exit 2 with nothing on either stream
  (**R.236** — the only exit-2 shape left on the door, which is why it leads its family in the queue), and a slice
  **returned** from a function answers one word — `print(n())` prints `1` where `ys = n()` prints the list, because
  the scan that classifies a `return` has no arm for a slice (**R.238**, ADR 0333 one construct further out).
  Bundling either would have hidden a second wrong-answer class inside a row about kinds.
- **Test rows are claims, and a claim copied from the tool is not a claim.** Two of my hand-written rows were
  wrong against CPython (`xs[None:2]` of a two-element list is `[1, 2]`, not `[1]`) and the parity leg failed them
  before anything was recorded; `recmerge` refused a third outright (`def n(k): return xs[1:k]` answers `1` here,
  `[2, 3]` there), which is how **R.238** was found — a refusing recorder is a measurement, not an obstacle.

## The conformance program is a measurement engine, not a celebration (L11.4, Gap R.233; ADR 0336; Gaps R.239, R.240, R.241 filed)

The row's behaviour landed green in one build (`/tmp/gustyc-r233`): 27 answered shapes, 28 raise rows, the catchable
rows, the fold's control, the IR assertion. Writing `integration/programs/slice_bounds.gy` — one program, its stdout
compared line for line against `python3` — then failed four times and each failure was a **new defect**, not a bug in
this row:

- **A shape the program needs may not exist.** `tup = (1, 2)` is `codegen: unsupported expression *lang.Tuple` at
  exit 1, so the tuple-bound row cannot name its tuple; written inline — `print(xs[0:(1, 2)])` — it raises the
  reference's `TypeError` correctly. The lesson is not "tuples are broken" (they are on the roadmap) but that the
  *program* must be written in the subset the language answers, and the *test table* must say which spelling it means.
- **Two doors, one copy: `print([x * 2 for x in xs[0:2]])` refuses while `zs = xs[0:2]` then
  `print([x * 2 for x in zs])` answers `[2, 4]`** (**Gap R.239**). The same asymmetry this cycle made illegal for a
  subscript (ADR 0334) survives for a comprehension's iterable, because the door asks a literal, `range()`, or a
  recorded variable — and a `*Slice` node is none of those. Its refusal even speaks about texts ("the reference
  iterates a text one character at a time"), so the copy never reaches this row's own gate: a bad bound inside a
  comprehension is refused, not raised.
- **`len` of a slice of a text refuses with `len requires an inline list/dict/set literal`** (**Gap R.240**) while
  `len(s)` answers `4`, `len(xs[0:2])` answers `2`, and the fold that prints `s[1:3]` holds the count. Three doors
  own the fact; the fourth names a literal that is nowhere in the program — ADR 0249 again, a refusal whose sentence
  describes a different shape.
- **An `except` arm that *calls* a user function takes the run down with the exception it already handled**
  (**Gap R.241**): the arm prints, the traceback prints, the statement after the `try` never runs, exit 3 — and the
  same arm with `print` in it exits 0. That pair *is* the diagnosis: every user call ends its own block with the
  post-call check on the module-wide `@exn_flag`, and ADR 0218 put `clearExn` on the edges **out** of an arm, never on
  the edge **into** one. It reproduces with a plain `print(xs[9])`, so it is filed as the exception road's and not
  smuggled into a row about slices — and `docs/language.md`'s ADR 0218 bullet, which claimed the shape away, was
  re-measured and corrected in the same commit.
- **A conformance program asserts only its own row's doors.** Each of the four above is absent from
  `programs/slice_bounds.gy` and present in a filed table with the reference's answer beside what the toolchain says
  today; the program is `match` on both legs, and the refusals stay visible instead of being laundered into it.
- **A roadmap row label is a machine-read field.** The Open queue's Pri cell must match `^[0-9]+[a-z]?$`
  (`roadmap_snapshot_test.go`'s `queuePri`): a 27th row in the `26…` family cannot be `26aa`, and the failure mode is
  spectacular rather than quiet — `TestTheRoadmapSnapshotIsMeasuredNotRemembered` stopped seeing the rows after the
  first one and reported "32 of 45 queue rows" for a 157-row queue. New rows take a fresh numeric label and sit
  physically beside their family (`130/131/132` here).
- **The parser has no `except <Type> as e:`** (Gap R.113, open since 2026-10-02), so a catchable row can assert
  `except TypeError:` and `except:` but not a named exception object. Where a row wants the name, the row is the
  parser's.

## The row that could not be witnessed was the worst one in the family (L11.4, Gap R.236; ADR 0337; Gaps R.242, R.243 filed)

`print(xs[::0])` did not answer, did not refuse and did not raise. `rt_slice` walked `for (i = low; i != high; i +=
step)` with `step = 0`, the index never moved, the harness's budget expired, and the CLI came back with **exit 2** —
the code ADR 0166 reserves for a *compiler* bug — with nothing on either stream. Its neighbours answered `[]` at exit
0 (`xs[0:2:0]`: the bounds stopped the loop the stride never moved) and refused (`print("abcd"[::0])`: `cannot fold
string slice`). One program, three behaviours, and the reference's one `ValueError: slice step cannot be zero` for all
three.

- **A defect the suite cannot assert is a lead, not a nuisance.** Gap R.236 sat in the filed tables as a *note*
  because a killed run returns nothing to compare — which is exactly why it ranked above the rows that did have
  expectations. The closure's first job was to make it assertable: raise, and the row becomes 19 rows of class and
  message with exit 2 forbidden.
- **Three behaviours to one question means the question is missing.** The kind gate (ADR 0336) could not have caught
  this: `0` is a perfectly good integer. `ValueError` and `TypeError`, two messages, two DoDs — the value question
  shares the file and the call site, never the predicate.
- **Split the fix by what the compiler can read, and make the negative control a row.** A step read as zero raises
  with no `@rt_slice(` and no counter advanced (ADR 0273's purity — a gate that bumps `heapSeq` on its way out is a
  gate with a side effect); a step it cannot read carries `icmp eq i32 %step, 0` beside the call; a step read as
  anything else emits **nothing**. `TestTheZeroStepGuardIsInTheModuleWhereTheValueIs` asserts all three shapes, and
  the third one is the row that fails if someone "simplifies" the guard into an unconditional tax on every
  `xs[::2]`.
- **The trap stays in codegen.** A helper that raised would own exception state the codegen cannot see and hand back
  an uncatchable trap (ADR 0214 — `except ValueError:` is language surface); a helper that treated a zero step as 1
  would have printed `[1, 2]` where the reference raises, which is the worst trade this contract knows — a wrong value
  at exit 0 dressed up as a fix. `rt_slice`'s signature and body are unchanged; the guard rides beside it, after the
  bounds are evaluated, because that is where the value is *and* the order the reference raises in.
- **The house style was hiding a priority-1 defect.** Measuring the zero step with no spaces (`xs[::0]` needs none)
  found that the lexer emits `-1` as a single token whenever a minus is followed by a digit, with no question about
  the previous token — so `y = x-1` parses as `y = x` plus an expression statement `-1` and **answers `x` at exit 0**,
  while `print(1-1)`, `print(x-1)`, `print(len(xs)-1)` and `for i in range(3-1):` are parse errors. `print(2- 3)` is
  right, and `print(x - 1)` is right: every program in this repository writes the spaced form, so a fully green suite
  had never seen it (the ADR 0187/ADR 0232 lesson for the third time — a defect survives in the one spelling nobody
  writes). Filed as **Gap R.242** with the twelve-row table, and its closure owes the **token stream** both ways, not
  just the rendered answer, because "the tests pass" is what the spaced spelling has been saying all along.
- **A refusal can be the honest remainder of a fix, if it is named.** ADR 0337 answers the zero step on the road that
  can stride and leaves `s[::k]` refusing — `rt_str_slice` has no stride argument — as **Gap R.243**, with the
  code-point rule (L11.5) written into its fix cell so the next cycle cannot "just add a step parameter" and make
  `"café"[::2]` count bytes.
- **The recorder keeps being the best oracle.** `recmerge` cross-checks the compiled leg against CPython and refused
  nothing this time — five sources went in (four answered stride shapes and the grown conformance program), record
  6484 — and the program still asserts only its own row's doors: no comprehension over a copy, no `len` of a text
  slice, no call in an `except` arm, no user-call in the handler that Gap R.241 makes fatal.

## The most ordinary arithmetic in the language was wrong, silently, in the one spelling nobody writes (L11.2 lexer surface, Gap R.242; ADR 0338; Gap R.244 filed)

```
x = 5
y = x-1
print(y)      # CPython: 4 — this toolchain: 5, exit 0, nothing on stderr
print(1-1)    # CPython: 0 — this toolchain: parse error at 1:8: expected ")"
```

`case c == '-' && i+1 < n && unicode.IsDigit(rune(src[i+1]))` read `-1` as one integer wherever a minus was followed
by a digit, never asking what came *before* it. `y = x-1` therefore was `y = x` and an expression statement `-1`: the
subtraction was not mis-evaluated, it was never parsed, and the program printed the value the subtraction never
produced. The other face — `print(1-1)`, `print(x-1)`, `print(len(xs)-1)`, `print(xs[2-1])`, `print(3.5-1)`,
`for i in range(3-1):`, `def g(n): return n-1` — was refused by the parser. `x - 1` was right. That space is why a
green suite had never seen it (the ADR 0187 / ADR 0232 / Gap R.236 lesson, now for the fourth time).

- **A wrong answer is a *token boundary* before it is a wrong output, so the tests had to be written at that
  altitude.** `INT:-1` beside `OP:- INT:1` is the entire difference between `5` and `4`. Thirty-one rendered token
  streams (both halves of the rule), the predicate on its own over 19 hand-built streams, and — the assertion that
  actually pins the defect — the parse: `y = x-1` is **one** statement whose value is a `*BinOp`, and `x = -1` is one
  statement whose value is an `*IntLit` of `-1`, not a `*UnOp` the parser rebuilt. That last half is what rejects the
  tempting "just lex a bare `-` always" fix, which answers the arithmetic and moves every index, key, default and
  `print(-1)` in the corpus.
- **A negative control earns its keep only if it can fail both ways.** Deleting the context check fails 17 of the
  token-stream rows (measured, not asserted); always splitting fails the sign rows; and the IR row requires `sub i32`
  in `@main`/`@gy_*` for four programs and its **absence** for four sign programs — the module for `y = x-1` held no
  arithmetic at all before the row, so that assertion is the defect's own shape in the emitted code, not a proxy.
- **"Every keyword begins a sign position" is wrong in exactly three keywords.** `True`, `False` and `None` are
  `TokKeyword` and they END an expression, so `print(True-1)` must be arithmetic (the reference answers `0`) and not a
  stray `-1`; every other keyword — `return`, `in`, `else`, `not` — begins one, which is what keeps `return -1` a
  literal. And the homoglyph path appends a `TokWarning` *after* an identifier, so a rule that reads the previous
  token has to skip the notes that are not part of the program.
- **The record is not a safety net for spellings nobody writes.** Eight recorded sources contain an `X-N` pair; all
  eight hold it inside a text or a comment (`print(int("-7"))`, `"-42".zfill(4)`), none changes answer, and no
  conformance program contained an unspaced subtraction. A priority-1 defect with 6 484 recorded programs and a
  200-program matrix had literally zero coverage of it — so the fix recorded 56 newly answered programs plus the new
  `programs/minus_operator.gy` (record 6541, programs 201, matrix 190 rows / 152 parity / 0 fail / oracle 137 `match`).
- **An IR assertion must know whose code it is reading.** The runtime's own helpers contain `sub i32` (`rt_str_index`
  counts backwards), so the first version of the IR row passed on the *negative* controls for the wrong reason; the
  file now extracts `@main` and the program's own `@gy_*` functions and nothing else. Same lesson as `cliMainBody`:
  a whole-module substring match on a module that ships the runtime attached asserts almost nothing.
- **Filed, not folded in.** `print(+1)` is refused (`unexpected token`) where CPython prints `1` — the grammar has no
  unary plus at all, and the number rule was not the parser's to fix: **Gap R.244**, with `+1.5`/`+True`/`-+1`/`x-+1`
  measured and cited. The comprehension over a list the compiler kept static still refuses, and that door belongs to
  L11.1/L11.2 (ADR 0192); pinning it here means the day either road grows an answer, the row fails and moves.
- **CLI trivia worth remembering:** `--emit-llvm` takes a *filename*, not a switch — `gustyc --emit-llvm --file p.gy`
  reads as `--emit-llvm "-file"` and reports `undefined name "file"`. IR assertions in tests go through
  `lang.Compile(src).IR`, which is the machine path anyway (ADR 0166's sibling: the IR is an artifact, not a stdout
  side effect).

## A citation is a claim about a file you have not just read (Gap R.245 filed; the correction of two claims in ADR 0338)

Before pushing ADR 0338, two of its sentences were checked against the source and both were wrong.

- It cited "roadmap **L11.2/Gap N.4** wants `.5`". `L11.2` is *"`str()` vs `repr()` are one pair per backend"*
  (`✅ DONE`), and there is no `Gap N.4` anywhere in the tracker. The construct was real, the row was invented.
- Its test table claimed `print(-.5)` lexes as one `FLOAT:-.5`. It does not: the merge rule requires a **digit**
  after the minus, and a `.` is not one, so the stream is `OP:- OP:. INT:5`. The row was written from a guess about
  the rule rather than from the rule.

The fix was not to soften the prose. `-` followed by `.` is a token stream, and `print(.5)` is a program: measured
against CPython (`0.5`, `1.5`, `-0.5`, `1.0`, and `x = .5` → `0.5`, all refused here at exit 1), it is a defect nobody
had filed — `Gap R.135` owns only the exponent marker — so it became a fresh row (**Gap R.245**) with a fresh ID, a
section in `docs/roadmap-details.md`, a paragraph in `docs/language.md`, and a pin in `pkg/lang/lexer_test.go` that
asserts the **token stream** of the refusal and the parse's refusal, with the reference's answer written beside each
row as a citation. One of those rows is the fix's own negative control: `obj.5` must stay a refusal, because the
reference gives it an `AttributeError` and a leading-`.` case that enters after a name would turn a refusal into a
wrong answer.

- **The rule generalises:** any ADR or roadmap cell that names an ID, a file, a line or a token is a claim that can
  be *read*, so read it before pushing. `grep -n "L11\.2" roadmap.md` costs nothing and returns a sentence that makes
  the citation false. An invented ID is worse than a missing one, because item IDs are permanent and something will
  eventually go looking for this one.
- **A refusal row is worth as much instrumentation as an answer row.** The `.5` defect had no probe, no matrix row
  and no test; three `Lex` dumps and one `Parse` gave it all four in a minute, and now the day someone grows the case
  the pin fails and the row moves instead of the defect being fixed in an unlogged commit.
- **Check the neighbour before borrowing its row.** `Gap R.135` (the exponent marker) is the same function and the
  same family, and it was tempting to widen it. It is a separate row because the exponent needs a marker *after* a
  fraction and this needs an entry condition *before* one — and because a fresh ID is what makes the two fixable
  independently.

## The loop had three roads and no question: an un-nameable container read as a repeat count (L11.1, Gap R.246; ADR 0339; Gaps R.247–R.253 filed)

`for v in sorted(xs)` reached `llc` as `%t1 = icmp slt i32 %_ctr1.ld1, @.lst1` — *global variable reference must
have pointer type*, exit 2, ADR 0166's bug class, on the most ordinary loop in the language. Five programs of that
shape, all five answered by CPython with `1 2 3`. The same five with a **literal** instead of a name did not crash,
and that is the one that should keep the lesson: `for v in sorted([3, 1, 2][0:2])` printed `0` at exit 0 (CPython:
`1`, `3`), and `for v in sorted(["b", "a"])`, `for v in reversed("abc")`, `for v in sorted(b())` printed **nothing
at exit 0** — the loop bound its variable to the counter, and the body dutifully printed whatever the counter's
word was. The `sorted` builtin had been correct the whole time (`print(sorted([3, 1, 2]))` answers `[1, 2, 3]`);
`case *ForStmt:` had three roads — unrolled literal, runtime container, numeric counter — and asked no question in
front of them, so anything the first two would not claim fell to the third, which asks the iterable for a *bound*.
A container's word is a global's address. Given a literal, the comparison succeeds and the program lies.

- **A fall-through road is the defect, not the missing arm.** The fix's most useful line is not the fold, it is the
  guard immediately *above* the counter road: a container that neither door claims is refused, naming the half that
  is missing. Deleting the guard fails the refused table and fails **nothing** in the answered table — which is the
  mutation test that proves the guard is a refusal and not an accidental source of values.
- **An AST-level fold must run before the rewriter that names things.** `case *ForStmt:` opened with
  `containerAnswerOperand(n.Iter)`, whose job is to turn a container-returning call into a fresh `__cansN` name —
  so by the time the case asked "what is this iterable?", `sorted([3,1,2])` was a *name* and both the literal fold
  and the builtin-name roads were unreachable. The three questions now run fold → materialise → name, in that
  order. Any road that rewrites the AST before a later road classifies it is a question taken away from that road.
- **A dispatch arm must not claim a shape it has not answered.** The container road's `*Call` arm matched *every*
  call and then did something only for generators; a non-generator call got nothing and fell through. Narrowing it
  to `forIterCallIsGenerator` let the handle road see the call at all. An `else`-less arm that matches a type and
  answers a subset is a silent sink.
- **Count the whole family before widening a shared predicate — and believe the regression, not the design.** The
  first version added `sorted`/`reversed` arms to `isContainerExpr`, `staticContainerKind` **and**
  `containerHandleOf`, on the "these are a pair" reading. It made `print(1 in sorted(xs))` — which answers `True`
  today — *refuse*, because the membership road asks the first question and then reaches for `containerOperand`,
  the fourth member nobody counted. Turning a working answer into a refusal is the one regression ADR 0233
  forbids, so the arms came out entirely, the row is local to the loop's own case, and the widening is
  **Gap R.253** with this measurement as its evidence. Before widening a predicate, list every road that asks it.
- **Naming beats handing over a handle, when the consumer keeps a notebook.** Routing the runtime copy through the
  generic `containerHandleOf` arm made the iteration *tagged*, and the tag stuck to the loop variable for the rest
  of the function: `for v in sorted(words)` then `for v in [7, 8]` printed `(null)`, and the same name used as a
  number met Gap R.146's sentence. Materialising the copy into a rooted `__srtN` slot, recording its element kind
  in the same notebooks an `xs = [...]` assignment fills, and walking the list-variable road is both simpler and
  the road ADR 0323 already made correct.
- **A loop variable's kind claim belongs to the loop that made it.** The container road set
  `g.internedVars[loopVar]` for a text iterable and nothing ever removed it, so `for v in words` (text) followed by
  `for v in xs` (numbers) printed `b`, `a`, `a`, `(null)` for CPython's `b`, `a`, `1`, `2`, and `for v in range(2)`
  after a text loop printed the *string table*. Two silent wrongs, both measured on this row's own first draft,
  both caught by the negative-control table rather than by a new test. Every road that binds a loop variable now
  either claims or clears the name — a counter is a number under no reading.
- **Zero matrix coverage is how a no-op survives.** A sorted literal in a loop position had no probe, no matrix row
  and no record entry, so the road that silently ignored `sorted` printed the record's own answer at exit 0 for as
  long as it liked: the record is a witness cut from the compiler being tested. 50 newly recorded sources and an
  89-line conformance program (`programs/for_iterables.gy`, generated from `/usr/bin/python3` and compared
  line-for-line) is what it cost to make that class unfree.
- **Rebuild before believing a failure — and grep the binary, do not `strings` it.** The first "the fix does nothing"
  reading was a stale `/tmp/gustyc-*` binary. `strings` on the rebuilt binary came back empty for a sentence that
  was verifiably in the source; `grep -a` found it. A tool that silently finds nothing is worse than a failing test,
  because it converts a build mistake into a design conclusion.
- **Two ADRs of one number, and six invented links in one header.** `docs/adr/` held a draft 0339 from earlier in
  the session beside the one being written now; `ls docs/adr | grep ^0339` catches that in one command. The retained
  draft's header linked six files that do not exist (`0249-a-refusal-names-what-is-missing-or-it-is-a-bug.md`,
  `0262-a-fold-and-a-renderer-must-not-move-apart.md`, `0273-a-gate-is-pure-…`, `0302-the-ast-interpreter-is-retired-…`,
  `0333-a-container-returned-from-a-function-is-a-named-thing.md`, `0196-the-for-loop-binds-its-variable-…`) and cited
  ADR 0117 for the integer repeat count, which is ADR **0207**. The whole header is now checked mechanically —
  extract every `(0NNN-…md)` link, `[ -f docs/adr/$f ]` — which is cheaper than being right, and returns a list
  instead of an apology. Real titles also disagree with in-code shorthand (`0249` is a slot-read question, `0233` is
  the implemented/refused/absent rule); the ADR file is what a reader can verify, so the ADR cites the real ones.
- **A refusal is only honest if the two doors' refusals are distinguishable.** The builtin refuses `key=` at its own
  door and the loop refuses an unwalkable iterable at its own; the CLI test therefore always requires `roadmap
  L11.1` and requires the loop's own markers (`ADR 0339`, `repeat count`) only when the sentence speaks as the loop.
  An agent that cannot tell which door refused cannot plan a workaround.

## The ordering builtins were reading options by position, not by name (L11.7, Gap R.249; ADR 0340; Gaps R.254–R.255 filed)

`print(sorted([3, 1, 2], key=abs))`, `print(sorted([3, 1, -2], key=abs, reverse=True))`,
`print(sorted([3, 1, 2], key=3))`, `print(min(3, 1, -2, key=abs))`, and
`print(min([3, 1, 2], key=abs))` were five faces of one parser: the ordering builtins took their *second slot*
as the reverse flag. The measured outcomes were not all refusals — some were the worst kind. The first refused
with a sentence about `reverse=`. The second printed a wrong order at exit 0. The third printed a descending
list where CPython raises `TypeError: 'int' object is not callable`. The fourth made `llc` reject the module
because `key=abs` had been lowered as if it were a candidate (`use of undefined value '%_abs'`). The fifth
refused because `key=abs` had been added to `min`'s candidate list and then read as a container.

- **Named options are not positional candidates.** `key=` and `reverse=` have to be read by name before any
  road lowers an argument. A positional parser turns the reference's TypeError into an answer, and it turns an
  option into an operand. The fix reads `pos, key, reverse, badKw` first; only then does the unkeyed road get
  its old documented repeat flag. The reference's `min` and `max` reject `reverse=` outright, and now the
  compiled backend does the same — as a raise, not a guess.
- **A callable argument should travel the ordinary call road, not a new builtin callback.** A key is just
  `key(element)`. Synthesising `Call{Fn: key, Args: [element]}` and lowering it with `g.value` reuses arity,
  default parameters, raises inside the callee, builtin behaviour, and the same IR the program could have
  written by hand. A separate ordering callback would have duplicated all of that and disagreed with ordinary
  calls the first time a callee raised.
- **A compile-time TypeError can be a wrong answer when the expression has effects.** `key=3` has no effect,
  so emitting the reference's raise is correct. `key=print(1)` is not — CPython must run `print(1)` first, then
  try to call `None`. The first draft inferred call-expression key results and statically raised, skipping the
  side effect. The honest answer is a refusal naming call-expression keys until the value word can carry and
  call their answers; it is filed as **Gap R.255**.
- **A tag is not the same question as a container's kind.** `key=xs` had to say `'list' object is not callable`,
  not `'int' object is not callable`. Asking only the element tag answered the list's element kind; asking only
  the notebooks missed constants. `keyWordKind` asks the same pair door other positions use, so the TypeError
  names the value the program actually wrote.
- **Stable order needs a rank, and rank placement needs the slot writer that does not own length.** The keyed
  road counts `#{ keys before mine } + #{ earlier equal keys }`, using `@rt_elem_gt` and flipping the two sides
  of the comparator for descending. The first placement used `@rt_set_elem`; that call bumps length, so sorting
  three elements produced six slots and `print` wrote `[1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0]`. The append call owns length;
  placement should use `@rt_put_elem`. Structural tests now assert `@rt_alloc`/`@rt_append_tagged`/`@rt_put_elem`
  and that a keyed module never *calls* `@rt_sort` (the runtime text may still define it for unkeyed roads).
- **Runtime gates must ask the same question from both halves.** Keyed `min` emits calls into heap-runtime
  helpers but allocates no heap object of its own, so `heapUsed` alone left the root globals data half out while
  the pulled runtime block referenced `@gc.kinds`. The emitted module failed with an undefined `@gc.kinds`. The
  gate now reads `needHeap` as well as `heapUsed`/`rooted`; this was found by a JIT run, not by a unit-only test.
- **A test that greps for a helper name must distinguish a definition from a call.** `strings.Contains(mod,
  "@rt_sort(")` failed because the runtime block legitimately defines `@rt_sort` even when the keyed road does
  not call it. The structural witness now matches a call instruction (`call ... @rt_sort(`), not the definition.
- **Table tests must not accidentally pin pre-existing debts as this row's promises.** Two rows thought to be
  unkeyed negative controls were old unrelated refusals/wrongs: `min(xs)` over a heap list is **Gap R.107**, and
  `print(reversed([1,2,3]))` answering its argument unreversed is **Gap R.251**. They were removed from the new
  row's answered tables and left in their own rows. A new feature commit may measure neighbors, but it may not
  inherit their promises.
- **Record what the reference answers, not what the table wants.** `tools/recmerge` refused the documented
  gusty-only positional repeat flag because CPython itself rejects a second positional argument to `sorted`;
  that row belongs to a CLI leg comparing compiled legs only. The keyed sources the reference answers moved to
  the record (6591 → 6665 for the family), while the refused key shapes remain in the refusal tables and cannot
  acquire records.

## A name's container kind was decided by six roads, none of them the binding that took the name over (L11.1, Gap Q.1; ADR 0341; Gaps R.256–R.257 filed)

`d = {1: 10}` then `d = [3, 4]` is two programs to the object and one program to the reader. The assignment
freed the dict, built a list, stored the handle — and the read asked a notebook the compiler had kept by
*name*. `print(d)` wrote `{3: 4, 0: 0}` and `print(d[0])` wrote `0`, both at exit 0; `print(d[1])` died
`KeyError: 1` where CPython prints `4`; `d.append(9)` grew a dict; `d.sort()` printed `{1: 2, 3: 0, 0: 0}`;
and `d = {1: "x"}` then `d = [2, 3]` handed `llc` a module it rejected. The asymmetry was the diagnosis:
`xs = [1,2]` then `xs = {1: 10}` answered, because the dict road happens to clear its two neighbours, while
the **list-literal road cleared nothing at all**. Six roads, fourteen claims — three kind bits, three "my slots
describe themselves" bits (`mixedLists`/`mixedDicts`/`mixedSets`) and eight element-kind notebooks
(`listElemStr`/`Int`, `setElemStr`/`Int`, `dictKeyStr`/`Int`, `dictValStr`/`Int`).

- **When a family looks symmetric, measure both directions before believing any of it.** "Rebinding works"
  was true in one direction and false in the other, and every prior green test had been written in the
  direction that worked. The row is six transitions × the read doors, not one program.
- **A door that clears everything is a broom, and the suite tells you so.** The first draft of
  `settleContainerKind` deleted every claim for the name; `print(xs[0])` of a literal list went back to
  refusing, because ADR 0241's fold record — the thing that licenses a static slot read — is exactly a claim
  the binding *agrees* with. The rule became: clear what **disagrees** with the binding in hand, leave what
  it agrees with for the caller to re-record. The negative-control row (seed another name with claims, settle
  this one, assert the other is untouched) is what keeps a "clear the map" fix from ever passing again.
- **A notebook is a fact about an object, not about a name.** `xs = ["a"]` then `xs = [1, 2]` was refused as
  "a compiled list holds either strings or numbers, not both" — Gap J.6's sentence, spoken about a list that
  had been freed. `recordElemKind` consults the opposite notebook before recording, so a literal binding that
  rewrites every slot has to retire the record first. The literal sibling door answers `[1, 2]`; the sentence
  stays honest for a container that *grows* into a second kind, which is J.6's row.
- **The structural witness is the test an answer-level test cannot write.** Counting the reader calls
  (`readerHelpers`: `@rt_get_elem`, `@rt_list_len`, `@rt_print_list`, `@rt_contains_tagged`, `@rt_dict_get`,
  `@rt_dict_has`, `@rt_dict_has_tagged`, `@rt_dict_print`, `@rt_set_find`, `@rt_set_print` and their siblings)
  counted inside the program's own `@main`/`@gy_*` bodies, seven rebound/single pairs were different programs
  before the row and are the same program after. Before, measured: the dict→list pair called `@rt_dict_get` 1,
  `@rt_dict_has` 1, `@rt_dict_has_tagged` 1, `@rt_dict_print` 1 and never `@rt_print_list`/`@rt_contains_tagged`,
  where the list-only program called `@rt_print_list` 1, `@rt_get_elem` 2, `@rt_list_len` 3,
  `@rt_contains_tagged` 1; the text→number pair refused outright. The definition-vs-call lesson from
  ADR 0340 paid for itself immediately: the runtime block *defines* every one of those helpers and calls them
  from each other, so a whole-module grep witnesses nothing.
- **A probe harness against CPython must know the exit-code contract.** `d = {1: 10}` / `d = [3, 4]` /
  `print(d[9])` "disagreed" with the reference in the first sweep — the trap is exit **3** here and exit 1
  there (ADR 0166's classes). Comparing `returncode` equality, not exit *class*, turns every correct raise
  into a fake defect and trains the reader to ignore the sweep.
- **Probe shapes you were not planning to fix; they surface the neighbours.** The alias lines added for
  coverage (`b = a`, `b = [7, 8]`, `print(a[1])`) exposed a use-after-free: `emitFreeOld` is a *name*-level
  statement, and `b = a` had made two names one object. It is filed as **Gap R.257**, with the reference's
  answer written into the row, and pinned as a debt — not fixed here, because the fix belongs to the handle
  copy. The same program is where the row's own answer is visible: `print(b[0])` answered `0` before the
  door and `7` after it.
- **A heap bug that depends on free-list order is a worse bug, not a milder one.** The alias shape answered
  `2` in a four-line program (stale bytes nobody had overwritten) and died `KeyError: 1` in the seven-statement
  program the debt row pins, where an earlier rebinding had put the freed slot up for reuse. Same object, same
  read, opposite verdicts — the difference is allocator history. A "works in the minimal case" check is not
  evidence for anything about a heap, and the row therefore pins the *longer* program.
- **The conformance corpus is a claim about what answers, so unrelated defects come out of it.** The alias
  read was removed from `programs/rebound_container_kind.gy` (it would have made a `match` row impossible)
  and moved into the filed-not-fixed tables with the reference's answer beside it. `tools/recmerge` also
  aborts on the first program the compiled leg refuses, so owed shapes — `max(d)` over a variable is
  **Gap R.107**, a set asked for a position is the newly filed **Gap R.256** — have to be filtered out of the
  sources file before recording, not after.
- **Ask the tables, not only the programs — that is where the stale bit was.** The door's first draft cleared
  the two rival kinds' "my slots describe themselves" bits and left the bound kind's own. `sealTheDeal` looked
  right — the door's own comment said "leave what the binding agrees with for the caller to re-record" —
  until the gate table seeded all
  fourteen claims and printed the survivors: a name that had been a mixed list and was rebound to a
  homogeneous literal kept `mixedLists` standing, because every road that builds an object writes that bit
  only in the branch where slots carry tags and **none of them writes `false`**. `xs = [1, "a"]` then
  `xs = [1, 2]` was printing CPython's answer through the per-slot-tag readers over tags nobody wrote. The
  three mixed bits are now cleared unconditionally; the element notebooks of the kind being bound are not, and
  the difference is exactly which claims a caller re-records. A program-level test cannot see either half —
  the answer is right in both — so the table, asked as a function, is what witnesses it.
- **A probe table measured against a stale binary is a fabricated table.** Twice in this row a `/tmp/gc-*`
  build misled the sweep: once it showed a defect (`xs = ["a"]` / `xs = [1, 2]` refusing Gap J.6's sentence)
  that the current tree does not have, and once it showed the *fix* not working. The rule that fixes it is
  not "rebuild often" — it is **build the baseline from the commit, not from a timestamp**: `git worktree add
  /tmp/prereq HEAD --detach` and build there, so "before" is HEAD by construction and "after" is the working
  tree. The before/after table in ADR 0341 and in the roadmap row is that pair of binaries, and the corpus
  half of the sweep (203 of the 204 conformance programs answering identically; the 204th is this row's own,
  which the commit before refused) is the same two binaries asked of the whole corpus.
- **`go test`'s 10-minute default is not enough for this suite, and two runs in parallel make it worse.**
  Both `integration` and `pkg/lang` panicked at `test timed out after 10m0s` when a background full run
  overlapped a targeted one. Long runs get `-timeout 40m`, and one full suite runs at a time.

## The suite was serial because it shared a process, so the process stopped being shared (ADR 0343; Gap R.258 filed)

**Feature (harness / test execution)**: `make test` was **11 m 43 s** for 2,246 top-level cases and 646 subtests on
a 20-core box, and `tools/testshards`' own header explained why no case dared overlap another: the runner took
fd 1 and fd 2 with `dup2` around a program it `dlopen`ed into the test process. ADR 0343 moved that state out
instead of working around it. The same tree now runs in **about 1 m 40 s**.

- **The reason a suite is serial is a list of facts, not a mood.** Before touching anything the four kinds of
  shared state were written down: (1) the program ran *inside* the test process (`captureFD`'s fd surgery,
  `dlopen`/`dlmopen`, one `@heap` and one intern table per process); (2) per-run facts were process facts
  (`SetStdlibDir`, `SetGCReport`, the resolver's global stdlib root and `os.Getwd()`); (3) package-level caches
  with no lock (`bodyBindingCache`, `pairClosedOut`, `recmerge`'s retargeted `recordPath`); (4) cases that
  genuinely own the process (`t.Setenv`, toolchain-command overrides, the in-process entry). Each got its own
  answer — child process, per-run option, mutex or return value, `//parify:serial` marker — rather than one
  blanket "don't parallelise". A rationale you cannot enumerate is a rationale you cannot retire.
- **Running the program in a child is the whole fix, and it is cheap.** Link to an executable, `cmd.Start`,
  collect two pipes, honour the tool budget with a context. The in-process path stays for the one case that
  exists to test it (`JITOptions{InProcess: true}`), and `linkSOOrExecutable` keeps the shared-object shape that
  path needs (`-Wl,-u,pyre_main`, no `-e main`, no `--gc-sections`) — a `.so` has no entry point of its own, and
  `--gc-sections` deletes the global the child would call. A death by signal is now reported as the compiler's
  bug in ADR 0302's own words ("this is the artifact, not the program") instead of being absorbed.
- **A serial suite is a coverage hole, and this one swallowed a `SIGSEGV`.** `x = sorted([3, 1, 2], reverse=True)`
  followed by `x` dies in `@rt_alloc`: the binding writes the *tag* half of a (payload, tag) pair into the one-word
  slot that should hold the heap handle, so the next allocation reads its index back as `0xffff`. Under the old
  in-process engine the crash came back as an empty answer and the case continued. The moment cases could overlap
  it became a drift divergence with a name. Filed as **Gap R.258** with the record's answer beside the compiled
  one, and the crash reproduces standalone through `--file` and `--build`, so nothing about the runner caused it.
- **`t.Parallel()` is a claim, not a witness.** The first version of `tools/parify` only refused to *insert* into
  unsafe bodies; a case that already called `t.Parallel()` was reported "already marked" and skipped. The v2 rule
  is that an existing call is a claim the tool must be able to falsify: the same walk runs, and a case that says
  parallel while reaching process state is a `-check` **failure**. Both directions are asserted by
  `TestACaseThatSaysParallelAndTakesTheProcessAnywayIsAFailure` — violation must flag with the reason, and the
  clean case must not, so "the marker is there" can never be what makes a check pass.
- **Analyse the package, edit only the tests.** `recordFile` originally scanned just `_test.go`, so a case that
  assigned `recordPath` — declared in `main.go`, not in a test file — looked clean. The tool now parses every
  `.go` file for package variables and helper bodies, and rewrites only test files. Same lesson one level down:
  a callee's body must be read with the *locals of the function being read*, or a `slots := map[string]string{}`
  inside a codegen helper is reported as writing the tool governor's `slots chan struct{}`, and every case that
  compiles anything is refused. Scope-blind name matching produces an analysis that is confidently wrong.
- **Two idioms are safe and had to be believed: `sync.Once` bodies and mutex-guarded spans.** Refusing package
  writes outright would have serialised every lazy cache and every ledger in the tree (`gapLedger`, `debtSeen`,
  `ledger` are all written under a mutex). `onceGuardedLits` marks the closure handed to `.Do(...)`; `lockIntervals`
  reads `Lock/Unlock`, `RLock/RUnlock` and `defer Unlock` (a deferred release holds the span to the end of the
  body), and a write inside an acquired span is not a race. The unit test that pins it is a ledger with a real
  mutex — minus the `mu.Lock()`, which must flip it back to serial.
- **Tier the process-wide acts by *who reaches for them*.** `dlopenRun` is in the runner's call graph — every
  compiled run passes through `JITWithOptions`, which contains a branch that calls it. Refusing anything that can
  reach it refused 155 cases for a branch they never take; refusing the case that walks to it **through its own
  test-file helpers** is the rule that means something. Hence two tables: `knownUnsafe` (followed everywhere) and
  `knownInTestCode` (followed only through functions defined in a `_test.go` file).
- **A rewrite tool that can produce unparsable Go is worse than no tool.** Insertion into one-line bodies
  (`if err != nil { t.Fatal(...) }`, `for ... { break }`, a closure on one line) needs a self-delimiting statement,
  and every generated file is re-parsed and gofmt-checked before it is written — a refusal to write, not a broken
  tree. `TestInsertionLandsInsideTheBrace` and `TestTheShapesThatBrokeTheFirstVersion` are the regression set, and
  the tool is idempotent so a second pass is a no-op.
- **The guard runs the documented command, not a library.** `integration/parallelism_guard_test.go` shells out to
  `go run ./tools/parify -check -quiet <patterns>` so the thing in `docs/operations.md` is the thing that reddens
  the build, and the failure quotes the census line (`2878 parallel, 2 serial, 12 marked serial`) rather than
  swallowing it. An off-tree analysis library would be a second source of truth with no user.
- **Shared fixtures are shared state with better names.** Two rows of `TestBuiltArtifactRunsForReal` are both
  labelled `simple`, and `writeSrc` wrote both programs to `dir/simple.gy` — one row ran the other's source and
  passed because both answers happened to be right. Every table row now gets its own leaf (`caseLeaf`: sanitized
  name + hash). A table is not a set of cases; it is a set of cases *and* a filesystem namespace.
- **A ledger row pinned to bytes that were never stable is a coin flip.** The unbound-`match` value-pattern row
  prints an object address; the compiled address is not the reference's. `unstable: true` says "re-measure the
  *shape*" (does it answer at all, does it keep its trap class), which is what that row can honestly claim.
- **Refactoring a package variable into a return value can silently drop half an answer.** Lifting
  `pairClosedOut` into `pairCallScan`'s second result returned `nil, nil` on the "no specs" exit — and codegen
  asks the closed-position question *independently* of whether the program ended up paired.
  `TestAPairAnswerHeldByAPositionThatKeepsOneWordStillRefuses` failed within seconds (`z = twice(y)` printed the
  truncated word `8` instead of refusing), and `TestTheClosedPositionSetSurvivesAnEmptySpecMap` now pins both
  halves — with its teeth checked by reverting the fix and watching that row fail.
- **`go test`'s ordering note is a fact about the harness**: parallel tests run *beside* the serial ones, not
  after them, so marking the offenders serial does not protect them. That is why the answer had to be removing
  the sharing, not scheduling around it.

## What `-race` found once the cases were allowed to overlap (ADR 0343, continued)

- **A parallel suite is a race detector's whole point, and it paid for itself on the first run.** Four
  `WARNING: DATA RACE` reports, one address: `(*irGen).installPowerReaders` writing the package-level
  `kindOfIntValue` function variable while another goroutine's `readIntLiteral` read it. The compiler's power
  predicates read a NAME the program bound to a literal int, and the reader was *installed* — a closure over the
  asking generator's module constants, behind a "wired once per generator" bit. Two generators at once made that
  a race on a function pointer; one at a time made it last-writer-wins, so a compile could be answered from
  another module's constants while the comment above it promised "scoped to this generator's module constants".
  **A hook is a global with a story told about it**; `powerFacts{kindOf, readInt}`, built per ask by
  `(*irGen).powerReaders()` and passed as a value, is the same information with nowhere to leak.
- **The serial suite could not have seen the second half of that bug at all.** The race is the visible half; the
  invisible half is a compile answered from the wrong module's constants, which needs an interleaving that a
  one-case-per-process suite never produces. Fixing a race by adding a mutex would have kept the wrong answer.
- **Assert the shape, then assert the behaviour.** `TestThePowerPredicatesReadTheProgramThroughAValueTheyAreGiven`
  fails if the hook or its installer returns (grepping the two files, which is how this file already checks that
  the print road asks `g.powerAnswersDouble(n)`);
  `TestCompilesAnswerTheirOwnPowerQuestionsUnderOverlap` compiles a batch of power programs alone, then the same
  batch concurrently, and requires each answer to be the answer it gave alone. The first cannot be fooled by a
  mutex; the second cannot be fooled by a comment.
- **`make testrace` is now a shipped target and the tree is clean under it** (`./pkg/... ./cmd/...
  ./integration/... ./tools/...`, 4m35s). The static check (`parify -check`) and the dynamic one (the detector)
  are not redundant: one finds a case that claims parallelism while touching process state, the other finds the
  cache nobody wrote down.

## The toolchain was process state, and one case's stub answered another case's program (ADR 0343, Gap R.260)

- **The first overlapping runs produced diagnostics that belonged to a test, not to a program.** `import math`
  reported `invalid module: my favourite complaint` — a string that exists only inside the stub `llc` written by
  a toolchain-error case — and a golden-record program came back `cannot open …/stub-llc`. Both are reads of a
  package variable (`llcCmd`) that a case had written to ask its own question. A serial suite has always run the
  cases in one order, so the only symptom was the rare cross-shaped failure; the moment the cases overlapped it
  became two ledger rows and a lie in a report.
- **"Package-level so tests can point at alternate installs" is a use case, not a safety argument.** The comment
  above those variables explained why the design is convenient and never asked who else was reading it. Gap
  R.259's power hook had the same structure ("wired once per generator", about shared storage). The rule that
  falls out: **a run-scoped fact is a value the run carries**; if only one caller can set it and every other
  caller reads it, it is process state with a story attached.
- **Absence is not the same question as "not named".** `ToolOverride`'s empty field means *keep the default* —
  which is what lets a case replace only the tool it is asking about. The optimizer case that needs *no `opt` at
  all* (to exercise the textual fallback) cannot spell that with an empty string, so it has its own name,
  `toolNamesWithoutOpt`. A single sentinel overloaded across "unset" and "deliberately none" would have made one
  of the two tests silently wrong.
- **Assert which binary ran, not which one the report mentions.** `TestTheToolchainNamedByOneRunIsNotTheOneAnotherRunReads`
  uses a stub `cc` that appends to one shared log before execing the real compiler, and asserts the log holds
  **exactly one** line after a run that named it executes beside a run that did not. A report can name the right
  tool while a different one executed; an invocation count cannot lie about that.
- **Check the new test has teeth by breaking the fix, not by reading it.** Setting `toolNamesFor` to ignore its
  argument turned all four override tests red (one of them by panic, in the classification path); restoring it
  turned them green. The same trick caught a second thing here: the first version of the override missed the `cc`
  link in `BuildWithOptions` because a `grep` for the old variable had been filtered too aggressively — the test
  that a bad `cc` must fail its own build is what noticed the missed call site.
- **The census is the deliverable.** `parify`'s line went from `2878 parallel, 2 serial, 12 marked serial` to
  `2892 parallel, 2 serial, 4 marked serial`: nine cases released from owning the process, four left, each of
  which (three `t.Setenv`, the in-process engine) takes the process by definition. A serial-marked case is fine
  when it is honest; the goal was never zero, it was *named*.

## The last serial markers were refactored away, not granted (ADR 0343, `tools/envprobe`, parify's callee rule)

- **The census ended at one marker.** `parify` now reports **2902 parallel, 2 serial, 1 marked serial** — the
  survivor being the case that asks for `JITOptions{InProcess: true}` and therefore owns fd 1 and fd 2. The
  target was never "zero markers"; a marker on a case that genuinely owns the process is the honest outcome. The
  target was *no marker that is a workaround*, and every one of those got a refactor instead.
- **A tunable knob stays process-wide — the test of it does not have to be.** `GUSTY_PYTHON` and
  `GUSTY_TOOL_TIMEOUT` are process-wide *by design*: that is what makes them settable from a shell. The mistake
  was testing them with `t.Setenv`, which both panics in a parallel case and retunes the process for every case
  running beside it. The fix has two halves: the decision becomes a function of an environment it is *given*
  (`pythonBinaryFrom(lookup)`, `budgetFrom(lookup, name, def, warn)`), which makes it a table — and one run of
  `tools/envprobe` keeps the process-wide entry point honest, because a probe reports what **its own process**
  resolved. The table would otherwise certify a resolver nobody calls.
- **Asserting the complaint, not just the fallback.** `budgetFrom` takes the writer it grumbles to, so
  "GUSTY_TOOL_TIMEOUT=90 is ignored" is now asserted as a sentence naming the variable and the default it fell
  back to. The old case could only assert the duration, because a `t.Setenv` case cannot capture stderr without
  owning the process — so the half of the requirement that mattered most ("a setting silently ignored is worse
  than one that does not exist") had no witness at all.
- **`parify`'s shadowing rule had to be extended from variables to callees, and the false positive was
  load-bearing.** A CLI case defines a local `run := func(...)` that execs the built binary; the package also
  has a helper called `run` that installs a standard-library root. Callee resolution was name-blind, so the case
  was refused for a call it never makes — and because a `//parify:serial` marker also grants exemption from
  `-check`, my own tool's bug had bought a case a permanent, unexamined excuse. `TestALocalNamedRunIsNotThePackagesRun`
  asserts both directions (the shadowing local runs free; the case that really calls the package's `run` still
  refuses), because "assume functions named `run` are safe" would have passed it too.
- **Rule of the campaign, said once more:** an unsafe-looking test is a design report. Every marker that came
  off was a piece of production state that should have been a parameter — the runner's fds, the stdlib root, the
  toolchain, the power predicates' reader, the environment knobs.

## CI that runs nothing looks like a quiet week, not like a failure (`.github/workflows/go.yml`, 37 pushes)

- **The signal was an email that said "No jobs were run", and it read like nothing happening.** Every Actions
  failure I had ever handled was a red step with a log. A workflow whose YAML does not **parse** produces no
  step at all: the run opens and closes in the same second, has zero jobs, and is named after the *file path*
  instead of the workflow's `name:` — because the parser died before the name. Conclusion `failure`, no check
  runs on the commit, no log to open, nothing to click. The diagnostic to keep: **a run whose `name` is the path
  and whose `updated_at == created_at` never parsed**. The API's `jobs` list comes back empty, and the commits
  API reports *zero check runs* for the SHA — that pair is the whole signature.
- **One character-class of bug, in a comment-adjacent line, took CI dark for a week.** The offending line was
  `- name: Unit tests (sharded: one test process per core)` — a plain YAML scalar ends at the first `": "`, so
  GitHub read a mapping whose value was `Unit tests (sharded:` and the job vanished with it (`mapping values are
  not allowed here`, line 100 col 34). It landed in the ADR 0313 commit that added the sharding step; the last
  run with jobs was the push before it. Nothing about the code was involved, and nothing in the repo could tell
  me, because the file is the only one in the tree that nothing in the suite reads.
- **So the suite now reads it.** `integration/ci_workflow_test.go` has three parts, and the middle one is the
  reason the other two are trustworthy: the structural rule in Go (a step/job name must not be a plain scalar
  carrying `": "`), **a table that feeds the rule the exact line that broke CI and requires it to refuse** — a
  guard written to match nothing would also have passed all week — and a real `yaml.safe_load` where `python3`
  has PyYAML (the oracle's own interpreter, so the dependency costs nothing), skipped rather than passed where it
  does not. The parse asserts the four things a runner needs before it can run anything: a `name`, an `on`,
  non-empty `jobs`, and a job with `steps`.
- **Verified both ways before pushing**: with the quoting removed, the two checks name line 100 and fail; with
  the fix in place they pass. `git log -- .github/workflows/go.yml` plus the run list's `created_at` is what
  localised it — the file's last change sat exactly between the last run with jobs and the first without.
- **A harness owns its own plumbing, including the plumbing nobody executes from a test.** The same instinct
  that produced `tools/testshards`'s self-tests and the `parify` guard should have covered the workflow file: if
  an artifact decides whether the suite ran at all, a case must read it.

## The decline was the answer nobody read (ADR 0344, Gap R.261)

- **What was measured, before any code changed.** Five programs, one preamble (`def g(): return 5`), each run
  against `python3` and against `/tmp/gustyc-head` built from the commit under work:
  `print(f())` over a list filled by `out.append(g())` printed `0` for `[5]`; over a set filled by `out.add(g())`
  printed `0` for `{5}`; over a dict filled by `out["k"] = g()` printed `0` for `{'k': 5}`; the same dict with a
  float-returning callee printed `0` for `{'k': 2.5}`; and `for v in f(): print(v)` printed **nothing at all** for
  `5`. All at exit 0. `str(f())` and `repr(f())` were already correct — and that asymmetry was the diagnosis
  waiting to be found: the render road hands the handle to `rt_str_of_container`, so the object was never the
  problem, only who had been handed it.
- **A function returning `[5]` printing `0` meant the print door was asked nothing at all.** The root cause was
  not in the printer, the runtime or the object layout: `containerAnswerScan` answers *two* questions and returns
  them as two maps, and every consumer in the tree read the first as the whole answer. A decline is a fact with a
  subject — "this is a container, and I cannot describe its slots" — and encoding it as absence from one map
  throws away the first clause, which is the only clause three doors needed.
- **The first fix was wrong, and the probe caught it.** Letting every position that can hold a handle take the
  answer is the natural move; it turned `for k in f(): print(k)` into `0` (the reference prints `k`). That is the
  row's real lesson: **"can hold the pointer" is not the same question as "asks the object"**. A loop reads each
  member back through notebooks the scan writes; hand it an answer with no notebooks and it does not fail, it
  *guesses*. The rule is now a method on the record (`takesRead(read)`), the reads are named (`Whole`, `Shape`,
  `Members`, `Slots`, `Walk`), and every door that does not name its read gets the strictest one — which makes
  the whole change provably monotone: a door can only widen from what it already was.
- **A refusal has to be unreachable by fall-through, not merely available.** Adding the loop's refusal meant
  putting a guard (`containerAnswerReadIsRefused`) where the door *declines*, because the code after a declined
  door is the road that prints the handle. `return refusal` sitting in a helper nobody calls is how a row that
  "handles" a case keeps the bug.
- **One question, asked twice, becomes two answers (ADR 0232 again).** The slot predicate lived in a closure
  inside `containerAnswerDescribesItsSlots`; the narrower judgement the membership and loop doors needed would
  have been a second copy of it. Lifting it to `containerAnswerSlotReader.slot` — a type holding the three records
  the question reads — kept both doors asking one question, and cost no behaviour.
- **Process: isolate the bug from the feature that found it.** The defect surfaced while bringing up L11.7's
  higher-order door, but it reproduces with no function values in the program at all. The pass was moved out of
  the tree (`/tmp/callable_value.go.pass`), the AST fields it needs reverted, and the container fix re-verified
  alone against `python3` — 18 programs, all matching, the two non-matches being honest refusals of unrelated
  limitations (`sum` over a call's answer, tuples). Three binaries side by side (`-head`, `-a` stale, `-b` fixed)
  is what made "is this mine?" a five-second question instead of a debate.
- **Guard the shape, not just the answer.** `TestTheRuleIsAskedOfTheRecordNotOfTheCaller` fails if a door starts
  deciding for itself again; `TestTheDeclinedAnswerIsPrintedByTheDoorThatAsksTheObject` asserts the answer reaches
  the printer as a rooted slot (`__cans…`) rather than as the ordinary road's word; and both test files forbid the
  refusal from leaking `*lang.`, `0x`, `%!s(` or a compiler temp. Every refused row carries CPython's answer in
  the table, so a door that grows later turns a passing row into a green answer rather than a guess.
- **A stale binary is a false memory.** Two "regressions" in this session were `/tmp/gustyc-a` having been built
  from an intermediate edit — one of them was my own first, wrong fix reporting itself as HEAD behaviour. Any
  claim about "what HEAD does" now gets re-measured with a binary built from `git commit` in a clean worktree.

## A function used as a value is a name the pass mints, not a word the value carries (ADR 0345, roadmap L11.7)

**Feature (codegen + front-end-adjacent pass)**: `print(apply1(inc, 41))`, `print(twice(d2, 3))`,
`g = d2` / `print(g(4))` and `print(sorted([3, 1, 2], key=lambda x: 0 - x))` were refused at exit 1 by seven
different doors wearing seven vocabularies, where CPython prints `42`, `12`, `8` and `[3, 2, 1]`. `defunctionalizeCallables`
(`pkg/lang/callable_value.go`) now runs as the first act of `GenerateIRReport`: read the program, plan a rewrite
or decline, deep-copy, write. A higher-order function is cloned per entry tuple, a lambda that must be named is
declared, an alias is retargeted, and everything the pass cannot prove comes back exactly as it went in.

- **The record is a witness, and a helper can quietly be the record.** `captureStdout`/`compiledPrints` in
  `pkg/lang` answers from `testdata/interpreter-golden.json` *when the record holds the source*, and falls back to
  the JIT otherwise. The reference-leg table I wrote used it, so four probes "passed" while the compiler was never
  asked — they were being read back out of a JSON file. `callable_value_test.go` now has its own
  `compiledRunIsTheBackend`, which is `RunSource` and nothing else. Anything that claims to be a *compiled* leg has
  to name the compiled entry point in its body, not in its comment.
- **A skip needs a floor.** The record-leg test skips probes the retired engine never saw — which is most of the
  new ones — and a table of skips is indistinguishable from a table of passes. Both that test and
  `TestTheKeyedOrdersAreOnTheRecord` now count how many rows reached a record and fail at zero. The same bug hid in
  the counting itself: the counters were filled by `t.Parallel()` subtests, which run *after* the parent function
  returns, so the guard read `0` while the real answer was still queued. A guard that counts subtest work cannot be
  a parallel parent.
- **`%p` is not a seed.** Names minted with `fmt.Fprintf(h, "%s|%p", base, node)` gave
  `print(sorted([3, 1, 2], key=lambda x: -x))` two different modules in two runs: Go randomises `%p` per process
  since 1.21. Determinism is load-bearing here — the golden record, the lit tests and every cached artifact read IR
  symbols — so `nodeSeed` numbers nodes by first ask within the plan, and
  `TestThePassRewritessTwiceToTheSameBytes` compiles every probe twice. Gap R.162 was filed against exactly this
  property on another pass; expect it wherever a name is minted.
- **A wrong answer showed up before a test did.** While the alias road was half-built, `print(apply1(inc, 41))`
  printed **`43`** — 41 plus two increments — at exit 0. It reached me only through a probe script, because the
  reference harness at the time compared against a CPython run of a *source that did not define `inc`*, so CPython
  printed nothing and "both printed nothing" looked like agreement. A reference leg has to run the *same program*;
  a harness whose reference silently produces the empty string turns every mismatch into a match. The arity audit
  (`callableInnerAgrees`, checked against the *declared* parameter count) is what makes the double-application
  shape impossible now, and the answer table would have caught it too — but only if it had been compared to
  something real.
- **The refusal's name is part of the refusal.** `too many arguments for g` passed an integration test that asked
  for `<lambda>`… except it did not: the row had been written to accept whatever came out, and only became a real
  check when the CLI table was rewritten to demand CPython's word. A lambda's surface name is `<lambda>` even when
  a name is bound to it, because that is what the reference prints; a clone's surface name is the function the
  program wrote (`twice`), because that is what the reader's file contains. Both decisions live in one function
  (`callableSurfaceName`) so the minted spelling never leaks, and `FuncDef.CloneOf` carries the source name into
  `--debug-info` and tracebacks.
- **Declining is a feature, and it wants to be legible.** Every unprovable shape returns the caller's untouched
  tree, which keeps the older honest refusal — the pass can only *add* answers. `--callables` prints why it
  declined (the `refused` field, cited to the roadmap row) with a schema definition behind it, because a rewrite
  whose decisions are unreadable is a rewrite nobody can debug without reading its source.
- **Every measurement I trusted was the one that had a reference beside it.** The seven new gap rows (R.263–R.269)
  each carry CPython's answer as measured, not as remembered — and three shapes I first believed were gaps turned
  out to be programs CPython itself stops (`apply1(twice, 3)` is a `TypeError`, not a value), which is why they are
  not on the list. The list came from one script that printed `ours`/`ref` side by side; that script is worth more
  than any table I could have written from intent.

## The gate was a serial command in a concurrent suite (AGENTS.md § Test gate, makefile)

**Change (loop contract)**: `AGENTS.md` told the cycle "run `go test ./...` before commit" while the makefile
had long since grown the concurrent runners — so the command an agent read from the contract was the slowest
correct one available (`make testparallel` is ~1m40s against the serial run's ~11m43s on the 20-core box,
ADR 0343), and it was also the one missing two flags. `AGENTS.md` now names `make testparallel` as the gate in
all three places a gate is stated (the Correctness bullet, loop step 5, the Testing rule), and a new
§ Test gate table lists the targets and when each one is right.

- **A hand-rolled copy of a makefile target is not the same command.** The bare `go test ./...` drops
  `-tags=llvm20`, and a suite built without the tag skips its LLVM legs — it reports a green that was never
  earned — and drops `-count=1`, which is the only thing standing between a doc guard and `go test`'s cache
  (ADR 0317: the cache key holds build inputs, not the `docs/*.md` and `roadmap.md` a guard opens at runtime).
  Pointing the contract at the *target* rather than a transcription of it is what keeps the flags attached.
- **A contract and a makefile drift the same way two modules do.** `tools/testshards/main_test.go` asserts the
  makefile's serial target keeps the tag and the flag but its comment claimed the serial run was "the gate
  AGENTS.md names" — true once, then only about the artifact-writing modes. The comment now says which half
  of that is still true, because a stale comment in the guard that watches the gate is the failure mode with
  no test to catch it.
- **Concurrency has an exception and it had to travel with the recommendation.** `GUSTY_GOLDEN_UPDATE` and
  `GUSTY_GOLDEN_MISSING` write per-run ledgers, so N concurrent runs would each overwrite the file with their
  own subset (ADR 0313, ADR 0315). A doc that says "run the parallel one" without naming the serial
  carve-out manufactures a corrupted ledger out of an agent who was following instructions.

## A refusal is an interface, so the code it is branched on is generated from the registry (ADR 0346, roadmap L11.8)

**Feature (CLI + machine path)**: a capability refusal reached a human as a sentence and a script as
`"error": "codegen: …"`, so an agent planning a compilation had to match on prose to learn what it had been
refused. `pkg/lang/capability.go` is now the one registry of 40 `lower.unsupported.<shape>` codes — code, shape,
suggestion, owning roadmap rows — read by `--json`'s `capability` member, by `gustyc --capabilities`, and by
`--schema`'s `capabilityRefusalCode` enum, which is spliced out of the registry at init rather than typed. No
`codegen:` refusal site was touched. The exit-code half of the row was already ADR 0211's.

- **A reworded sentence does not fail a branch, it stops firing one.** That is the whole argument for codes, and
  it inverted how I chose the mechanism: the comparison was never "typed errors vs a table", it was "which
  forgetting is silent". Wrapping 142 refusal sites in a typed error compiles happily with a site left out, and
  the coverage decays the first time someone adds a refusal in a hurry. A registry whose `Sample` no longer
  produces its refusal is a red test that afternoon. Pick the failure mode you can see.
- **The docs table advertised sentences the compiler had stopped saying.** The guard that reads every
  "Message substring" out of `docs/operations.md` and greps it from the package's own string literals found three
  dead rows (`strings inside runtime containers …`, `unsupported call "`, `cannot hold another container yet` —
  all retired underneath ADRs 0224/0232/0239) and one that had drifted (`operator "<op>" on a string` had grown a
  `(kind)` clause between the two halves of the quote). A doc that tells a script what to match on is code, and
  code that is never compiled against anything rots on exactly that schedule.
- **Cut a quoted sentence at its placeholders before you grep for it.** `%s`/`%q`/`<op>` are not in the docs and
  the docs' `…` is not in the source, so `capabilityFragments` splits on both and asks each surviving fragment ≥ 12
  characters separately. Fragments too short to be a sentence are dropped rather than allowed, because matching
  `operator` anywhere in `pkg/lang` certifies nothing.
- **Classify one message, not the payload.** The first coverage pass joined a program's diagnostics into one
  string and truncated it to 130 characters for the report — and the truncation cut through the markers, so real
  codes went missing from the tally. Same for level: `arithmetic on non-numeric operands` and
  `match is not exhaustive` are checker *warnings* about programs that compile, and counting them as refusals
  would have made the coverage claim about the checker's mood. Errors and hard failures only, and the allowlist
  says why for the rest.
- **A marker is measured or it is a guess wearing a contract.** `d.items()` was written into the registry as the
  sample for the dict-methods refusal and classified as `container-method-over-a-name` instead — the receiver
  question is asked before the method question, and only `for k, v in {"a": 1}.items():` reaches the sentence I
  had meant. Every entry got its sentence by compiling its sample and reading the answer back, which is why
  `Markers` and `Sample` live in the registry at all (`json:"-"`: how the entry is tested, not a field an agent
  should read).
- **Two hand-typed lists of one fact is the bug, not the drift.** The schema enum used to be a place a human
  added codes. Now `ASTIRSchema` is a template plus `withCapabilityCodes`, and a lost placeholder panics at init
  rather than shipping a schema that says no refusal has a code. The same reason made `capability` an always-present
  key rendered `null`: "absent" and "looked and found nothing" have to be distinguishable, or the reader is
  guessing about the classifier from the payload's shape.
- **Longest marker wins, and that is a determinism claim.** `tuple(…)`'s refusal contains the generic
