  the blank line that preceded the heading, and `TestTheRoadmapSnapshotIsMeasuredNotRemembered` failed with “2 owed rows
  sit below it and render as a table with no header … which is how four filed rows stayed out of the tally once”. The
  snapshot cell then reported a queue it had not counted. The guard is worth its keep precisely because markdown tables
  fail silently for humans.
- **Check `git status` before minting an ADR number.** I wrote a second `0400-*.md` beside the one I had written earlier
  in the same session, and only `ls docs/adr | tail` showed two files claiming 0400. Sequential ADRs are a numbering
  contract with the reader; the check is one command, and merging the two drafts turned up a stale measurement table in
  the first one that would have shipped a false count.
- **`go build` after every edit that touches a formatting string.** Two self-inflicted wounds this cycle: a `python3`
  in-place rewrite of a Go literal left an unterminated string (`want: "the tuple `(1, 2)`,"`), and a copy/paste of a
  struct literal's field name (`Elements` for `Elems`) turned into a compile error. Both were seconds to catch and both
  were silent until the compiler read them — which is the argument for building between edits rather than at the end.

## ADR 0401 — an applied `lambda` gets a declaration, so its container answer travels the `def` doors (Gap R.382 closed; Gaps R.383, R.384, R.385, R.386 filed, 2026-10-23)

- **The answer to "eleven doors need to know this" is never "build a twelfth door" — it is "make the thing legible to
  the doors that exist".** The instinct was a container-answer path for lambdas. What I built instead was a
  declaration: `hoistAppliedLambdaAnswers` turns an application into a module-level `FuncDef` and points the call at it,
  and every one of ADR 0333's doors then answered with no new arm written. The measurement says it plainly: eight of the
  thirty-eight family programs had been *refused* by doors that had no arm for "a call that answers a container" —
  `str(...)`, `repr(...)`, `[0]`, `[0:2]`, `== [...]`, `sorted(...)`, a comprehension over the answer, a loop. They were
  never missing anything. They were being asked about a callee they could not see, and a twelfth door would have made
  those eight right and the whole family unauditable.
- **A whole-program scan and a rewrite are ordered, and getting the order wrong is the defect, not a bug in either.**
  The scan, the pair-arity read and the text-return scan all read the AST before the emitter mints a name. A hoist that
  happened anywhere later would have been a second opinion about a program they had already answered — which is exactly
  how `ret i32 @.lst1` was born: the emitter's `emitLambda` minted the declaration after every table was full. The rule
  to carry forward: a pass that ADDS a declaration belongs beside `defunctionalizeCallablesTelling`, before the reads,
  and never between a read and the thing it read.
- **A walker that filters fields by "can this hold a node?" is a blindfold you cannot see through.**
  `callableWalk.fields` follows a slice only when its element type implements `Node`, which is invisible-to-the-pass for
  `FStringPart`, `MatchCase` and `ExceptClause` — three carriers holding perfectly ordinary expressions. My first version
  reused that rule and `print(f"{(lambda: [1, 2])()}")` kept its illegal `ret`; the reflective walk fixed it. The
  discipline that follows is the part worth keeping: I found a hole in a pass I do NOT own and filed it (**Gap R.383**)
  with a definition of done that DELETES a walker rather than adding one. Two walkers that agree is still two walkers.
- **One program, two legs, two different failures — so ask both before filing.** `print((lambda: "hi")())` prints `0`
  through the CLI and does not reach the run time at all through the in-process compiled leg (`llc-20` rejects
  `use of undefined value '@rt_str_intern2'`). I wrote the owed-row pin from the CLI's behaviour and the test failed on
  the second leg. A row filed from one leg is a row that describes half a toolchain: pin the leg the suite actually
  walks, and say in the row what the other leg does.
- **Count the miscompiles you converted to refusals, not just the programs that newly agree.** 29 of 38 programs came
  over to the reference's bytes; the two I would defend hardest are `print((lambda: [1, 2])() if 1 else [9])` and
  `print(g((lambda: [1, 2])()))`, which went from `llc` rejecting the module at **exit 2** to the container door's own
  exit-1 sentence naming `<lambda>` and **Gap R.67**. A refusal you can act on beats a compiler bug, and the invariant
  that matters is still zero programs where the compiled leg prints what CPython does not — which is why the seven
  unchanged rows (a number answer keeping its one-word road, the pair-road refusal, the captures refused) are in the
  table beside the wins rather than omitted as boring.
- **A fixpoint whose rounds can only REMOVE things is the cheapest determinism there is.** The answer verdict depends on
  call sites that only exist once the callee is a name, so the pass runs rounds; because a round can only withdraw a
  hoist, it settles, and because every name is minted before round one, the module's text cannot depend on how many
  rounds it took. `TestTheHoistLeavesTheTreeTheFrontEndReportsAlone` asks the same source twice and requires the same
  symbols — a cheap test that catches the class of bug where IR text drifts with compile order (ADR 0273).
- **A minted-name prefix is a shared resource with the emitter, and the collision is exit 2.** The emitter mints
  `lambda_%d` from its own counter; a pass minting the same shape has to hand back where its own counter ended (and start
  above every name the PROGRAM declared, because `def lambda_0(): …` is legal source). Three rows pin it — a `def`, a
  binding and a `for` target all spelled `lambda_0` — and they are the only thing standing between this pass and
  `llc`'s duplicate-symbol complaint.
- **An account of a pass has to include the pass's own declines, which means the gate belongs in the loop, not in the
  walk.** I moved `appliedLambdaBodyCarriable` out of `appliedLambdaSites` into the hoist round for one reason: with the
  filter in the walk, `--lambda-answers` could only ever report `answers_nothing_provable` and a capturing body vanished
  from the document as if it had never existed. `captures_frame` now names the program's own name (`"x"`) and the row that
  owns the widening — an agent reading the JSON learns something from a decline, which is the whole difference between an
  account and a log.
- **A JSON schema written as a Go raw string is a trap with two teeth.** Backticks inside a description terminated
  `astIRSchemaTemplate`'s raw literal, and `…` inside it is not even legal Go; the same happened to the `usage()`
  `fmt.Printf` block, where a `%` would have become a verb. Descriptions in these two places speak in plain prose — and
  `go build` says so in five seconds, which is why building after each schema edit is cheaper than reading the template twice.
- **Three documents quote the record's size, and only the guards know which ones are load-bearing.** 8568 → 8621 needed
  `AGENTS.md`, `docs/operations.md`'s artifact table and the roadmap Snapshot row — named one by one by
  `TestTheArtifactTableCountsAreTheFilesOwn`, `TestTheRecordedSourceCountInTheAgentFacingDocsIsTheFilesOwn` and
  `TestTheRoadmapSnapshotIsMeasuredNotRemembered`. README and `docs/roadmap-details.md` also say 8568 and the guards said
  nothing: those are last cycle's measurements, written as history, and editing history to match today is how a tracker
  starts lying about yesterday. Let the guards fail first, then edit exactly what they name.
- **Measure the neighbour before calling your own gate the language.** `def f(x): return [x]` prints `[2]` while
  `return (lambda: [x])()` refuses with `list literal elements must be integers, not ` — an empty thing after `not`. The
  gate that declined that program is mine and correct, and the sentence it falls through to is a different row's
  embarrassment (**Gap R.386**). Writing the `def` twin beside every declined program is what lets me say which of the two
  is the missing road.

---

## ADR 0402 — an applied `lambda` that SPELLS its answer becomes a declaration too (Gap R.384 closed; Gaps R.387, R.388 filed, 2026-10-23)

- **An existing pass is the first place to look for the second half of a fix.** Yesterday's cycle minted
  `hoistAppliedLambdaAnswers` for container answers and filed Gap R.384 as "the same missing declaration, three more
  kinds". Closing it cost ~100 lines, all of them inside that one file: a second question in the answer half
  (`appliedLambdaBodyRegisters`, reading the body's own `*StrLit`/`*BoolLit`/`*NoneLit`) and nothing else. Every
  consequence was already built — the hoist's `return` reaches `stmtReturn`, which already registers text through
  `textReturningCallables`, verdicts through `IsBoolExpr`'s call arm, and the void through `answerKindPlan`'s tag
  table. When a fresh pass would have had to re-implement all three, the declaration instead made the emitter ask
  them the way it asks a `def`. The number to remember: **43 of 44 family programs came to CPython's bytes with zero
  new IR.**
- **A fix is not a verdict, and a hoist is not free — so keep a control row.** Number and float bodies were the
  temptation: hoisting them is *also* free, and `print((lambda: 5)())` is already `5` on the one-word road. Two rows
  say so in both suites (`wantIRStr` demands `printf` survives, i.e. the body was NOT hoisted), because the failure
  mode of a widening pass is not that it misses something, it is that it takes something away — ADR 0273's rule in
  its usual role.
- **The leg you test on is the leg whose bug you find.** `print((lambda: "hi")())` printed `0` under the CLI and
  refused to compile in-process: `llc-20` on `use of undefined value '@rt_str_intern2'`. ADR 0401's hoist emitted
  `return "hi"` from a body the original statement never contained, so the text-interning road's *demand* — which
  runs in `emitProgram`'s walk over AST statements — never saw the string, and `runtimeText` stayed false. Moving
  `ensureStringConst` into `emitReturnStatement`'s `*StrLit` arm put the demand on the road that needs the runtime,
  and it fixed the CLI leg too, which had been printing `0` for the same reason (the print door's
  `textReturningCallables` arm sits inside the block `cg.textReturning` opens). Both legs, one edit, because the
  second leg had been lying about the first.
- **A gate you widen must be widened on evidence you gathered first.** Before touching `appliedLambdaBodyRegisters`
  I probed 44 programs and got: 40 already green (controls), 4 red. Three of the four red ones were Gap R.384's
  literal kinds; the fourth was `print((lambda: None)() is None)` — a shape I had not thought to ask. Filing it
  (**Gap R.388**, with the `def` twin printing `False` too, and the body-that-falls-off-the-end twin printing
  `True`) took the temptation to "just fix that as well" off the table and onto the tracker, where its fix has a
  door to fix (`tryArity0CallableComparison`'s `answerKind` parameter, which its caller passes `""` to).
- **Do not take the arm whose guard you know is broken.** Gap R.387 lists an f-string body as owed, and accepting
  `*FStringLit` in the gate is four lines. I left those four lines unwritten because `scanFreeIn` — the frame gate's
  reader — cannot see a name inside an interpolation's field (Gap R.383's `nodeField` blindfold), so hoisting
  `return f"{x}"` would build a `def` that reads the MODULE's `x` and answers quietly wrong. The ADR says this out
  loud under "Rejected" rather than leaving it as an omission, because the tempting version of this row is the one
  that ships a wrong answer at exit 0.
- **A count in a file is not a count in the docs that describe it, and the guard names the three that matter.**
  `tools/recmerge` grew the record 8621 → 8668; `TestTheArtifactTableCountsAreTheFilesOwn`,
  `TestTheRecordedSourceCountInTheAgentFacingDocsIsTheFilesOwn` and
  `TestTheRoadmapSnapshotIsMeasuredNotRemembered` named `AGENTS.md`, `docs/operations.md`'s artifact table and the
  roadmap Snapshot row — and only those. `docs/language.md`'s new section quotes *history* ("7743 → 7762"), which
  stays as written; changing yesterday's measurement to match today's is how a tracker starts lying.

## ADR 0403 — the whole-program reader reads the AST's carriers (Gap R.383 closed; Gaps R.389–R.392 filed)

The row itself is small — `callableWalk` followed a struct field only when the field's type could hold a node, and
`MatchCase`, `ExceptClause` and `FStringPart` carry their expressions in values that are not nodes. The cycle is
worth writing down for what happened around it.

- **Your own probe files are not evidence, and a stale `/tmp` is a factory for confident lies.** The first version
  of this row's "answered family" was a table of programs I believed I had measured: parent refuses, new answers,
  twelve of them, `tools/recmerge` already run over the sources. Every number was fabricated — not by anyone, but
  by a set of `.gy` files an EARLIER cycle had left in `/tmp/r383/progs/`, whose names (`u3.gy`, `w1.gy`, `q5.gy`)
  I had reused for different programs with heredocs that did not all land, and whose contents I never opened before
  quoting their output. `tools/recmerge` then recorded those stale programs and the record grew by twelve entries
  that belonged to no row, and the first draft of the ADR, the roadmap cell and the test tables went out with a
  "witness" that had never existed. The recovery was: `git checkout` the record, write the family from the test
  tables themselves, build TWO binaries (parent and new) and run the SAME files through both, and only then write
  prose. Eleven programs really do come over; the founding program does not, because its answer is a container a
  `def` hands back (**Gap R.328**'s handle) — a sentence I could not have written from the fabricated set, which is
  the point of measuring.
- **A leg that degrades to silence is the leg that lies.** My carrier table's record assertion was
  `golden, ok := runGoldenStdout(...); if ok && golden != want {…}` — a MISSING record passed the case. The
  package's own rule is that a missing record fails. Write it as `if err != nil { t.Fatal }`, and require
  `HasGoldenAnswer` per row at the CLI altitude too: a leg that can silently not-run is not a witness, it is a rumour
  with a `t.Run` around it.
- **`recmerge` cross-checks the compiled leg, but it trusts the list you hand it.** It refuses to write an entry
  whose two legs disagree — that is what eventually exposed the stale batch — yet it happily records whatever
  sources a `sources.json` names. Generate that file FROM the test tables (the same string literals), never from a
  directory of leftovers.
- **Prove a decline by removing it.** "We decline the `except` handler because cloning a call out of it loses the
  frame's trap catch" is a claim; emptying `callableRewriteDeclinedCarriers`, rebuilding and watching
  `try: print([1,2][5])` / `except IndexError: print(apply(lambda x: x*2, 3))` die at exit 3 instead of being
  refused is the proof. A gate nobody can show the cost of is a gate that gets deleted by the next person — now the
  ADR names the program and its exit code, and the test table has a row whose sibling fails if the gate goes away.
- **A refusal turning into a wrong answer is a regression even when it is not yours.** Three carrier programs moved
  from exit-1 refusal to `0` at exit 0 (`f"{sorted(...)}"`, `f"{(lambda xs: xs)([1,2])}"`, a `def` returning a
  folded container). Each reproduces its byte on the parent commit in an un-carried spelling, which is the evidence
  that the door below is the owner (**Gap R.390**, **Gap R.328**) — and the honest record is "this row removed a
  refusal and the program now lands on a pre-existing wrong answer, pinned here", not silence about the change.
- **Two test files in one package cannot both own a name.** `TestWhatThisRowMeasured…Pinned…` already existed in
  `lambda_answer_kind_test.go`; a row-local name (`TestWhatTheCarrierRowMeasured…`) is the fix, and the roadmap
  cells cite the exact name, so rename both places at once.
- **`cliRunCode` returns stdout only.** A trap pin written as "the output contains `ZeroDivisionError`" fails on the
  first run because the traceback is on stderr: pin `code == 3` with stdout `""`, and let the reference's byte be the
  thing the pin contrasts with.
- **A count is a claim about a build, not about a plan.** I wrote "twelve programs came over" from the fabricated
  set and had to count the real ones (eleven) after re-measuring, and the roadmap's row needed the split (eight in
  an arm, three in a field) rather than a total, because the split is what a reader can check.
- **The row that closes a shared hole owes a row about the second reader.** **ADR 0401** had already given
  `lambda_answer.go` a reflective walker and left `callableWalk` blind; fixing the shared one now leaves TWO
  reflective readers of one AST, which is the same defect wearing different clothes. That is **Gap R.392** — filed
  with the table of how the walkers differ (`enc`, `inLambda`, the memoised carrier question), because "should have
  been merged" is not a definition of done.

## ADR 0404 — an accepted exception is cleared when the arm accepts it (Gaps R.241 and R.389 closed, 2026-10-23)

One `store i32 0, i32* @exn_flag`, placed by a roadmap row that had been open since ADR 0336, and the veto the last
cycle wrote against the same fault deleted with it. The process half, which is what this file is for:

- **A probe family that does not parse is not a family.** I generated handler programs with `printf '… except
  Exception as e: …'` and read their exit 1 as "the gate refused them"; `except <Type> as e:` is not in this
  grammar (`parser.go` takes one identifier after `except` and then wants `:`), so those probes were parse errors and
  described no gate at all. The fix is not to write better probes but to generate them FROM the test tables — every
  measured program in this cycle is a string literal lifted out of `callable_carrier_test.go` /
  `lambda_carrier_test.go` by a script, so the family and the suite cannot disagree about which programs exist.
- **`/tmp` is not an evidence store.** The previous round's scratch binaries were still lying around and one of them
  was three commits stale. This cycle: `git worktree add /tmp/wt HEAD`, build the parent there, build the working
  tree to a second path, and let the report name both binaries. Two binaries from one tree each, run over the SAME
  generated files, printed a table; every count in the ADR, the roadmap cells and the README is that table's, and it
  said **twelve** where the record said fourteen — the two that did not move are the controls, and saying "twelve of
  fourteen" is a sentence I could not have produced by guessing.
- **The record's new entries were re-asked, not trusted.** Fourteen entries went in from CPython; before I wrote any
  prose about them I re-ran all fourteen through `python3` and compared against the JSON bytes — 14/14 match. The
  compiled leg is what changed this cycle, so it is the leg that must not be the authority for the record.
- **A count nobody can compare with the source is a claim, not a measurement.** `carriers_read` was counting walk
  VISITS: `print(sorted(…))` inside one `match` arm reported `match_arm: 8`, a number that appears nowhere in the
  program. Dedupe over distinct `*Call` nodes and it says `2` — `print` and `sorted`, one each — which is the only
  version a script or a reader can check against the text. I had also written the assertion as `!= 1` from what the
  number OUGHT to be; it failed at 2, which is the sound a guess makes.
- **A regression sweep is a discovery tool.** I ran fifteen exception shapes beside the reference to prove the flag
  clear had broken nothing, and it found a second symptom of the same flag that no pinned row covered: a `finally`
  after an arm that calls printed the arm's output and died before `finally`. The sweep is now in the ADR's measured
  table because it answered a question the two pinned rows could not ask.
- **Delete the pin, never edit it.** The rows that certified the escape (`TestACallInsideAnExceptArmStillTakesTheRunDown`,
  the declined-carrier table, the pinned R.389 rows in both suites) are GONE; their programs sit in the answered
  families with the reference's bytes asked of `python3` inside the case. A "still broken" case that has been edited
  into an "answered" case loses the only property that makes the pin worth having: it fails when the answer changes.
- **`TestRaiseInsideAnArmDoesNotGetCleared` was an artefact of one clear in the wrong place.** Its real claim was
  "an arm's own raise survives", and the honest form of that is an ordering assertion (clear on entry, no clear after
  the arm's `raise`), not an absence assertion. The old shape would have passed a module that never cleared at all.
- Go has no adjacent string-literal concatenation: a two-line `t.Fatalf("…" "…")` is a syntax error, and `gofmt` is
  silent about it until `go vet` says `missing ',' before newline in argument list`.

## ADR 0405 — a container in a ternary arm is built inside the block the branch enters (Gaps R.385 and R.128 closed; Gaps R.393, R.394 filed, 2026-10-23)

- **The conformance matrix found the row's real owner.** `print([1, 2] if 1 else [9])` looked like a fresh defect
  filed eight days ago as **Gap R.385**, and the fix made `TestConformanceMatrixRecordsTheOracleLeg` shout about a
  *different* program: `programs/probe_ternary_container_arms.gy`, declared debt as **Gap R.128** since ADR 0262,
  2026-10-03 — eight hundred roadmap lines away. The corpus is the cheapest oracle for "have I just re-fixed something
  somebody filed long ago", because its drift check compares every declared state with what the legs now do. Paying
  the debt meant three deletions, not one: the registry row's `reason`/`ref`/`pins`, the exit-6 contract row in
  `integration/bool_element_test.go`, and the probe's membership of `conformanceProbes()` — a probe cannot fail, which
  is exactly why a paid one moves to `conformanceStandalone`.
- **A shared predicate asked at 25 call sites is not widened for one door.** The obvious fix — give `isContainerExpr`
  and `staticContainerKind` a `*Comp` case, since a comprehension IS a container — is true, and it is a bundle: those
  two questions are asked by the membership test, the comparison, the loop, the truthiness door, the `%` road, the
  logic road and the argument roads. One commit per feature won, so the widening lives in exactly one place
  (`isContainerArm`/`staticContainerArmKind`, which the ternary's arms ask), and the comment says who should eventually
  fold it into the module-level pair. The rejected alternative is written into the ADR with the number of call sites,
  because "I did not do the obvious thing" needs a reason a future reader can check.
- **The failing family is larger than the failing shape.** The row was `[1, 2] if 1 else [9]`; the test-table probes
  found the comprehension arm (`[v for v in [1, "a", True]] if 1 else [9]`) still printing `0`, and it needed both the
  arm question widened AND `CompGenerator` kept out (a generator's eager-list answer is another row's divergence). A
  second probe asked whether the list printer was right for a comprehension arm whose elements carry different tags —
  the module-level road prints those with `rt_print_list_mixed` — before any expectation was typed into a table.
- **A silent wrong answer and a crash are different classes, and the report has to keep them apart.** Of the 20
  answered programs that moved: 12 off **exit 2**, 5 off a **silent `0` at exit 0**, 3 off a **refusal in words** — and
  separately 4 pairs off exit 2 into an exit-1 refusal. "17 fixed" would have been true, cheaper to write, and useless:
  the silent five are the ones that could have been shipping, and the four refusals are a *change of exit class* in the
  direction ADR 0166 asks for, which is not the same claim as "it prints now".
- **A pinned refusal has to be pinned three ways.** Exit code, message, AND empty stdout: a program that does not run
  prints nothing, so a refusal that also printed something is a different bug wearing a refusal's exit code. (The
  house pattern is `integration/module_slot_scope_test.go`, which pins an owed exit-2 with the same triple.)
- **Parallel CLI cases need per-subtest directories.** I copied `lambda_carrier_test.go`'s shape — one `t.TempDir()`
  outside the loop, every parallel subtest writing the same filename into it — and then did not copy it: same-name
  writes from parallel cases let one program's bytes be run under another's name. Fixed before the first run rather
  than after a flake.
- **The count guards are the doc editor.** Instead of guessing which numbers moved, I ran
  `TestTheRoadmapSnapshotIsMeasuredNotRemembered` first and it named all seven: programs 244 → 245, matrix rows
  230 → 231, parity 200 → 202 (two asserted rows arrived: my new program and the promoted probe), divergences
  30 → 29, `match`/`debt` 186/22 → 188/21, record 8709 → 8753, queue rows 298 → 300 with owed still 180 (two closed,
  two filed). Every one of those numbers is the artifact's; the docs just have to keep up.
- **`--json` is the machine path for a refusal too**, not only for an answer: `{"backend":"aot","exit":1,"ok":false,
  "phase":"codegen","error":"… roadmap Gap R.385 …"}`. A refusal that only exists as prose on stderr is a refusal an
  agent cannot route on.

## Tracker hygiene — Gap M.2 was owed nothing (queue row closed, 2026-10-23)

- **A retirement has to be propagated to the tracker, not just to the code.** Gap M.2 ("flip `gustyc
  --file` to the compiled backend", Pri 20, ⏳ PLANNED since 2026-08-03) was waiting for the second
  backend to stop being the default. **ADR 0302** removed that backend, `evalSrcOrFile` has one
  execution call (`lang.JITWithOptions`) and no evaluator call survives in the CLI — and the row still
  sat at the top of the queue claiming work, with a DoD clause (`--interp stays the escape hatch`) that
  describes a flag the tool now rejects as a usage error. A queue that lists finished work is worse than
  an empty queue: the loop's rule is "take the top row", so a stale row is a mis-directed cycle.
- **Measure a row before you accept it as owed.** Three CLI invocations — `--file` printing `5` at exit
  0, `--json --file` reporting `"backend": "aot"`, `--interp` exiting 4 — plus the artifact's `fail 0 /
  drift 0 / 202 asserted rows` decided the row in under a minute. The witnesses were already in
  `cmd/gustyc/main_test.go` (`TestCLIReportsWhichBackendRan`, `TestCLIShowBackendGoesToStderr`,
  `TestCLIPositionalSourcePathRuns`, the two retired-flag rows); the row had simply never been re-read
  against them.
- **Fix the ripple in the same commit.** The row was cited in four places (queue row, ledger row, the
  details record, and two "still-open gap-shaped items" sentences, one of them in `roadmap.md`'s
  sequencing note). Closing only the queue row would have left three claims that the flip is future
  work — and the `Rows owed` guard then recomputed 180 → 179 of 300, which is the tracker checking my
  own arithmetic.


## ADR 0406 — an `except … as name:` arm binds what the exception writes (Gap R.113 closed; Gaps R.395, R.396, R.397 filed, 2026-10-23)

**What was measured, not remembered.** The row was written 2026-10-02 and had never been re-asked; before writing a
line I ran the idiom through the parent binary (`5985031`) and through `python3` in one temp dir. Parent: exit 1,
`parse error at 3:26: expected ":"`. CPython: `division by zero`. That is the whole justification for the cycle, and
it is also the reason the row had stayed open for three weeks — nobody had asked whether the sentence in the ledger
still described the binary on the machine.

**The decision, in one sentence.** The reference hands an arm an exception OBJECT; this backend's value word is one
`i32`, so the arm is handed what that object **writes** — the message — interned by the one door every other text
uses, and the doors that ask the *object* a question are refused instead of answered with the message wearing the
object's clothes.

**The two-record split was the whole trick.** `print(err)` needs `printsAsInternedStr` to say yes; `len(err)` needs
`exprIsString` to say no. Both read `internedVars`, so a single record forces one of the two to lie — and the wrong
way to lie is the exit-0 one (`len(err)` → `16`, `err.upper()` → `DIVISION BY ZERO`, `err == "division by zero"` →
`True`). A separate `caughtVars`, consulted by the print/formatter roads only, is the split the reference itself
draws. It is a *deliberate* exception to ADR 0229's "one question, asked once", and the ADR says so out loud rather
than leaving a reader to find two predicates that disagree.

**Three lessons worth keeping.**

1. **The binding road, not a copy of it.** `bindCaughtName` builds an `AssignStmt` over a node the parser never
   produces (`ExnMessage`) and hands it to `stmtAssign`. Every record the family depends on — ADR 0172's
   latest-binding reset, the ADR 0228 written-flag, GC rooting, the float-slot decision — is then written by the road
   that already knows how. My first attempt emitted the slot and store by hand; it printed the *previous* binding's
   constant (`err = "stale"` before the `try` won the read) precisely because it skipped the road's records.
2. **"undefined name" came from four censuses, not one.** After the parser change, the arm's own `print(err)` still
   failed: `bodyBoundNames`, `collectModuleBindings`, `moduleBindingNames`, the written-flag walk in `boundflags.go`,
   `params.go`'s rebinding census and escape analysis's `nonListAssign` each had to learn that the arm binds. The
   `with … as` clause was the precedent at every one of them — when adding a binding form, grep for the existing
   binding form rather than for the statement you are adding.
3. **Ask the reference the question the row does not ask.** `print(type(err))` was written into a probe table as an
   ordinary way to ask what the arm caught, and it came back `parse error at 4:11: unexpected token`: `type` is in the
   lexer's keyword table, so *no program in this language can call `type()`*. That is Gap R.396, and it would never
   have been found by reading the roadmap, because the roadmap only lists questions anybody thought to ask. Same for
   `except (A, B):` (Gap R.397).

**What the pins hold.** `TestWhatTheCaughtNameStillOwesPinsTheDivergence` and its CLI twin carry nine rows of
"still wrong", each with the reference's bytes beside this backend's, and each written to fail if it ever starts
agreeing — the only shape of a regression test that cannot decay into a rumour. The corpus program
`integration/programs/except_as_name.gy` was byte-compared with `python3` before it was registered, and the matrix
moved 231 → 232 rows with `oracle_match` 188 → 189.

## The module's literal container reaches a compiled body — as a binding (Gap R.35 container half, ADR 0407)

**What I set out to do** was finish a row that had been open since the tracker began: a compiled function that reads
the module's list. **What I shipped** is half a mechanism, and the interesting part of the session is the half I
deleted.

1. **I built the interception first, and it looked like the better door.** A `moduleContainerAnswer` hook in the
   subscript and concatenation roads, answering a read from the container-answer table, measured **49 of 80 probes**
   agreeing with CPython. The frame binding — one call in the entry prologue that synthesises `xs = <the literal>` and
   hands it to `stmtAssign` — measured **40 of 80** on the same subset. I nearly kept the winner. What flipped it was
   asking *why* the interception lost rather than counting what it won: every position the interception declined fell
   through to the general road, and the general road refuses anything whose name resolves to module state. The binding
   declines nothing, because it does not answer anything — it puts the name in the state a local container is already
   in, and two hundred ADRs of roads that have been right about that state answer the module's object for free. The
   interception is gone. **An interception answers the positions it recognised; a binding answers the positions
   somebody else wrote.**
2. **The stale-table instinct fired, and the house rule caught it.** `TestACompiledBodyIsHandedTheModulesContainer`
   failed on shapes where the general road already refused; my hand went to the expectation. The rule ("a row that
   stops being true FAILS, and the case is DELETED rather than edited") pushed me to measure the *function-local*
   analogue instead — which is how I found that `def f(): xs = ["a", "b"]; return xs[1]` prints **`1`** today. The
   constant-index fold names a machine word, the word has no tag, and the index arrives where the element's payload
   should have been. That single measurement produced the door's last clause, three roadmap rows, and the reason the
   door asks a body what its `return` reaches before it hands anything over.
3. **Decline, do not refuse.** My first version raised the family's module-state error when a body's `return` reached
   an unnameable slot. It cost 16 probes: a body that reads three containers lost two of them because the third had a
   double in it. Declining the name keeps the declined name's parent-build behaviour and frees the other two to be
   answered. A gate that answers "no" too loudly is answering "no" to its neighbours.
4. **The position, not the shape.** The same `return` question mis-fired twice more before it was right: `return xs[0]
   + xs[2]` (an addition over slots) and `return not xs` (a count question) were both refused as if they handed the
   object back. The predicate was never "mentions the container" — it is "the answer is BUILT out of the object",
   which is a fact about the operand's position and not about the expression tree. `containerOperand` is now three
   lines and correct, and the two refusals it cost are the two probes that should have cost them.
5. **Sibling files are the type checker.** My first cut wrote `*LLVMCodeGen`, `TupleLit`, `DictLit.KVs`,
   `StringLit`, `walkChildren` — none of which exist. This emitter is `irGen`, building IR *text* into a
   `strings.Builder`, with `containerAnswer{kind, arms, fullyDescribed}`, `Tuple`, `DictLit.Keys/Vals` and its own
   walker per file. Reading `module_float.go` and `container_return.go` before writing cost me one build cycle;
   writing first cost me four.
6. **Two of my probe rows were born wrong and stayed wrong.** `[1.5, 2.5]` → `2` and `[True, False]` → `0` are
   byte-identical on the parent build, which is the difference between "this door broke it" and "this door found it".
   The A/B harness makes that distinction mechanically, so the sentence in the ADR is a measured claim and not a
   hunch about blame.

## ADR 0408 — the join seam is the concatenation (Gap R.403 closed; Gaps R.404, R.405, R.406 filed, 2026-10-24)

`n = 3` / `print("-".join([f"a{n}", "z"]))` printed `a3-z` in the reference and exited **1** here with
`join() list elements must be constant strings`. `str.join` was a fold over `*StringLit`s, and one interpolation in
the list dropped the program out of the road. The row is closed, and the interesting part is not the seam.

1. **A refusal is not the boundary of a feature — it is often a wall in front of three wrong answers.** The first
   probe family over "what should `join` answer" measured 3 of 33 agreeing on the parent build. After the seam
   landed, three programs began reaching exit 0 with wrong bytes: `def f(): return "-".join([f"a{n}", "z"])`
   printed **`6`**, the same body through a frame-local `s` printed `6` and `10`, and a join arm beside a number arm
   printed `a-b` and `(null)`. `6` is the `@str_tab` **index** of `a3-z` — the number the intern table stores that
   text under — printed as a number. Every one of them was a **pre-scan** verdict: a caller holds one word and a
   name, and the scan that decides which printer gets that word had never heard of `join`. Had I stopped at "the
   refusal is now correct", all three would have shipped.
2. **"One door per construction" is a measurement, not a taste.** My first draft of the ADR said the row *needed* a
   runtime join. It did not: `@rt_str_cat` has built texts while the program ran since **ADR 0229**, on the `+` road,
   interning into the same `@str_tab`; a join is that concatenation with the separator between the neighbours. The
   guard now asserts the module gains **no `define`** from this row and that the all-constant program still emits **no
   `@rt_str_cat`** — a claim about absence has to be a test, or the next "helpful" rewrite silently un-folds the easy
   case and nobody notices for forty ADRs.
3. **A fact the compiler asks twice is a fact that answers yes once.** `join` was already in the method fold's
   table of text-answering methods (`textMethodAnswersText`) and in none of the shape predicates the pre-passes ask
   (`isStringExpr`, `isStrUnder`) — which is exactly how a method answers *as a text* in one position and *as an
   index* in another. The fix is **ADR 0232**'s rule again: `joinShapeIsText` joins the formatting door (**ADR 0360**)
   and the repeat door (**ADR 0365**) in the shape predicate, `isStrUnder` answers `join` beside the case family, and
   the print road, the parameter census, the `return` road and the answer-kind census all start seeing the same
   thing. The per-node alternative — special-case a join operand at the print door — is what **ADR 0407** measured at
   49-of-80 against a binding's 111-of-178; interception answers positions it recognises, and the census answers
   everywhere.
4. **Walk the body before judging the body.** `scanStringBindings` asked "does this `def` hand back a text?" *before*
   walking its own statements, so a frame-local `s = <text>` was not yet in `internedVars` when the function's answer
   was typed. Moving the walk above the judgement changed exactly one class of verdict — the one a body earns from its
   own bindings — because a `def` written later already saw those names either way. Ordering bugs in a pre-pass are
   invisible until a program is written that depends on the missing fact; the program here was twelve characters long
   (`s = ` … `return s`).
5. **The answer-kind census has an arm shape it cannot see, and the control row is what filed it.** A body with a
   join arm and a number arm should be *carried* by the **ADR 0368** plan (mixed bodies answer, they are not refused);
   it was not, because `answerArmOf` classifies a literal, an interpolation, a text door and a call — not a **name**
   `internedVars` holds — so the body looked one-kind and got one printer. The evidence that this is the census's and
   not `join`'s: the same body spelled `s = "ab".upper()` prints `AB` / `(null)` on the parent build too, byte for
   byte. That control is a test row now, beside the join row, both pinned at the wrong bytes with the reference's
   answer next to them (**Gap R.406**). A wrong answer you can attribute is a row; one you cannot is a rumour.
6. **A raise belongs to the program, a refusal belongs to the compiler.** An element the compiler can *see* is not a
   text now traps at exit **3** with the reference's `TypeError: sequence item 1: expected str instance, int found`
   (`bool` spelled `bool`, `None` spelled `NoneType`), catchable by the program's own `except TypeError:`; an element
   whose kind it cannot read is refused at exit 1. The fold-era road had this backwards — exit-1 prose for the case the
   reference answers by raising. `--json` gives the trap its `exception` / `exception_message` / `frames`; a refusal
   gives a `capability` code. Those two faces must not be conflated, or an agent reads a program's bug as the
   compiler's limitation.
7. **The recorder's refusals are the rows.** `tools/recmerge` wrote 33 entries for this family from CPython
   (`8851 → 8884`) and refused four programs; those four refusals are **Gap R.404**, **Gap R.405** and the two
   **Gap R.406** pins (**ADR 0309**). A table whose expectations the backend wrote would have called all four green.
8. **Trust the grep, not the memory.** Twice this cycle I reasoned from a "read" of a file that turned out not to hold
   what I remembered — `isTextShape`, `tagForTypeName`, `funcReturnType` are not in this package, and acting on them
   cost failed builds and one wrong diagnosis ("the fold mixes string objects with the string struct", which was a
   story about code I had not actually re-read). The discipline that fixed it: before editing on the strength of a
   remembered body, `grep` for a distinctive token from it, and if the token is absent, re-read the file. A model's
   confidence is not evidence about a file; the file is.

## ADR 0409 — the truth of a text is its length (Gap R.407 closed; Gaps R.408, R.410 closed, R.409 filed, 2026-10-24)

Found by asking the roadmap's own next action a question: **L11.1** names "the interpolation as a text value" with a
list of shapes, so I measured all of them against CPython. 54 of 60 agreed; the six that did not pointed at one
wrong question in a door I had not touched — `if f():` where `f` hands back a text printed the else arm at **exit 0**.

1. **A refusal is a wall, not a boundary — and an exit-0 wrong answer is a wall with a green light on it.** The join
   row last cycle was a refusal hiding three wrong answers; this row was twelve wrong answers with no refusal in
   front of them. `def f(): return "abc"` / `if f():` → `f`, `while f(i):` never entered, `not f()` → `True`,
   `"y" if f() else "n"` → `n`, a method's text answer → false, `s = f()` / `if s:` → else arm, `except … as err:` /
   `if err:` → else arm. The condition road's fallback tests the operand against zero, and a text's value is an
   `@str_tab` **index**: the question it asked was *which table entry*, not *how many characters*. Entry 0 is the
   first text a program interns, so every failing program is a two-liner and every passing one is a program that
   interned something first — the worst possible distribution of a bug, because the failures look like toys.
2. **The door existed before the road did.** `rt_str_len` is the arm `@rt_pair_truth` takes for the text tag, and the
   unrolled loop item has asked it since **ADR 0386/0393** for exactly this reason. The condition road never got the
   memo because there was no road: `if f():` could not even be *asked* until the container-answer door (**ADR 0333**)
   and the answer-kind gate (**ADR 0368**) made a call's answer answerable. Each later ADR widened what an answer can
   be and left one reader with its old guess. **ADR 0232** — one question, asked by every road — is not a style rule;
   it is the only thing that keeps a widening from becoming a divergence.
3. **Do not wait for the representation to fix the answer.** The tempting framing was "this is L11.1's tagged word;
   file it and move on". The tagged word would fix this family, and would first need **Gap R.324**'s four bare-payload
   doors and **Gap R.406**'s name arm. Meanwhile the exit-0 wrongness is answerable today with a helper that already
   exists. A representation change is a reason to *simplify later*, never a reason to leave a wrong answer shipping.
4. **Assert the absence, not just the presence.** The IR guard checks that a call's-text condition emits
   `@rt_str_len` **and** that a literal condition emits none. Only the second half keeps the fold honest; a suite with
   just the first passes contentedly after someone routes the easy case through the runtime.
5. **Controls are how you keep a widened door from eating its neighbours.** The answered family sits beside a control
   family (a call's number, a call's container, a mixed-kind body, a loop item, a pair parameter, `and`/`or`,
   an ordering, the fold) run against both builds. It found nothing broken this time — and found that two of the
   controls' diffs were identical byte-for-byte on the parent build, which is how **Gap R.409** (mixed-kind parameter)
   and **Gap R.131** (`bool([1])`) got filed against the right owners instead of against this commit.
6. **A refusal without a code is a sentence only a human can read.** Walking the family surfaced two refusals —
   `print(bool([1]))` and `w(0)` beside `w("a")` — that resolve to **no capability code**, which is the **L11.8** /
   **ADR 0346** contract broken in place. The tell: the sentence quoted a roadmap row (`Gap R.131`) and still nobody
   could branch on it programmatically. Codes are the machine path for refusals; `ClassifyCapabilityRefusal` returning
   false on a sentence a program can reach is a bug in its own right (**Gap R.408**).
7. **Environment is state, and subprocesses inherit it.** Running the artifact mode exactly as documented —
   `GUSTY_GOLDEN_UPDATE=1 go test ./integration/` — came back having rewritten **`pkg/lang`'s** drift ledger down to
   one row. The parallelism guard shells out to a `-run`-filtered `go test ./pkg/lang/`, and the ledger is adjudicated
   by whichever process finishes. Same class as **ADR 0343**'s toolchain globals, one level up: a run-scoped fact
   travelling as inherited process state. Fixed by scrubbing the four `GUSTY_*` artifact variables in `parifyEnv`, with
   a case that sets each in the parent and asserts the child never sees it (**Gap R.410**). The general rule for this
   repo: if the correctness of an artifact depends on how a person invokes the suite, the suite has to refuse the
   invocation that would break it.
8. **What I did with the roadmap's "next action" cell.** It names ~26 interpolation shapes as the work owed on L11.1.
   Measuring it was cheaper than trusting it: 54/60 already answered, so the row's next action is stale prose, and the
   real work was in a door the list never mentioned. A tracker row is a pointer to a measurement, not a substitute for
   one — and when the measurement says the row is answered, the row changes and the loop moves on.

## ADR 0410 — the slot a `pop()` removes leaves the list wearing what it was stored as (Gap R.411 closed; Gaps R.412, R.413, R.414 filed, 2026-10-24)

The tracker's open queue named **L11.1** — the tagged value word — and pointed at "the slot a container method
removes". Three programs, found by writing the ordinary ones: `xs = [1, 2, "a"]` / `xs.pop(0)` / `print(xs)` wrote
`[2, 0]` at **exit 0**; `xs = ["a", 1]` / `xs.pop(0)` / `if xs[0]:` died at **exit 139** with nothing on stdout;
`print(xs.pop(0))` answered `0` for a text, `1` for a double, and an arena slot for a nested list. One defect, three
failure kinds.

1. **A slot is two words and a door that moves one of them is the bug, not the reader.** `@rt_pop` shifted the
   payload array, shrank the length, returned the removed payload — and never touched `@heap_tags`. So the tail wore
   the kind of the slot it landed on, and the popped answer wore whatever kind the removed slot's *last tenant*
   carried, because the tag array is not cleared on free. That last clause is the one to remember: an answer that
   depends on the program's **history** instead of its source looks like a heisenbug and is only a missing store.
2. **The precedent was in the same file.** `rt_reverse` swaps the tag with the payload (**ADR 0187**),
   `rt_set_discard_tagged` shifts both, the indexed store drops the old tag. `pop` was the third positional door and
   the one nobody had walked. When a rule already has two implementers in one file, the fix for the third is to read
   the file, not to invent a representation — and the resulting helper signature change (`@rt_pop` growing an
   `i32* %outt`) added **no new runtime entry point**, which is what kept this a codegen row rather than a memory-model
   cycle.
3. **A pair answer has to travel through doors that already exist, or you have written a second printer.** The
   temptation was to render the popped value where it is produced. Instead the removal hands `(payload, tag)` to the
   positions that already ask a door — the printer, `str`, the truth road, `==`, the ordering, the tagged arithmetic
   door, a literal's element, a function's parameter — each given exactly one popped arm. The version that failed
   first: I answered the pair inside `numericExprPair`, which stepped around `taggedArithPair`'s refuse arms, and
   `print(xs.pop(0) > 1)` printed `False` where the reference raises. A gate paid to step around a door's refusal is
   **Gap R.296**'s bug restated; routing through `arithWouldRefuse` turned that wrong answer into the reference's
   raise.
4. **A gate and a door must be asked the same question in the same test.** `popAnswerShape` answers three things —
   the object's own tag for a self-describing list, the notebook's claim for a single-kind list, **DECLINE** for a
   kind no notebook describes — and `TestThePopAnswerShapeHasThreeAnswers` puts the gate's answer and the door's IR
   in one table (**ADR 0249**). Guessing `TagInt` for an undescribed container would have shipped a quieter version
   of the bug this row exists to remove (**ADR 0166**), so the third answer is a decline and the decline is pinned.
5. **The record leg refused to testify twice, and both refusals were correct.** `tools/recmerge` wrote **79** entries
   from CPython (**8912 → 8991**) and declined `xs = ["a", 1]` / `print(xs.pop(0) + 1)` because this backend's
   sentence (`unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'str' and 'int'`) is not the reference's (`can only concatenate str
   (not "int") to str`) — same class, wrong words, so the program is **Gap R.413**'s and not the record's. And when I
   put a program the record *does* answer — a dict's `pop` over a name, which this backend refuses — into a CLI case,
   the `integration` drift guard failed the run until the row was adjudicated into the ledger (**19 → 20**). Both
   mechanisms are the same one: the compiled leg never writes an answer, and a compiled refusal is never an answer.
6. **A test that asks the record a question inherits the record's debts.** The dict case was written as "assert the
   refusal sentence", which is reasonable until the helper notices the record disagrees and files a divergence on your
   behalf. The lesson is not to dodge the helper — it is to ask refusals through `Compile`, which witnesses nothing,
   and to ask answers through the record, which does.
7. **Two sentences, because the reference has two.** `pop from empty list` for the empty list, `pop index out of
   range` for the rest. This backend had one, for the empty case. Nobody files a roadmap row for a missing article in
   an exception message; it only surfaces when the program that asks is written down, which is the argument for
   measuring a family rather than the defect that started it.
8. **What stayed wrong, and why that is the commit's shape.** **35 of 63** programs moved to the reference's answer,
   **17** controls held, **11** still differ — and each of the 11 is a row (**Gap R.412** the popped slot against
   `None`, **Gap R.413** a popped text in an arithmetic position in three shapes, **Gap R.414** a body whose `return`
   *is* the popped slot, plus the refusals **Gap R.35**, **Gap R.174**, **L11.3** already own). R.414's control is the
   best finding in the file: `return xs[1]` is *refused* while `return xs.pop(1)` prints `0`, which localises the bug
   to the pop road rather than to the slot, and is the difference between a row someone can start and a row that reads
   "the pair system is wrong somewhere".

## ADR 0411 — the identity question asked against the void is asked of the TAG (Gap R.412 closed; Gaps R.415, R.416, R.417, R.418 filed, 2026-10-24)

**ADR 0410** left its own honest table with one row that bothered me more than the bug it fixed:
`xs = [None, 1]` printed `None` for the popped slot, printed `True` for `xs.pop(0) == None`, and printed **`False`**
for `xs.pop(0) is None`. One value, one question, three readers, two answers — and the two readers that were right
were right because of a door `is` had never been allowed through.

1. **The fold was not broken; it was being asked a question it cannot answer.** The None-equality road's own comment
   says it "decides the result statically, from what the source says each side is". That is sound whenever the source
   states the kinds (`print(1 is None)` must cost no call) and is a **guess** when the kind lives in a container the
   program built. And it is a guess with a specific failure mode: the payload a void leaves behind is `0`, which is
   also what an `int` slot carries, what the intern table's first entry is, and what the arena's first slot is. A
   fold that tests the payload is testing which number is in the box — **ADR 0172**'s collision, wearing the identity
   road's clothes. The lesson generalises: *a static decision procedure is only sound over operands the source can
   settle*, and the check "what does this road actually key on?" is cheap to ask of every fold in the file.
2. **The correct-sounding widening was the one to refuse.** Letting every `is` through the pair door is a three-line
   diff and answers `[1] is [1]` `True` — because `@rt_payload_eq` compares containers by **content** (**ADR 0189**),
   and content equality is the wrong answer to an identity question. So the door admits the void (a singleton, where
   identity and equality genuinely coincide) and declines everything else, and the shape it declines is filed with
   the assembler's own line beside it: `print([1] is [1])` dies on `icmp eq i32 @.lst1, @.lst2` at **exit 2**
   (**Gap R.418**). Choosing between a wrong answer at exit 0 and an obvious failure at exit 2 is not a style
   question; the second one cannot be shipped by accident.
3. **A door has to be hung in every road that asks its question, or the suite can't tell which one answered.**
   `print(x is None)` lowers through the value road, `if x is None:` through the condition road — two functions, one
   `BinOp`. **ADR 0232** learned this for the tagged equality and hangs it twice; my first cut widened only the value
   side, and the only reason that showed up is that the family contains `if xs.pop(0) is None:` and
   `while xs.pop(0) is None:`, which disagreed with each other. Both hooks, one door, and an IR case that counts
   `rt_payload_eq` calls per question.
4. **Assert the fold is still a fold.** The IR guard runs in both directions: the popped slot's `@main` carries one
   `call i32 @rt_payload_eq(i32 %popped, i32 %tag, i32 0, i32 3)`, and the four literal controls carry **no pair call
   at all**. A one-directional version of that test passes happily after someone routes the easy case through the
   runtime, which is a slower, vaguer version of the same bug (**ADR 0385**).
5. **Four of the seventeen "fixes" were refusals turning into answers.** A slot read of a mixed list, a tuple's slot,
   a loop element over a named list, a pair-bound name: each of those positions used to be refused because it wanted
   one word and the read carries two. Measuring "moved to the reference" without separating refusal→answer from
   wrong→right hides the part users feel, so both columns are now in the row's evidence cell.
6. **The residue was localised by controls, not by reading the code.** `ys = xs` / `print(ys.pop(0))` prints `0`
   (**Gap R.415**) while `xs.pop(0)` prints `None`; `for v in xs` answers while `for v in [None, "a"]` does not
   (**Gap R.416**); `if v:` inside a callee answers while `return v is None` does not (**Gap R.417**). Each sibling
   pair says which notebook is missing an entry, and each is byte-identical on the parent build — that last clause is
   the sentence that separates a filed debt from a regression, and it is why I keep a parent binary alive through the
   whole cycle.
7. **A paid row's pin gets deleted, not edited.** Two owed-table rows in the pop family were this row's program
   wearing a `False`. Editing them to `True` would have left a "owed" table that pins reference answers and hides the
   fact that the debt is gone; deleting them and moving the programs to the answered table is the only spelling that
   distinguishes a paid debt from a rewritten one.
8. **Numbers are recomputed, never remembered.** The record went **8991 → 9025** (`tools/recmerge`, from CPython,
   refusing nothing because the compiled leg agreed on every source claimed as paid); the snapshot's ADR cell moved
   to **402 records, highest 0411**, rows owed to **194 of 324**. The Open-queue blank-line guard caught my own
   formatting on the way (`countQueueRows` counts rows under a stray blank line as `hidden` and fails), and the
   snapshot test would have failed the run rather than bless a remembered number (**Gap R.204**).

## ADR 0412 — the alias of a list answers what the name that built it answers (Gap R.415 closed; Gap R.419 filed, 2026-10-24)

**ADR 0411** filed it as residue and I found it the way most of these are found: by writing the ordinary program
beside the door. `xs = [None, 1]` / `print(xs.pop(0))` prints `None`; add one line — `ys = xs` — ask the same
question of `ys`, and the same backend prints **`0`** at **exit 0**. Two programs, one object, one name different.

1. **The renderer had the right rule and was handed the wrong words.** `print` asks the `(payload, tag)` pair;
   under the alias it received a payload and nothing else. The reason is that `ys = xs` shares the *handle* and
   the notebook — `mixedLists`, `listElemStr`, `listElemInt` — is keyed by **NAME**. Fixing the printer would have
   bought one road and left `ys[0]`, `for v in ys`, `if ys.pop(0):` and `str(ys.pop(0))` to be repaired one at a
   time. The localising question is not "which road renders it wrongly" but "which notebook never got written".
2. **Three halves, and the measurement says all three are load-bearing.** Copy the claims at the binding: without
   it the mutation doors read an empty record for the alias and store an *untagged* payload into a tagged
   container, and the read-back is a **SIGSEGV** (`ys.append("a")` / `print(xs.pop(2))`). Keep the link and follow
   it at read time: without it the copy is a claim about the moment of the binding and `xs = []` / `ys = xs` /
   `xs.append("a")` is an event after it. Tell the promotion to every sharer: without that, `xs.append("a")` leaves
   `ys` claiming integers about a list whose next slot is a text. Each of the three is a test table, because each
   is a *half*-fix that passes the obvious cases.
3. **A link is a lookup, not a redirection.** The handle is still loaded from the name the read is written against
   (`%_ys` in the module) — only the *claims* resolve to the name that built the object. That distinction is what
   makes `xs = [None, 1]` / `ys = xs` / `xs = [2, None]` / `print(ys[0])` answer for the FIRST list: the copied
   claims describe the object `ys` holds, and `forgetContainerAlias` kills the link when either name is handed
   another object. Had I redirected the read instead, the alias would have followed a rebinding it must not see.
4. **One lookup, asked by every door.** The gate (`popAnswerShape`) and the door (`popAnswerPair`) read the SAME
   `listElementClaims` table, and the slot read and the loop's tagged arm read `mixedListRead` — because **ADR
   0249**'s rule is not stylistic: my first cut resolved in the door only, and the gate said "not a tagged list"
   while the door said "served", which is a wrong answer wearing a refusal's clothes. The gate test asks all three
   answers (object's tag / record's claim / DECLINE) from one table with the door asked beside it.
5. **The decline is the answer a fix tries to lose.** Following a link into an empty record is not a licence to
   guess a kind — a guessed kind is how a payload gets printed under a label the object never gave it (**ADR
   0166**), which is the bug this row exists to remove. The cycle (`a = b` above `b = a`) is pinned behind a
   watchdog too: an infinite walk would be the compiler's fault, not the program's.
6. **No new road, and the IR proves it.** The alias's removal goes through the one `@rt_pop(i32, i32, i32*)`
   **ADR 0410** hung; the guard counts one call per removal, checks the out-parameter and the alias's own handle,
   and names four helpers that must never appear (`@rt_pop_aliased`, `@rt_pop_alias`, `@rt_alias_`,
   `@rt_tag_elem_aliased`). A name is not a new kind of container, and the temptation to write `…_aliased` shows
   up the moment a fix is described in terms of the alias instead of in terms of the object.
7. **Its sibling containers are a row, not a footnote.** I stopped at the list, because `recordContainerAlias`
   copies the claims whose doors exist. `e = d` / `e["b"] = "x"` / `print(d)` writes `{'a': 1, 'b': 1}` — the
   intern index under a label — and `t.add("a")` and `e[7] = 2` segfault. All three byte-identical on the parent
   `8aa3029`, which is the sentence that makes them **Gap R.419** rather than this commit's damage; `w(ys.pop(0))`
   printing `0` is **Gap R.417** reached through the alias, byte-identical to the non-alias twin, and a slot bound
   and asked as a condition is **Gap R.146**'s one-word position refused exactly as its non-alias twin is.
8. **Measurement discipline paid for itself.** 42 answered programs, parent build beside this one, each asked of
   the pinned CPython: **26 moved, 16 controls held, 0 regressions, 0 of the family still differing**. My first
   harness counted 45 and reported 18 controls because it harvested `want` strings and format strings out of the
   Go tables as "programs" that trivially agreed (both legs printed nothing). Filtering those is not cosmetic: an
   inflated control count is a lie about coverage, and the number that goes in the row is the number a reader can
   reproduce.
9. **Paid pins are deleted, and the harvest is the record's, not mine.** The void family's owed table lost
   `the same list under a second name` outright — the program moved into this file's answered family — which is
   **ADR 0411**'s precedent applied a second time. `tools/recmerge` wrote the **36** entries (**9025 → 9061**) and
   refused nothing, because the compiled leg agreed on every source claimed as paid; and when I could not say *why*
   the file had grown 36 entries during development, the answer was to restore it from HEAD and re-record it through
   the sanctioned writer rather than trust a diff I could not attribute (**ADR 0309**'s rule is only worth what
   you're willing to prove about it). The guards caught the rest, as they always do: the snapshot's record cell, the
   queue-row total (**194 of 325** — the new **Gap R.419** row) and the ADR cell (**403 records, highest 0412**) are
   the artifacts', not my memory (**Gap R.204**).

## ADR 0413 — the alias door is a CONTAINER door (Gap R.419 closed; Gaps R.420, R.421, R.422 filed, 2026-10-24)

**ADR 0412** paid the list's shared-handle binding and named the dict and the set as "the same defect one
container over". Their bytes were already pinned in the owed table, so this cycle was a widening rather than a
discovery — and it still taught me twice.

1. **An empty notebook is not ignorance, it is a confident wrong answer.** The dict store door decides whether an
   incoming value needs a tag written with it by asking `dictValInt[name]`/`dictValStr[name]`. Handed an alias with
   *nothing recorded*, it does not abstain — it concludes *nothing contradicts*, stores the entry unlabelled, and the
   printer renders `{'a': 1, 'b': 1}`: the text's intern index under a label the object never gave it. I had been
   describing the missing-copy bug as "the door can't see the record". It can't see it *and it answers anyway*, which
   is why the fix is the copy and not another `if` at the door.
2. **The same door, widened — not a second door.** Every container already had its store, its add, its printer; they
   read the same name-keyed maps for every program in the corpus. So `containerKindHeld` + per-kind copying + the
   `mark*Mixed` trio walking `containerSharers` is the whole change, and the IR is unchanged: `rt_dict_put_tagged`
   and `rt_set_add_tagged` are still the only lowering. If a fix for a *name* needs an `…_aliased` helper, the fix
   has grown a second answer to one question (**ADR 0249**'s rule, now with a second example).
3. **The promotion walk stopped being decoration on the second container.** For the list, copying alone got me most
   of the way; for the dict, writing `d["b"] = "x"` through the alias promotes the *object*, and clearing the
   single-kind claim on the mutated name alone left the other name printing every slot through a table it had
   outgrown — the row's own wrong answer, arriving from the opposite side of the alias. One event, one object, every
   name.
4. **Three of the "alias" defects had nothing to do with aliases.** The dict rebound under its own alias prints the
   *second* dict (the rebinding's `rt_free` releases an object the alias still roots and the allocator hands the same
   slot straight back); a set with a void member prints `{1, None}` where CPython prints `{None, 1}`; and
   `s.discard("a")` over `{1, 2}` removes `2`, comparing the payload where the pair is the discriminator. Each
   reproduces with no alias in the program and on the parent build — that column is what kept them as rows
   (**Gap R.420**, **R.421**, **R.422**) instead of smuggling three unrelated fixes into a notebook commit.
5. **A refusal and a wrong answer are different debts, and a harness that conflates them hides one.** The CLI owed
   table only knew "answered wrongly", so the two **Gap R.417**/**R.174** refusals I moved into it failed with
   *"the shape was REFUSED rather than answered wrongly — move this row"*. The fix was a `refuses` arm that requires
   exit 1 and forbids exit 2 (**ADR 0006**, **ADR 0166**), because "still refused" and "still wrong" must each be able
   to fail independently.
6. **Measure with a battery, verify with the parent.** 37 dict/set programs, parent `8aa3029` beside this build,
   each asked of CPython: **15 agreeing → 31, none moved away**. Keeping the parent binary alive is the only reason I
   can say "this one is older than me" about six of the seven leftovers — and the battery caught two shapes (`t.add(None)`,
   `discard`) that no table I had written would have asked about.
7. **Numbers are the artifacts', never mine.** The record went **9061 → 9084** (`tools/recmerge`, from CPython, 23
   entries, none refused because the compiled leg agreed on all of them), the snapshot's cells to **404 records,
   highest 0413** and **196 of 328** rows owed, and the guards failed the run until every doc repeated the file's own
   number rather than my note about it (**Gap R.204**).

## ADR 0415 — a set keeps its members in the reference's bucket order, at the door that inserts (Gap R.421 closed; Gaps R.423, R.424 filed, 2026-10-24)

1. **An order is not cosmetic when two doors read one array.** The row arrived as "the printer puts the void
   last", and the printer is exactly where it must not be fixed: `print(s)` and `for x in s` are two doors over the
   same `@heap` slots, and CPython answers them with one sequence because it has one table. A sort inside
   `rt_set_print_mixed` would have printed `{None, 1}` while the loop went on printing `1, None` — two orders for one
   set, one of them invisible until someone writes the loop. The loop program is therefore pinned in the same table
   as its `print` twin, so a future printer-sort fails the row instead of passing it.

2. **Copy the reference's RULE, not its shape.** The bucket is `hash(x) mod size`; an int hashes to itself, and
   CPython's own documented exception — `hash(-1) == -2`, so that `-1` never wears the value the C API reserves for
   an error — is not a quirk to invent around but part of the rule worth carrying. The void hashes to a constant that
   lands it in bucket 0, which is the whole of "the void prints first". And where the reference's hash is not a
   function of the payload at all — a text's is salted per process, and four runs of `{"a", None}` really did give two
   different orders — the answer is `8`, "not participating", and the member keeps its insertion position. Guessing a
   bucket for a text would have broken the record-agreed `{1, 2, 'a'}` to chase a coin flip.

3. **A shift is a shift is a shift.** Making `add` insert meant moving the tail right by one, and the pair rule of
   **ADR 0410** applies verbatim in the other direction: move payload and tag together or every moved member wakes up
   wearing the kind of the slot it landed on. The three doors are now `rt_pop` (left), `rt_reverse`'s swap, and this
   one (right) — the same sentence in `codegen_ir_set.go`'s comment keeps them from drifting apart.

4. **The measured boundary became two rows, not two hedges.** `{5, 3, 9, 1}` and a 9-member set that trips the
   reference's resize are wrong at exit 0 after this commit exactly as before it — differently wrong, which is worse
   to read and no worse to a user. They are **Gap R.424** with the reference's bytes and this backend's pinned side by
   side, in both owed tables, rather than a rule quietly extended until the two tables happen to agree. **Gap R.423**
   is the discovery underneath — and the claim I had to take back. The set literal has two fill roads: its mixed arm
   goes through the ordered door (`s = {1, None, 3}` prints `{None, 1, 3}`), its single-kind arm fills positionally with
   `rt_set_elem` beside `rt_tag_elem` (`s = {3, 1, 2}` keeps the source's order). My first statement blamed the missing
   order on a missing tag; a build of the tree showed `rt_tag_elem` beside every positional member, exactly as **ADR
   0187**/**ADR 0189** require. What that arm withholds is the PLACE, not the tag — and a row's root-cause sentence is a
   claim about the artifact, so it was corrected the same day rather than left to rot. One road, one rule — the literal belongs at the same door as
   `s.add(v)`, and that is the row.

5. **Numbers are the artifacts', never mine — and `--emit-llvm`'s argument shape bit me twice.** `--emit-llvm`
   consumes the next argv, so `--emit-llvm --verify --file x.gy` reported `undefined name "verify"`: the CLI is
   `--file x.gy --emit-llvm`, or ask `tools/gymap`. The record is **9084 → 9094** from `tools/recmerge` (10 sources,
   none refused, the compiled leg agreeing on every one), and the snapshot cells moved to **405 records, highest
   0415** and **197 of 330** only after the guards read the files and told me the numbers they had already earned.

6. **A sibling worker's uncommitted change can falsify your pins; park it, do not adopt it.** Halfway through this
   cycle the tree held someone else's uncommitted **Gap R.420** work (`rt_release`, a root-aware release, in
   `codegen_gc.go` and `codegen_ir_arena_globals.go`) — which made the R.420 pins this session had just committed fail
   with *"already paid — delete it"*, and made my gate red over a change I neither wrote nor could finish. I copied
   both files aside with their md5s, restored them to HEAD so the suite measured my change alone, gated and committed
   that, and put the work back. Two rules fell out of it: **never commit another worker's in-flight change to pay for
   your own green**, and **leave a number you did not earn unissued** — `ADR 0414` belongs to that change, so this row
   cites `0415` and says why in its Status cell.

## ADR 0414 — a released container is asked who still holds it, at the door in front of the free list (Gaps R.420 and R.257 closed; Gaps R.426, R.427 filed, 2026-10-24)

1. **A free list is a queue of slots, and a slot cannot be both free and rooted — so the question has to be
   asked before the push.** The obvious fix was in the collector: `rt_gc` marks the whole free list dead (`2`)
   before it marks from the roots, and `rt_gc_mark` only marks a slot whose mark is `0`, which is why a rooted
   object that had been released stayed pushable. Letting the root mark override that dead mark looks like a
   two-line repair and is a corruption machine: the slot stays on the free list, live, and the next `rt_alloc`
   hands a live object to a fresh container. The mark array is one pass's scratch; ownership lives in the free
   list. Every "fix it in the GC" instinct about this family has to survive that sentence first.

2. **The parked change was the right shape, and finishing it was cheaper than rewriting it.** **ADR 0415**'s
   session set aside another worker's uncommitted `rt_release` and deliberately left `ADR 0414` unissued for it.
   This round picked that change up: it already had the door, the kind-byte gate and the clear-before-release
   order, and it already answered the row's two programs. What it did not have was the witnesses, and the
   difference between the two states is the whole commit — see rule 6. Adding `g.heapUsed = true` inside
   `emitFree` (the road that emits a call into a gated block claims the block, **ADR 0173**) also stopped the
   change depending on the textual block-usage probe noticing a call the flag was supposed to assert.

3. **A witness is a claim about the artifact, and for a release-order bug the artifact is the instruction
   sequence.** Two runs of the same source can differ here depending on whether the freed slot happens to be up
   for reuse: the same disease showed itself as `KeyError: 1` at exit 3 in one program and as a silently plausible
   number in another. Output-only tests certify whichever case the allocator was in the mood for. So the suite now
   reads the emitted `define` blocks: `@rt_free` has exactly one caller in a module and it stands inside
   `@rt_release`; and the six positions of a rebinding — `load %_d` → `rt_root_clear %_d` → `icmp ne` →
   `rt_release` → `rt_alloc` → `store %_d` — are compared pairwise, each adjacent pair load-bearing (clear-before-load
   releases an untested word, release-after-store frees the NEW object, alloc-before-release hands the freed slot
   straight to the new dict).

4. **Ask the kind, never the payload — and prove it with the arena's own number.** The first draft of the door
   compared "does any root's word equal this handle?", which is the conservative collector's failure re-opened: an
   `int` variable holding `3` would veto the release of slot `3`, and every program with a small integer in scope
   would leak. The gate is the kind byte, exactly as in the collector's mark phase (**ADR 0181**). The test that
   keeps it honest does not read a comment: it pads a program with twelve int roots whose words are the indices
   `0..12` and requires the collector's `headroom=` to be identical to the same program without them.

5. **A row paid by a mechanism it did not name still closes — and its `Blocked on` cell is where the residue goes.**
   **Gap R.257** asked for a refcount carried by the object; what answers it is a question asked of the names,
   because the names are what the root table holds. Its Definition of done (pinned program, loop form that forces
   the freed slot round the arena, two negative controls) is met, so it closed and its debt pin was DELETED — which
   is what that pin's own failure message said to do. But the mechanism chose the row's boundary: an object that
   survives only in another container's SLOT is invisible to a table of names, so `xs = {"a": 1}` / `d = {"k": xs}` /
   `xs = {"b": 2}` / allocate / `print(d["k"])` still prints the second dict. That is **Gap R.427**, filed with the
   list twin (which is right, because that road allocates before it releases) pinned beside it, and the row links
   back to R.257's `Blocked on` for the count that would settle it.

6. **"It works when I run it" is not a commit.** The parked change already made both row programs print the
   reference's bytes; it had no test file, no record entries, no docs, and the two owed-table pins that its own fix
   invalidates were still in the tree failing. Half of this round was the parts that make a behaviour a fact: 17
   answered shapes on the compiled leg AND the record leg, the traps beside them, the two IR-shape suites, the CLI
   family against a live `python3`, two corpus programs plus their matrix rows, 30 records from `tools/recmerge`,
   and the deletion of the pins that the fix had silently paid (`TestWhatTheAliasRowStillOwesIsFiledNotFixed`, its
   CLI twin, and `TestTheAliasedContainerIsADebtRowNotAnAnswer` — whose failure was the only reason I found
   **Gap R.257** had been paid too).

7. **Guards found the second row; eyeballs would not have.** `sorted(d)` over `{"a": 1, "b": 2}` answering
   `['a', 1]` turned up because I wrote a family case asking a held dict's keys and diffed against CPython — the
   dict's array holds two words per entry while its `len` counts entries, the same stride question `rt_gc` was
   taught in **ADR 0350**. Filed as **Gap R.426** with the parent build named, not adopted: one commit, one feature.

8. **Numbers are the artifacts'.** `tools/recmerge` took the record **9094 → 9124** (30 entries, none refused), the
   corpus grew two programs and two matrix rows, and the snapshot moved to **406 records, highest 0415** and
   **198 of 333** — every one of them written after a guard quoted the file's number back at me, and two of the
   owed-table rows I closed being counted before I noticed they were closed. The `TestEmptyBindingNeverFreesHandleZero`
   guard also had to be re-pointed at the door that exists (`rt_release` behind its null test) rather than the push
   underneath it; its slot-0 half is unchanged, and the file says who asks what now.

## ADR 0417 — a dict is sorted by its keys, at the door that copies it (Gap R.426 closed; Gaps R.429, R.430 filed, 2026-10-24)

1. **"Ask the base what it is" is a rule, not a fix.** Three doors walk a dict's payload array — the collector, the
   printer, and `sorted` — and two of them had been *told* the stride separately (`rt_gc`'s `stride = isDict ? 2 : 1`,
   `rt_dict_print_mixed`'s `idx = mul i32 %i, 2`). The third one was never told; it just copied and sorted. A door that
   reaches for a word in an arena it has not identified is the defect, and the row is the third instance of it. The
   lesson to keep: when a fix lands on one container, the control family is where the next row is, and the fix should
   not be considered done until the containers it did *not* touch are pinned as still answering.

2. **The record leg found the second half of the bug, not the first.** The first version of the door read each key's tag
   out of `@heap_tags` and printed `['b', 'a']` as `[1, 0]` — the two indexes into `@str_tab` — because a *single-kind*
   dict is filled by the UNTAGGED `rt_dict_put` and keeps its kind only in the compiler's tables. That is a fact about
   **ADR 0232**'s own design (the tag array is not cleared on free, which `rt_append_tagged`'s comment has always said),
   read in the wrong direction: "the slot describes itself" is true only of slots somebody tagged. Fix: one question to
   the record (texts), one question to the slot (everything else), both answered by the codegen that chose the comparator.

3. **Sorting produces a LIST, and every list door has to be told.** `print(sorted(d))` was right while
